    Topics

    How the marks work

    Chemistry mark schemes list the marking points separately. Each point (labelled M1, M2 and so on) is worth one mark. The same words come up again and again in them:

    TermMeaning
    M1, M2…Separate marking points, one mark each. Some depend on an earlier point (for example, a calculation mark needs the right method).
    ecfError carried forward. If you get an early value wrong but use it correctly later, you can still earn the later marks.
    owtte"Or words to that effect": the idea matters, not the exact wording.
    allow / ignore / rejectAlternatives that also score, extra words that don't change the mark, and answers that score nothing even if part of them is right.
    Three habits that save marks

    Always give state symbols when an equation asks for them. Give answers to the number of significant figures the data supports (usually 3). Write units on every final answer.

    Command words

    WordWhat to do
    StateGive a short answer with no explanation.
    DefineGive the precise meaning. Learn the definitions on this site word for word.
    DescribeSay what happens or what something is like, including observations such as colours.
    ExplainGive reasons, usually in terms of particles, bonding or electrons.
    DeduceReach a conclusion from the information given.
    SuggestApply what you know to an unfamiliar situation. More than one answer may be accepted.
    CalculateWork out a number, showing your working.
    SketchDraw the general shape, with labelled axes and key features, not to scale.

    The Data Booklet

    In every theory paper you get a Data Booklet with a Periodic Table and tables of data. You don't need to memorise these values:

    QuantityValue
    Avogadro constantL = 6.02 × 1023 mol−1
    molar gas constantR = 8.31 J K−1 mol−1
    Faraday constantF = 9.65 × 104 C mol−1
    charge on an electrone = −1.60 × 10−19 C
    molar volume of a gasVm = 22.4 dm3 mol−1 at s.t.p. (273 K and 101 kPa); Vm = 24.0 dm3 mol−1 at room conditions
    ionic product of waterKw = 1.00 × 10−14 mol2 dm−6 at 298 K
    specific heat capacity of waterc = 4.18 kJ kg−1 K−1 (that is, 4.18 J g−1 K−1)

    The booklet also lists ionisation energies, bond energies, standard electrode potentials, atomic and ionic radii, and the infrared and NMR absorption tables. Values in different books differ slightly, so in the exam always use the values printed in the booklet or in the question. The questions on this site give any data you need.

    About the questions

    The questions here are written in the style of 9701 papers and test the same skills. They are not copies of official papers. For genuine past papers and mark schemes, use the Cambridge School Support Hub or ask your teacher.

    Almost everything in chemistry comes down to electrons: where they are, how strongly the nucleus holds them, and how easily they are lost or shared. This topic builds that picture, from the particles in the atom to orbitals and ionisation energies.

    Inside the atom

    An atom is mostly empty space. At its centre is a very small, dense nucleus that contains the protons and neutrons. The nucleus is about 10−15 m across, while the whole atom is about 10−10 m across, roughly 100 000 times larger. The electrons are found in shells (energy levels) in the space around the nucleus.

    ParticleWhere it isRelative massRelative charge
    protonnucleus1+1
    neutronnucleus10
    electronshells around the nucleus1/1836 (often written as negligible)−1

    Distribution of mass and charge: nearly all the mass of an atom is in the nucleus, which is positively charged. The negative charge is spread through the much larger volume around it. An atom is neutral because it has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

    Beams of particles in an electric field

    If beams of protons, neutrons and electrons travel at the same speed between two charged plates:

    • Protons are deflected towards the negative plate.
    • Electrons are deflected towards the positive plate, and through a much larger angle because their mass is about 1/1836 of a proton's, but the size of their charge is the same.
    • Neutrons are not deflected because they have no charge.
    Exam tip

    For ions, the same rule applies: deflection ∝ charge/mass. A 2H+ ion is deflected half as much as a 1H+ ion, and a 4He2+ ion the same amount as 2H+.

    Counting protons, neutrons and electrons

    Proton number (atomic number), Z
    The number of protons in the nucleus. It identifies the element.
    Nucleon number (mass number), A
    The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

    A nuclide is written 3717Cl, with the nucleon number at the top and the proton number at the bottom. So:

    • number of protons = Z
    • number of neutrons = A − Z
    • number of electrons = Z − (charge on the ion). A 2+ ion has lost 2 electrons; a 2− ion has gained 2.
    SpeciesProtonsNeutronsElectrons
    3717Cl172017
    4020Ca2+202018
    3216S2−161618
    2713Al3+131410

    Atomic radius and ionic radius

    The atomic radius is usually measured as half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms of the same element. Two trends matter:

    Across a period: radius decreases

    The nuclear charge increases by one each time, but the electrons go into the same shell, so shielding hardly changes. The outer electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus.

    Down a group: radius increases

    Each element has one more shell of electrons. The outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded by the inner shells, which outweighs the larger nuclear charge.

    Ions compared with atoms

    • Positive ions are smaller than their atoms. A metal atom such as Na loses its whole outer shell, and the remaining electrons are pulled in more strongly because there are now more protons than electrons.
    • Negative ions are larger than their atoms. The extra electron(s) increase repulsion between electrons, while the nuclear charge stays the same, so the electron cloud spreads out.

    An isoelectronic series (ions with the same number of electrons) shows the effect of nuclear charge clearly. All of these ions have the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6:

    IonN3−O2−F−Na+Mg2+Al3+
    Protons789111213
    Ionic radius / nm0.1710.1400.1360.0950.0650.050

    Ten electrons are held by more and more protons, so the radius falls steadily.

    Across Period 3

    NaMgAlSiPSCl
    Atomic radius / nm0.1860.1600.1430.1170.1100.1040.099
    IonNa+Mg2+Al3+Si4+P3−S2−Cl−
    Ionic radius / nm0.0950.0650.0500.0410.2120.1840.181

    The cations Na+ to Si4+ all have 2 shells of electrons and rising nuclear charge, so they get smaller. The anions P3− to Cl− have 3 full shells, which is why there is a jump in size between Si4+ and P3−. They then get smaller too, as nuclear charge rises.

    Isotopes

    Isotopes
    Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

    For example, chlorine has two isotopes, 3517Cl (18 neutrons) and 3717Cl (20 neutrons). Carbon has 126C, 136C and the radioactive 146C.

    Same chemical properties

    Isotopes have the same number of electrons in the same arrangement. Chemical reactions involve the electrons, so isotopes react in the same way.

    Different physical properties

    Different numbers of neutrons give different masses, so isotopes (and their compounds) have different masses and densities. For example, "heavy water", D2O, is about 11% denser than H2O.

    Shells, sub-shells and orbitals

    Shell
    A main energy level, numbered by the principal quantum number, n = 1, 2, 3, … The higher n is, the further the electrons are from the nucleus and the higher their energy.
    Sub-shell
    A group of orbitals of the same type within a shell: s, p, d or f.
    Orbital
    A region of space around the nucleus that can hold up to two electrons, with opposite spins.
    Ground state
    The lowest-energy arrangement of the electrons in an atom.
    Sub-shellNumber of orbitalsMaximum electrons
    s12
    p36
    d510
    f714
    Shell, nSub-shellsOrbitalsMaximum electrons (2n2)
    11s12
    22s, 2p48
    33s, 3p, 3d918
    44s, 4p, 4d, 4f1632

    The order of filling

    Three rules decide where the electrons go in the ground state:

    1. Lowest energy first: electrons fill the sub-shell of lowest energy first, so 4s fills before 3d.
    2. Two per orbital: an orbital holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins (shown ↑↓).
    3. Single first (Hund's rule): in a sub-shell with several orbitals of equal energy, electrons go into separate orbitals with parallel spins before they pair up. This is because two electrons in the same orbital repel each other more than two electrons in different orbitals.

    Writing electronic configurations

    The full configuration lists every sub-shell with the number of electrons as a superscript. The shorthand form starts with the previous noble gas in square brackets.

    AtomFull configurationShorthand
    N (7)1s2 2s2 2p3[He] 2s2 2p3
    Na (11)1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1[Ne] 3s1
    Cl (17)1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5[Ne] 3s2 3p5
    K (19)1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1[Ar] 4s1
    Fe (26)1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6 4s2[Ar] 3d6 4s2
    Cr (24)1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d5 4s1[Ar] 3d5 4s1
    Cu (29)1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s1[Ar] 3d10 4s1
    Br (35)1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s2 4p5[Ar] 3d10 4s2 4p5

    Cambridge writes 3d before 4s, grouping each shell together, even though 4s fills first. Either order is accepted.

    The two exceptions: chromium and copper

    Chromium is [Ar] 3d5 4s1, not [Ar] 3d4 4s2, and copper is [Ar] 3d10 4s1, not [Ar] 3d9 4s2. The 3d and 4s energies are very close. For Cr, putting one electron in each of the five 3d orbitals avoids pairing two electrons in 4s, which lowers the repulsion. For Cu, a full 3d sub-shell with one 4s electron is the lower-energy arrangement.

    Configurations of ions

    • Negative ions: add electrons in the normal filling order. O2− is 1s2 2s2 2p6.
    • Positive ions of the d-block: remove the 4s electrons first, then 3d. Once the 3d orbitals contain electrons, 4s is the higher-energy, outer sub-shell.
    IonConfigurationIonConfiguration
    Fe2+[Ar] 3d6Cu2+[Ar] 3d9
    Fe3+[Ar] 3d5Cr3+[Ar] 3d3
    Zn2+[Ar] 3d10Cl−[Ne] 3s2 3p6

    Electrons in boxes

    Each box is an orbital and each arrow is an electron. Arrows in the same box point in opposite directions. Use the explorer below to see the boxes for any element up to krypton, and for its ions.

    Shapes of s and p orbitals

    Orbitals in higher shells are the same shape but larger: a 2s orbital is bigger than a 1s orbital.

    Free radicals

    A free radical is a species with one or more unpaired electrons. It is shown with a dot, for example the chlorine atom Cl• and the methyl radical CH3•. Nitrogen monoxide, NO, and nitrogen dioxide, NO2, are also free radicals because each molecule has an odd number of electrons. Radicals are very reactive, as you will see in Topic 14.

    Ionisation energy

    First ionisation energy
    The energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms, forming one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
    Mg(g) → Mg+(g) + e− first ionisation energy of magnesium, +738 kJ mol−1
    Mg+(g) → Mg2+(g) + e− second ionisation energy of magnesium, +1451 kJ mol−1

    Each successive ionisation removes one more electron from the ion formed in the step before. All ionisation energies are positive (endothermic), because energy is needed to pull an electron away from the attraction of the nucleus. Always include the (g) state symbols.

    What decides the size of an ionisation energy?

    Ionisation energy measures the attraction between the nucleus and the electron being removed. Four factors control it:

    1. Nuclear charge: more protons attract the electron more strongly.
    2. Distance from the nucleus (atomic or ionic radius): an electron further out is attracted less.
    3. Shielding: inner shells and sub-shells repel the outer electron and reduce the attraction it feels.
    4. Spin-pair repulsion: an electron sharing an orbital with another is repelled by it, so it is slightly easier to remove.

    Trends in first ionisation energy

    Across a period: general increase

    Nuclear charge increases, the electrons are in the same shell with similar shielding, and the atomic radius decreases. The outer electron is held more strongly.

    Down a group: decrease

    The outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner shells. This outweighs the increase in nuclear charge.

    There are two small dips in each period, which give evidence for sub-shells:

    DipExplanation
    Be → B and Mg → AlThe electron removed from B is in a 2p orbital (from Al, 3p). This is higher in energy than the 2s (3s), slightly further from the nucleus, and shielded by the filled s sub-shell, so less energy is needed.
    N → O and P → SIn O ([He] 2s2 2p4), one 2p orbital contains a pair of electrons. The repulsion between the paired electrons makes one of them easier to remove than any 2p electron in N, where all three are unpaired.

    The big drop from a noble gas to the next Group 1 metal (Ne → Na) happens because the outer electron of Na is in a new shell, further away and shielded by two full inner shells.

    Successive ionisation energies

    For any element, each successive ionisation energy is larger than the one before. After each electron is removed, the remaining electrons are attracted by the same number of protons, there is less repulsion between them, and the ion is smaller.

    A big jump appears whenever the next electron has to come from a shell closer to the nucleus. Counting the electrons removed before the first big jump gives the number of outer-shell electrons, and so the group.

    Worked example: finding the group

    The first five ionisation energies of an element X, in kJ mol−1, are 578, 1817, 2745, 11 577 and 14 842. Which group is X in?

    1. Look at the ratio between each pair: 1817/578 ≈ 3.1, 2745/1817 ≈ 1.5, 11 577/2745 ≈ 4.2, 14 842/11 577 ≈ 1.3.
    2. The big jump is between the 3rd and 4th ionisation energies, so 3 electrons are in the outer shell.

    X is in Group 13. (These are the values for aluminium, [Ne] 3s2 3p1.)

    Questions

    Questions 1 to 5 are multiple choice, like Paper 1. Questions 6 to 8 are structured, like Paper 2.

    1Paper 1 style

    How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in one 5626Fe3+ ion?

    1. 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 26 electrons
    2. 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 23 electrons
    3. 26 protons, 56 neutrons, 23 electrons
    4. 30 protons, 26 neutrons, 29 electrons

    Protons = Z = 26. Neutrons = 56 − 26 = 30. A 3+ ion has lost 3 electrons, so 26 − 3 = 23 electrons.

    2Paper 1 style

    Which species has the electronic configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d5?

    1. Cr
    2. Fe2+
    3. Fe3+
    4. Cu+

    Fe is [Ar] 3d6 4s2. Fe3+ loses the two 4s electrons and one 3d electron, leaving [Ar] 3d5. Cr is [Ar] 3d5 4s1 (it still has a 4s electron), Fe2+ is 3d6 and Cu+ is 3d10.

    3Paper 1 style

    In which pair does the second element have a lower first ionisation energy than the first element?

    1. C, N
    2. N, O
    3. O, F
    4. Na, Mg

    Oxygen's first ionisation energy is lower than nitrogen's because the electron removed from O is one of a pair in a 2p orbital, and spin-pair repulsion makes it easier to remove. The other pairs follow the normal increase across the period.

    4Paper 1 style

    A beam of particles passes between two charged plates. The beam is deflected towards the positive plate, through a larger angle than a beam of protons travelling at the same speed. What could the particles be?

    1. neutrons
    2. 2H+ ions
    3. 4He2+ ions
    4. electrons

    Deflection towards the positive plate means the particles are negative. Electrons have a charge of −1 and a tiny mass, so their charge/mass ratio is far larger than a proton's.

    5Paper 1 style

    The first five ionisation energies of an element, in kJ mol−1, are 590, 1145, 4912, 6491 and 8153. In which group of the Periodic Table is the element?

    1. 1
    2. 2
    3. 13
    4. 14

    The biggest jump is from 1145 to 4912, after the second electron. So there are 2 outer electrons and the element is in Group 2. (These are the values for calcium.)

    Stoichiometry is the arithmetic of chemistry: using formulas and balanced equations to work out how much of each substance reacts and forms. Almost every Paper 2 question and every titration in Paper 3 uses it, so practise until it is automatic.

    Relative masses

    Atoms are far too light to weigh in grams, so their masses are compared with a standard, the carbon-12 atom.

    Unified atomic mass unit, u
    One twelfth of the mass of one atom of carbon-12. (1 u = 1.66 × 10−27 kg.)
    Relative isotopic mass
    The mass of one atom of an isotope compared with one twelfth of the mass of one atom of carbon-12.
    Relative atomic mass, Ar
    The weighted average mass of the atoms of an element (taking account of the abundance of its isotopes), compared with one twelfth of the mass of one atom of carbon-12.
    Relative molecular mass, Mr
    The weighted average mass of a molecule, compared with one twelfth of the mass of one atom of carbon-12. It is the sum of the Ar values of the atoms in the molecule.
    Relative formula mass
    The same idea for ionic compounds, which do not contain molecules, for example NaCl. It is often still written Mr.

    Relative masses have no units, because they are ratios.

    Worked example: relative atomic mass from isotopic abundances

    Chlorine is 75.77% 35Cl and 24.23% 37Cl. Calculate Ar(Cl).

    1. Multiply each relative isotopic mass by its percentage abundance and add: 35 × 75.77 + 37 × 24.23 = 2651.95 + 896.51 = 3548.46
    2. Divide by the total abundance, 100.

    Ar(Cl) = 35.48, so 35.5 to 3 significant figures.

    The abundances often come from a mass spectrum, where the height of each peak is proportional to the abundance of that isotope. See Topic 22.

    The mole and the Avogadro constant

    Mole
    The amount of substance that contains 6.02 × 1023 particles (atoms, molecules, ions or electrons). This number is the Avogadro constant, L.
    Molar mass, M
    The mass of one mole of a substance, in g mol−1. It has the same numerical value as Ar or Mr.
    Amount from massn = mMLearn it
    Number of particlesN = n × LLearn it
    Gas at room conditionsn = V (dm3)24.0Vm in Data Booklet
    Solutionn = c × V (dm3)Learn it

    Worked example: particles

    How many molecules, and how many atoms, are in 9.0 g of water? (Mr of H2O = 18.0)

    1. n = 9.0/18.0 = 0.50 mol
    2. molecules = 0.50 × 6.02 × 1023 = 3.01 × 1023
    3. Each molecule has 3 atoms, so atoms = 3 × 3.01 × 1023 = 9.03 × 1023

    3.0 × 1023 molecules and 9.0 × 1023 atoms (2 s.f., matching the data)

    Formulas

    Ions you must know

    The charge on a simple ion can be predicted from the group: Group 1 forms 1+, Group 2 forms 2+, Group 13 forms 3+, Group 15 forms 3−, Group 16 forms 2− and Group 17 forms 1−. Learn these compound ions and two common d-block ions:

    IonFormulaIonFormula
    nitrateNO3−ammoniumNH4+
    carbonateCO32−hydrogencarbonateHCO3−
    sulfateSO42−phosphatePO43−
    hydroxideOH−zincZn2+
    silverAg+These nine are the ions the syllabus lists.

    For elements with more than one possible charge, a Roman numeral gives the oxidation number: iron(II) is Fe2+, iron(III) is Fe3+, copper(II) is Cu2+, and manganese(IV) oxide is MnO2.

    Writing formulas of ionic compounds

    The total positive charge must equal the total negative charge. Use brackets when there is more than one compound ion.

    CompoundIonsFormula
    aluminium sulfateAl3+ and SO42−: 2 × (+3) = 3 × (−2)Al2(SO4)3
    calcium phosphateCa2+ and PO43−: 3 × (+2) = 2 × (−3)Ca3(PO4)2
    ammonium carbonateNH4+ and CO32−(NH4)2CO3
    iron(III) hydroxideFe3+ and OH−Fe(OH)3
    silver carbonateAg+ and CO32−Ag2CO3

    Equations

    A balanced equation has the same number of each type of atom, and the same total charge, on both sides. State symbols show the physical state: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water.

    An ionic equation shows only the species that change. Spectator ions, which are present but unchanged, are left out.

    ReactionIonic equation
    Any acid with any alkaliH+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(l)
    Silver nitrate solution with sodium chloride solutionAg+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(s)
    Zinc with copper(II) sulfate solutionZn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s)
    A carbonate solution with an acidCO32−(aq) + 2H+(aq) → CO2(g) + H2O(l)
    Barium chloride solution with a sulfate solutionBa2+(aq) + SO42−(aq) → BaSO4(s)

    Empirical and molecular formulas

    Empirical formula
    The simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound.
    Molecular formula
    The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of the compound.

    For example, ethane C2H6 has the empirical formula CH3. Glucose C6H12O6 has the empirical formula CH2O.

    Worked example: from percentage composition

    A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass. Its Mr is 56.0. Find its empirical and molecular formulas.

    CH
    mass in 100 g85.714.3
    ÷ Ar85.7 ÷ 12.0 = 7.1414.3 ÷ 1.0 = 14.3
    ÷ smallest12.00

    Empirical formula CH2, with empirical formula mass 14.0. Then 56.0 ÷ 14.0 = 4.

    The molecular formula is C4H8.

    Worked example: from combustion data

    Complete combustion of 0.230 g of a compound containing only C, H and O gives 0.440 g of CO2 and 0.270 g of H2O. Find its empirical formula.

    1. C: n(CO2) = 0.440/44.0 = 0.0100 mol, so 0.0100 mol C, mass 0.120 g
    2. H: n(H2O) = 0.270/18.0 = 0.0150 mol, so 0.0300 mol H, mass 0.0300 g
    3. O by difference: 0.230 − 0.120 − 0.0300 = 0.0800 g, so 0.0800 / 16.0 = 0.00500 mol O
    4. Ratio C : H : O = 0.0100 : 0.0300 : 0.00500 = 2 : 6 : 1

    The empirical formula is C2H6O.

    Hydrated salts

    Hydrated
    A crystalline compound that contains water molecules in its lattice, such as CuSO4·5H2O.
    Water of crystallisation
    The water molecules that are part of the crystal structure of a hydrated salt.
    Anhydrous
    A substance with no water of crystallisation, such as CuSO4. It forms when the hydrated salt is heated.

    Worked example: finding the water of crystallisation

    5.00 g of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO4.xH2O, is heated to constant mass. 3.20 g of anhydrous CuSO4 remains. Find x.

    1. n(CuSO4) = 3.20/159.6 = 0.0200 mol
    2. mass of water lost = 5.00 − 3.20 = 1.80 g, so n(H2O) = 1.80/18.0 = 0.100 mol
    3. ratio = 0.100 ÷ 0.0200 = 4.99, which rounds to 5

    x = 5, so the formula is CuSO4·5H2O. Heating "to constant mass" makes sure all the water has gone.

    Reacting masses and percentage yield

    To find the mass of a product: (1) find the moles of the substance you know, (2) use the ratio from the balanced equation, (3) convert back to mass.

    Worked example

    Iron is extracted by Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2. What mass of iron can be made from 800 g of Fe2O3? (Mr: Fe2O3 159.6; Ar: Fe 55.8)

    1. n(Fe2O3) = 800/159.6 = 5.01 mol
    2. 1 mol Fe2O3 gives 2 mol Fe, so n(Fe) = 10.0 mol
    3. mass = 10.03 × 55.8 = 559 g

    559 g of iron. If only 500 g is actually obtained, the percentage yield = 500 / 559 × 100 = 89.4%.

    Percentage yield% yield = actual yieldtheoretical yield × 100Learn it

    Yields are below 100% because the reaction may be reversible or incomplete, side reactions form other products, and some product is lost when it is separated and purified.

    Volumes of gases

    One mole of any gas occupies the same volume at the same temperature and pressure: 24.0 dm3 at room conditions, or 22.4 dm3 at s.t.p. So for gases, the ratio of volumes equals the ratio of moles in the equation.

    Worked example: finding a hydrocarbon's formula from gas volumes

    10 cm3 of a gaseous hydrocarbon CxHy is burned in 80 cm3 of oxygen (an excess). After cooling to room temperature, 60 cm3 of gas remains. This decreases to 30 cm3 when the gas is passed through sodium hydroxide solution, which absorbs CO2. All volumes are at room conditions.

    1. After cooling, the water is a liquid, so the 60 cm3 is CO2 plus unreacted O2.
    2. NaOH removes CO2: volume of CO2 = 60 − 30 = 30 cm3. The 30 cm3 left is unreacted O2.
    3. O2 used = 80 − 30 = 50 cm3.
    4. Ratio CxHy : O2 : CO2 = 10 : 50 : 30 = 1 : 5 : 3, so x = 3.
    5. C3Hy + 5O2 → 3CO2 + y/2H2O. Balancing O: 10 = 6 + y/2, so y = 8.

    The hydrocarbon is propane, C3H8.

    Solutions and titrations

    Concentration is the amount of solute in 1 dm3 of solution, in mol dm−3. Multiply by M to get g dm−3. Volumes measured in cm3 must be divided by 1000 to get dm3.

    Worked example: a titration

    25.0 cm3 of sodium carbonate solution is titrated with 0.100 mol dm−3 hydrochloric acid. The mean titre is 22.50 cm3. Find the concentration of the sodium carbonate.

    Na2CO3(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)

    1. n(HCl) = 0.100 × 22.50/1000 = 2.250 × 10−3 mol
    2. ratio 1 : 2, so n(Na2CO3) = 1.125 × 10−3 mol
    3. c = 1.125 × 10−3/(25.0/1000) = 0.0450 mol dm−3

    0.0450 mol dm−3, which is 0.0450 × 106.0 = 4.77 g dm−3

    Limiting and excess reagents

    The limiting reagent is the one that is completely used up. It decides how much product forms. The other reagent is in excess, and some of it is left over. To decide which is which, use the equation to find how much of one reactant is needed to react with all of the other.

    Worked example

    5.00 g of zinc is added to 50.0 cm3 of 2.00 mol dm−3 hydrochloric acid. Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g)

    1. n(Zn) = 5.00 / 65.4 = 0.0765 mol. n(HCl) = 2.00 × 0.0500 = 0.100 mol.
    2. 0.100 mol HCl reacts with only 0.0500 mol Zn, so HCl is the limiting reagent and zinc is in excess.
    3. n(H2) = 0.100 ÷ 2 = 0.0500 mol, so volume = 0.0500 × 24.0 = 1.20 dm3.
    4. Zinc left = (0.0765 − 0.0500) × 65.4 = 1.73 g.
    Significant figures

    Give your answer to the same number of significant figures as the least precise data (usually 3). Keep at least one extra figure in intermediate steps, and only round at the end. Rounding too early is a common way to lose the final mark.

    Questions

    Use Ar values: H 1.0, C 12.0, O 16.0, Mg 24.3, S 32.1, Ca 40.1. Questions 1 to 5 are multiple choice. Questions 6 to 8 are structured.

    1Paper 1 style

    Which sample contains the greatest number of atoms?

    1. 1.0 g of H2
    2. 4.0 g of He
    3. 9.0 g of H2O
    4. 16 g of O2

    Moles of atoms: A 0.50 mol H2 × 2 = 1.0 mol; B 1.0 mol; C 0.50 mol H2O × 3 = 1.5 mol; D 0.50 mol O2 × 2 = 1.0 mol. So C has the most atoms.

    2Paper 1 style

    A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. What is its empirical formula?

    1. CHO
    2. CH2O
    3. C2H4O
    4. CH3O

    C: 40.0 / 12.0 = 3.33; H: 6.7 / 1.0 = 6.7; O: 53.3 / 16.0 = 3.33. Dividing by 3.33 gives 1 : 2 : 1.

    3Paper 1 style

    5.00 g of calcium carbonate is heated until it has completely decomposed: CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g). What volume of carbon dioxide forms, measured at room conditions?

    1. 0.600 dm3
    2. 1.12 dm3
    3. 1.20 dm3
    4. 2.40 dm3

    n(CaCO3) = 5.00 / 100.1 = 0.0500 mol, giving 0.0500 mol CO2. At room conditions, 0.0500 × 24.0 = 1.20 dm3. (B uses the s.t.p. value, 22.4.)

    4Paper 1 style

    25.0 cm3 of 0.100 mol dm−3 sodium hydroxide is exactly neutralised by 20.0 cm3 of sulfuric acid. What is the concentration of the sulfuric acid?

    1. 0.0625 mol dm−3
    2. 0.125 mol dm−3
    3. 0.0500 mol dm−3
    4. 0.250 mol dm−3

    2NaOH + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + 2H2O. n(NaOH) = 2.50 × 10−3 mol, so n(H2SO4) = 1.25 × 10−3 mol. c = 1.25 × 10−3 / 0.0200 = 0.0625 mol dm−3. Answer B forgets the 2 : 1 ratio.

    5Paper 1 style

    What is the formula of aluminium sulfate?

    1. AlSO4
    2. Al2SO4
    3. Al3(SO4)2
    4. Al2(SO4)3

    Two Al3+ ions (+6) balance three SO42− ions (−6).

    6Paper 2 style

    A student heats 2.46 g of hydrated magnesium sulfate, MgSO4.xH2O, until all the water of crystallisation is removed. 1.20 g of anhydrous MgSO4 remains.

    (a)
    Explain what is meant by water of crystallisation.
    [1]
    (b)
    Calculate the value of x.
    [3]
    (c)
    Describe how the student could make sure that all of the water had been removed.
    [1]
    • Water molecules that are part of / chemically bonded within the crystal lattice
    • n(MgSO4) = 1.20 / 120.4 = 9.97 × 10−3 mol
    • mass of water = 1.26 g, so n(H2O) = 1.26 / 18.0 = 0.0700 mol
    • ratio 0.0700 / 0.00997 = 7.02, so x = 7
    • Heat, cool and weigh repeatedly until the mass stays the same (heat to constant mass)
    7Paper 2 style

    4.00 g of magnesium ribbon is added to 100 cm3 of 0.800 mol dm−3 hydrochloric acid.

    (a)
    Write the equation for the reaction, including state symbols.
    [1]
    (b)
    Show by calculation which reagent is in excess.
    [2]
    (c)
    Calculate the volume of hydrogen formed at room conditions.
    [1]
    (d)
    Calculate the mass of magnesium left at the end.
    [1]
    (e)
    Write the ionic equation for the reaction.
    [1]
    • Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)
    • n(Mg) = 4.00 / 24.3 = 0.165 mol; n(HCl) = 0.800 × 0.100 = 0.0800 mol
    • 0.0800 mol HCl needs only 0.0400 mol Mg, so Mg is in excess
    • n(H2) = 0.0400 mol, so V = 0.0400 × 24.0 = 0.960 dm3
    • 4.00 − 0.0400 × 24.3 = 3.03 g
    • Mg(s) + 2H+(aq) → Mg2+(aq) + H2(g)
    8Paper 2 style
    (a)
    When 10.0 g of calcium carbonate is heated strongly, 4.80 g of calcium oxide is obtained. Calculate the percentage yield.
    [2]
    (b)
    Suggest one reason why the yield is less than 100%.
    [1]
    (c)
    20 cm3 of ethane, C2H6, is burned completely in 100 cm3 of oxygen. Calculate the total volume of gas left after cooling to room temperature, and state what it consists of. All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.
    [3]
    • Theoretical mass of CaO = (10.0 / 100.1) × 56.1 = 5.60 g
    • % yield = 4.80 / 5.60 × 100 = 85.6%
    • Decomposition was incomplete (not heated for long enough) / some solid was lost
    • 2C2H6 + 7O2 → 4CO2 + 6H2O, so 20 cm3 C2H6 uses 70 cm3 O2
    • 40 cm3 CO2 forms, and 30 cm3 O2 is left over (water is liquid after cooling)
    • Total 70 cm3: 40 cm3 CO2 and 30 cm3 O2

    Bonds hold atoms together; intermolecular forces hold molecules together. This topic explains both, shows you how to draw dot-and-cross diagrams, and uses electron-pair repulsion to predict the shapes of molecules.

    Electronegativity

    Electronegativity
    The power of an atom to attract electrons to itself (in a covalent bond).

    Electronegativity depends on the same factors as ionisation energy: nuclear charge, atomic radius and shielding by inner shells and sub-shells. A small atom with a large nuclear charge and little shielding attracts bonding electrons strongly.

    Across a period: increases

    Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays about the same and the radius decreases, so bonding electrons are attracted more strongly.

    Down a group: decreases

    The atoms get bigger and have more shielding, so the bonding electrons are further from the nucleus and attracted less.

    Fluorine is the most electronegative element. On the Pauling scale (values given in the exam when needed):

    HCNOFNaMgAlSiPSClBrI
    2.202.553.043.443.980.931.311.611.902.192.583.162.962.66

    Predicting the type of bond

    The difference in electronegativity between two atoms tells you how unevenly the bonding electrons are shared:

    DifferenceBondExamples (difference)
    zeronon-polar covalent: electrons shared equallyCl2 (0), H2 (0)
    small to moderatepolar covalent: electrons shared unequally, giving partial charges δ+ and δ−HCl (0.96), O–H (1.24), AlCl3 (1.55)
    large (roughly 2 or more)ionic: electrons transferredNaCl (2.23), MgO (2.13), NaF (3.05)

    There is no sharp cut-off, so treat the boundary as a guide. Aluminium chloride is a useful case: its difference (1.55) is too small for ionic bonding, and it is indeed a covalent compound that forms Al2Cl6 molecules.

    Ionic bonding

    Ionic bonding
    The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (positive cations and negative anions).

    Ions form when a metal atom transfers its outer electrons to a non-metal atom, so that both end up with a noble gas configuration. In a dot-and-cross diagram, show only the outer shells, put each ion in square brackets, and write the charge at the top right.

    In the solid, each ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge in a giant ionic lattice (Topic 4). Ionic bonding is stronger when the ions have larger charges and smaller radii, which is why magnesium oxide (2+ and 2−) melts at 2852 °C and sodium chloride (1+ and 1−) at 801 °C.

    Metallic bonding

    Metallic bonding
    The electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.

    The outer electrons of the metal atoms are not tied to any one atom: they move freely through a lattice of positive ions (a "sea" of delocalised electrons). Metallic bonding is stronger when there are more delocalised electrons per atom and the ions are smaller and more highly charged. This explains why the melting points rise from Na (98 °C) to Mg (650 °C) to Al (660 °C), and why metals conduct electricity.

    Covalent bonding

    Covalent bond
    The electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of two atoms and a shared pair of electrons.

    Each shared pair is one bond. Two shared pairs make a double bond and three make a triple bond. Pairs that are not shared are called lone pairs.

    Expanding the octet

    Elements in Period 2 can hold at most 8 electrons in their outer shell, because the second shell has only 2s and 2p orbitals. Elements from Period 3 onwards can use empty d orbitals, so they can have more than 8 outer electrons. Examples: sulfur dioxide (10 electrons around S), phosphorus(V) chloride PCl5 (10 around P) and sulfur hexafluoride SF6 (12 around S). This is why nitrogen forms only NCl3 but phosphorus forms both PCl3 and PCl5.

    Coordinate (dative covalent) bonding

    Coordinate bond
    A covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair come from the same atom.

    The donor atom needs a lone pair, and the acceptor needs an empty orbital. Once formed, a coordinate bond is identical to any other covalent bond. It is often drawn as an arrow from the donor to the acceptor.

    Ammonia and hydrogen chloride: the gases react to form white solid ammonium chloride. The lone pair on N forms a coordinate bond to H+: NH3(g) + HCl(g) → NH4Cl(s). All four N–H bonds in NH4+ are then identical, and the ion is tetrahedral.

    Aluminium chloride: in AlCl3 the aluminium has only six outer electrons, so it has an empty orbital. In the vapour at lower temperatures, two AlCl3 molecules join to form Al2Cl6: a lone pair on a chlorine atom of each molecule forms a coordinate bond to the aluminium of the other.

    σ and π bonds

    A covalent bond forms when orbitals on two atoms overlap, so that the shared pair is attracted to both nuclei.

    • A σ (sigma) bond forms by direct, end-on overlap of orbitals between the two nuclei. Every single bond is a σ bond.
    • A π (pi) bond forms by sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals, with electron density above and below the σ bond. A double bond is one σ + one π; a triple bond is one σ + two π.
    Moleculeσ bondsπ bondsNotes
    H210overlap of two 1s orbitals
    ethane, C2H6706 C–H and 1 C–C
    ethene, C2H4514 C–H, and C=C is 1 σ + 1 π
    hydrogen cyanide, HC≡N22C–H, and C≡N is 1 σ + 2 π
    nitrogen, N212the two π bonds are at right angles to each other

    Hybridisation

    Carbon's 2s and 2p orbitals mix (hybridise) to form a set of identical hybrid orbitals, which form the σ bonds. The number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of orbitals mixed.

    HybridMade fromArrangementLeft overExample
    sp3one s + three p4 orbitals, tetrahedral, 109.5°noneC in methane and ethane
    sp2one s + two p3 orbitals, trigonal planar, 120°one p orbital, which forms the π bondC in ethene
    spone s + one p2 orbitals, linear, 180°two p orbitals, which form two π bondsC in HCN and ethyne

    In ethene, the π bond can only form if the p orbitals on the two carbons are parallel. So the molecule is planar and there is no rotation about C=C. This is the origin of cis/trans isomerism (Topic 13).

    Bond energy and bond length

    Bond energy
    The energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state.
    Bond length
    The internuclear distance between two covalently bonded atoms.

    Some bond energies are exact: for a diatomic molecule such as H2 there is only one bond in one environment. Others are averages: a C–H bond in methane has a slightly different energy from a C–H bond in ethanol, so the table gives a mean value.

    BondEnergy / kJ mol−1Length / nmBondEnergy / kJ mol−1Length / nm
    C–C3500.154H–H4360.074
    C=C6100.134O=O4960.121
    C≡C8400.120N≡N9440.110
    C–H4100.109Cl–Cl2420.199
    C–O3600.143Br–Br1930.228
    C=O7400.122I–I1510.267
    O–H4600.096H–Cl4310.127
    N–H3900.101H–I2990.161
    • Multiple bonds are shorter and stronger: C≡C > C=C > C–C. But C=C is less than twice C–C, because the π bond is weaker than the σ bond.
    • Longer bonds are generally weaker: the shared pair is further from the nuclei. H–Cl (0.127 nm, 431) is stronger than H–I (0.161 nm, 299), which is why hydrogen iodide decomposes much more easily (Topic 11).
    • Strong bonds mean low reactivity: N≡N (944 kJ mol−1) is one of the strongest bonds known, so nitrogen gas is very unreactive (Topic 12).

    Shapes of molecules

    Valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) theory: pairs of electrons around a central atom repel each other and move as far apart as possible. The shape depends on the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs.

    • A double or triple bond counts as one region of electron density, just like a single bond.
    • Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, because they are closer to the central atom. The order is lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair. Each lone pair squeezes the bond angles by about 2.5°.
    • The shape is named from the positions of the atoms, not the lone pairs.
    Bonding pairsLone pairsShapeBond angleExample
    20linear180°CO2, BeCl2
    30trigonal planar120°BF3
    40tetrahedral109.5°CH4, NH4+
    31pyramidal107°NH3, H3O+
    22non-linear (bent)104.5°H2O
    50trigonal bipyramidal120° and 90°PF5, PCl5
    60octahedral90°SF6

    Worked example: predicting a shape you haven't seen

    Predict the shape of the oxonium ion, H3O+, and of sulfur dichloride, SCl2.

    1. H3O+: O has 6 outer electrons. Each H adds 1 (total 9), and the positive charge removes 1, leaving 8 electrons = 4 pairs. Three are bonding pairs (to H) and one is a lone pair, so the shape is pyramidal, about 107°, like NH3.
    2. SCl2: S has 6 outer electrons, and each Cl adds 1 for its bond (total 8) = 4 pairs. Two bonding pairs and two lone pairs give a non-linear shape with an angle of about 104.5°, like water.

    More analogous examples: NH2− is non-linear (2 bonding, 2 lone pairs); CO32− and NO3− are trigonal planar (3 regions, no lone pairs on the central atom); SO2 is non-linear, about 120° (2 double bonds and 1 lone pair on S); PCl4+ is tetrahedral; PCl6− is octahedral.

    Intermolecular forces

    Van der Waals' forces is the general name for all the attractive forces between molecules, other than those due to bond formation. There are two types in this course:

    Instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (id-id) forces

    Also called London dispersion forces, these act between all molecules, polar or not. Electrons are always moving, so at any instant the electron cloud may be unevenly spread, giving a temporary (instantaneous) dipole. This induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule, and the two attract. The forces are stronger when:

    • there are more electrons (larger molecules), so bigger dipoles form. Boiling points rise from F2 (−188 °C) to Cl2 (−34 °C), Br2 (59 °C) and I2 (184 °C).
    • there is more surface contact between molecules. Pentane (straight chain, bp 36 °C) boils higher than its isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane (nearly spherical, bp 10 °C).

    Permanent dipole–permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces

    A polar molecule has a permanent dipole: one end δ+ and the other δ−. The δ+ end of one molecule attracts the δ− end of the next. These forces act in addition to id-id forces. For example, propanone (CH3COCH3, Mr 58, bp 56 °C) boils much higher than butane (C4H10, Mr 58, bp −1 °C), which has a similar number of electrons but no permanent dipole.

    Hydrogen bonding

    Hydrogen bonding is a special, strong case of permanent dipole–permanent dipole attraction. It happens between molecules where hydrogen is bonded to a highly electronegative atom. In this syllabus, that means molecules with N–H or O–H groups, such as ammonia, water and alcohols. (H–F also forms hydrogen bonds.)

    1. The N–H or O–H bond is very polar, leaving the small H atom with a large δ+ charge.
    2. This H is attracted to a lone pair on an N or O atom of a neighbouring molecule.
    3. The three atoms O–H···O are in a straight line (180°), because this keeps the electron pairs as far apart as possible.

    The unusual properties of water

    Each water molecule has two H atoms and two lone pairs, so it can form up to four hydrogen bonds. This explains why water:

    • has relatively high melting and boiling points. Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than the id-id forces in H2S, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules. Water boils at 100 °C; H2S, which has more electrons, boils at −60 °C.
    • has a high surface tension. Molecules at the surface are pulled strongly inwards and sideways by hydrogen bonds.
    • is less dense as ice than as liquid water. In ice, each molecule forms four hydrogen bonds in a regular tetrahedral arrangement, which holds the molecules further apart in an open lattice. When ice melts, some hydrogen bonds break and the molecules move closer together.

    Bond polarity and polar molecules

    A bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar: the more electronegative atom gets a δ− charge. A molecule has an overall dipole moment (it is polar) only if its bond dipoles do not cancel out, which depends on its shape.

    Polar molecules (dipoles don't cancel)Non-polar molecules with polar bonds (dipoles cancel)
    H2O (non-linear), NH3 (pyramidal), HCl, CHCl3, CH3Cl, propanoneCO2 (linear), BF3 (trigonal planar), CH4 and CCl4 (tetrahedral), SF6 (octahedral)

    How strong are the forces?

    In general, ionic, covalent and metallic bonds are much stronger than intermolecular forces. Breaking a covalent bond takes hundreds of kJ mol−1. Hydrogen bonds are typically 5 to 40 kJ mol−1, and other van der Waals' forces are usually weaker still. When a simple molecular substance melts or boils, only the intermolecular forces are overcome. The covalent bonds inside the molecules stay intact.

    Dot-and-cross diagram checklist

    • Show outer-shell electrons only, unless the question asks for all shells.
    • Use dots for one atom's electrons and crosses for the other's, so the reader can see where each shared pair came from.
    • Put shared pairs in the overlap between the two atoms, and include every lone pair.
    • For ions, use square brackets and show the charge. For a coordinate bond, both electrons of the pair have the donor's symbol.
    • Species with an odd number of electrons are allowed, such as the methyl radical CH3•: C has 3 shared pairs and 1 unpaired electron.

    Questions

    Questions 1 to 6 are multiple choice. Questions 7 to 9 are structured.

    1Paper 1 style

    Which molecule has a bond angle closest to 107°?

    1. H2O
    2. NH3
    3. CH4
    4. BF3

    NH3 has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair: pyramidal, 107°. Water is 104.5°, methane 109.5° and BF3 120°.

    2Paper 1 style

    Which molecule contains polar bonds but is not polar overall?

    1. NH3
    2. CHCl3
    3. CO2
    4. HCl

    CO2 is linear, so its two C=O dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel. The others have dipoles that do not cancel.

    3Paper 1 style

    How many σ bonds and π bonds are there in one molecule of hydrogen cyanide, HCN?

    1. 2 σ and 2 π
    2. 1 σ and 3 π
    3. 3 σ and 1 π
    4. 2 σ and 1 π

    H–C is one σ bond. C≡N is one σ and two π bonds. Total: 2 σ, 2 π.

    4Paper 1 style

    Hydrogen bonds form between molecules of which substance?

    1. methane, CH4
    2. hydrogen chloride, HCl
    3. methoxymethane, CH3OCH3
    4. methanol, CH3OH

    Only methanol has an H attached to O. Methoxymethane has O with lone pairs, but no O–H, so its molecules can't hydrogen bond with each other.

    5Paper 1 style

    Which species contains a coordinate (dative covalent) bond?

    1. NH4+
    2. CH4
    3. H2O
    4. CO2

    NH4+ forms when the lone pair on N bonds to H+, which has no electrons of its own.

    6Paper 1 style

    The boiling points of the halogens increase from fluorine to iodine. What is the main reason?

    1. The covalent bonds in the molecules get weaker.
    2. The molecules become more polar.
    3. The number of electrons increases, so the instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces get stronger.
    4. Hydrogen bonding gets stronger.

    Halogen molecules are non-polar, so only id-id forces act between them. These increase with the number of electrons. Boiling doesn't break the covalent bonds at all.

    7Paper 2 style

    Ammonia, NH3, reacts with boron trifluoride, BF3, to form the compound H3NBF3.

    (a)
    Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for NH3 and BF3, showing outer electrons only.
    [2]
    (b)
    State the shape of each molecule and its bond angle.
    [2]
    (c)
    Explain how a bond forms between N and B in H3NBF3.
    [2]
    (d)
    Suggest the F–B–F bond angle in H3NBF3. Explain your answer.
    [2]
    • NH3: three N–H shared pairs and one lone pair on N
    • BF3: three B–F shared pairs, three lone pairs on each F, and only 6 electrons around B
    • NH3 pyramidal, 107°
    • BF3 trigonal planar, 120°
    • The lone pair on N is donated to B…
    • …which has an empty orbital (electron deficient), forming a coordinate (dative covalent) bond
    • About 109.5° (allow 107° to 109.5°)
    • B now has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so the arrangement around B is tetrahedral
    8Paper 2 style
    (a)
    Draw a diagram to show a hydrogen bond between two water molecules. Include partial charges and the relevant lone pair.
    [3]
    (b)
    Explain why water has a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulfide, H2S.
    [2]
    (c)
    Explain why ice is less dense than liquid water.
    [2]
    (d)
    Explain why the boiling points increase from H2S to H2Se to H2Te.
    [2]
    • Two water molecules, with δ+ on H and δ− on O
    • Lone pair shown on the O of the second molecule
    • Hydrogen bond drawn between the H and that lone pair, with O–H···O roughly in a straight line
    • Water molecules are held by hydrogen bonds; H2S has only (weaker) van der Waals' forces (id-id and pd-pd)
    • Hydrogen bonds are stronger, so more energy is needed to separate the water molecules
    • In ice, each molecule forms (four) hydrogen bonds in a regular, open (tetrahedral) lattice
    • This holds the molecules further apart than in the liquid, where some hydrogen bonds are broken
    • The number of electrons in the molecules increases
    • So the instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces get stronger and need more energy to overcome
    9Paper 2 style
    (a)
    Describe how the σ bond and the π bond form in the C=C double bond of ethene.
    [2]
    (b)
    State the hybridisation of the carbon atoms in ethene and the H–C–H bond angle.
    [2]
    (c)
    The bond energy of C=C is 610 kJ mol−1 and of C–C is 350 kJ mol−1. Explain why the C=C bond energy is less than twice the C–C bond energy.
    [1]
    (d)
    Nitrogen, N2, is much less reactive than ethene, even though both contain a multiple bond. Use the data N≡N 944 kJ mol−1 to suggest why.
    [2]
    • σ: direct / end-on overlap of (sp2 hybrid) orbitals between the two carbon nuclei
    • π: sideways overlap of p orbitals, with electron density above and below the σ bond
    • sp2
    • 120°
    • The π bond is weaker than the σ bond, because there is less overlap of the p orbitals
    • N≡N has a very high bond energy, so a lot of energy is needed to break it
    • N2 is also non-polar, so it doesn't attract electrophiles or nucleophiles

    The properties of a substance depend on its particles and on the forces between them. This topic covers how gases behave, how to use the ideal gas equation, and how the four types of structure explain melting points, conductivity and solubility.

    The gaseous state

    In a gas, the particles move rapidly and randomly in straight lines between collisions. Gas pressure comes from the particles colliding with the walls of the container: each collision exerts a force on the wall, and pressure is the total force per unit area.

    Ideal gases

    An ideal gas is a model that follows the gas laws exactly. Its key assumptions are:

    • the particles have zero volume (they are points)
    • there are no intermolecular forces of attraction between the particles
    • (also) the particles move randomly and their collisions are perfectly elastic

    Real gases

    Real gases behave most like an ideal gas at high temperature and low pressure. They deviate when:

    The pressure is high

    The particles are pushed close together, so the volume of the particles themselves is no longer negligible compared with the volume of the container.

    The temperature is low

    The particles move slowly, so intermolecular forces have a significant effect: the particles attract each other and hit the walls less hard.

    Gases with small, non-polar particles, such as helium and hydrogen, are closest to ideal. Gases with strong intermolecular forces, such as ammonia (hydrogen bonding) and steam, deviate the most.

    The ideal gas equation

    Ideal gas equationpV = nRTLearn it
    Using mass and molar masspV = mMRT, so M = mRTpVLearn it
    SymbolQuantitySI unitConversion
    ppressurePa1 kPa = 103 Pa
    Vvolumem31 dm3 = 10−3 m3; 1 cm3 = 10−6 m3
    namountmoln = mass ÷ M
    Rmolar gas constant8.31 J K−1 mol−1given in the Data Booklet
    TtemperatureKT / K = θ / °C + 273
    The most common mistake

    Forgetting to convert cm3 to m3 (× 10−6) and °C to K. If your Mr comes out a million times too big or small, check your units.

    Worked example: relative molecular mass of a volatile liquid

    0.150 g of a volatile liquid is injected into a gas syringe in an oven at 100 °C. It vaporises completely, and the vapour occupies 50.0 cm3 at a pressure of 101 kPa. Calculate Mr.

    1. Convert units: p = 101 000 Pa, V = 50.0 × 10−6 m3, T = 373 K
    2. n = pVRT = 101000 × 50.0 × 10−68.31 × 373 = 1.63 × 10−3 mol
    3. M = mn = 0.1501.63 × 10−3 = 92.1 g mol−1

    Mr = 92.1 (this could be methylbenzene, C7H8, Mr 92.0)

    Using the ideal gas equation shows where the molar volume comes from: at 20 °C and 101 kPa, V = nRT/p = 1 × 8.31 × 293 / 101 000 = 0.0241 m3 = 24.1 dm3, close to the 24.0 dm3 used for room conditions.

    Bonding and structure

    Solids are classified by the particles in their lattice and the forces between them. There are four types:

    Giant ionic: sodium chloride and magnesium oxide

    A regular lattice of positive and negative ions held by strong ionic bonds in all directions. In sodium chloride, each Na+ ion is surrounded by six Cl− ions and each Cl− by six Na+ (6 : 6 coordination). Magnesium oxide has the same arrangement, with Mg2+ and O2− ions.

    Simple molecular: iodine, buckminsterfullerene and ice

    Small molecules held in a lattice by weak intermolecular forces. The covalent bonds inside each molecule are strong, but only the weak forces between molecules are broken on melting.

    • Iodine: I2 molecules held by id-id forces. It forms shiny grey-black crystals that sublime on gentle warming to a purple vapour.
    • Buckminsterfullerene, C60: 60 carbon atoms joined in a hollow ball of 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons. The C60 molecules are held by id-id forces, so it is soft, has a much lower sublimation point than diamond, does not conduct, and dissolves in non-polar solvents such as methylbenzene.
    • Ice: H2O molecules held in an open tetrahedral lattice by hydrogen bonds (Topic 3), which is why ice floats on water.

    Giant molecular (giant covalent): diamond, graphite and silicon(IV) oxide

    • Diamond: each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement (109.5°), forming a 3D network. Very hard, very high melting point, does not conduct (no delocalised electrons).
    • Graphite: each carbon is bonded to three others in flat layers of hexagons. The fourth outer electron of each carbon is delocalised over the layer, so graphite conducts electricity along the layers. The layers are held together by weak id-id forces, so they slide over each other: graphite is soft and slippery and is used as a lubricant and in pencils. Its melting point is still very high because the covalent bonds within the layers must break.
    • Silicon(IV) oxide, SiO2: each Si atom is bonded to four O atoms tetrahedrally, and each O atom to two Si atoms. Hard, high melting point (about 1700 °C), insoluble and non-conducting.

    Giant metallic: copper

    A regular lattice of positive copper ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. The metallic bonding is strong and non-directional, so copper has a high melting point (1085 °C). It conducts electricity because the delocalised electrons move through the structure. It is malleable and ductile because layers of ions can slide over each other without the metallic bonding breaking.

    How structure explains properties

    StructureMelting and boiling pointsElectrical conductivitySolubility
    Giant ionicHigh: many strong ionic bonds must be brokenNot as a solid (ions can't move); conducts when molten or dissolved (ions free to move)Often soluble in water (ions attracted to polar water molecules); insoluble in non-polar solvents
    Simple molecularLow: only weak intermolecular forces are overcomeDoes not conduct: no ions or delocalised electronsUsually soluble in non-polar solvents; water only if they can hydrogen bond with it (e.g. ethanol, sugar)
    Giant molecularVery high: many strong covalent bonds must be brokenDoes not conduct, except graphite (delocalised electrons)Insoluble in all solvents
    Giant metallicUsually high: strong metallic bondingConducts as solid and liquid: delocalised electronsInsoluble (some react with water)

    Worked example: deducing the structure from data

    SubstanceMelting point / °CConducts as a solid?Conducts when molten?Soluble in water?
    W801noyesyes
    X1085yesyesno
    Y114nonovery slightly
    Z1710nonono

    W is giant ionic (conducts only when its ions are free: sodium chloride). X is giant metallic (conducts as a solid: copper). Y is simple molecular (low melting point: iodine). Z is giant molecular (very high melting point, never conducts: silicon(IV) oxide).

    Questions

    Use R = 8.31 J K−1 mol−1. Questions 1 to 4 are multiple choice. Questions 5 and 6 are structured.

    1Paper 1 style

    What volume does 0.50 mol of an ideal gas occupy at 300 K and 100 kPa?

    1. 12.5 dm3
    2. 1.25 dm3
    3. 0.0125 dm3
    4. 125 dm3

    V = nRT/p = 0.50 × 8.31 × 300 / 100 000 = 0.0125 m3 = 12.5 dm3. Answer C is the value in m3 written with the wrong unit.

    2Paper 1 style

    Under which conditions does a gas behave most like an ideal gas?

    1. helium at high temperature and low pressure
    2. ammonia at low temperature and high pressure
    3. helium at low temperature and high pressure
    4. ammonia at high temperature and low pressure

    Helium has small, non-polar atoms with very weak forces between them. High temperature and low pressure make intermolecular forces and particle volume least important.

    3Paper 1 style

    Which substance has a giant molecular (giant covalent) structure?

    1. carbon dioxide
    2. iodine
    3. sodium chloride
    4. silicon(IV) oxide

    SiO2 is a 3D network of Si–O covalent bonds. CO2 and I2 are simple molecular, and NaCl is giant ionic.

    4Paper 1 style

    Why does graphite conduct electricity?

    1. It contains ions that move through the layers.
    2. Each carbon atom has one electron that is delocalised along its layer.
    3. The layers can slide over each other.
    4. The forces between the layers are weak.

    Each carbon uses three electrons in σ bonds to its neighbours; the fourth is delocalised and moves along the layer when a voltage is applied.

    5Paper 2 style

    A sample of a gas has a mass of 0.355 g. At 27 °C and 98.0 kPa, it occupies a volume of 128 cm3.

    (a)
    Calculate the relative molecular mass of the gas.
    [3]
    (b)
    State two assumptions of the kinetic theory for an ideal gas.
    [2]
    (c)
    Explain why the gas would deviate more from ideal behaviour at a very high pressure.
    [1]
    • Correct units: 98 000 Pa, 1.28 × 10−4 m3, 300 K
    • n = pV/RT = 98 000 × 1.28 × 10−4 / (8.31 × 300) = 5.03 × 10−3 mol
    • Mr = 0.355 / 5.03 × 10−3 = 70.6 (it could be chlorine, Cl2, 71.0)
    • The particles have zero / negligible volume
    • There are no intermolecular forces between the particles (allow: collisions are elastic; random motion)
    • At high pressure the particles are close together, so their own volume is significant compared with the volume of the container (and intermolecular forces become significant)
    6Paper 2 style
    (a)
    Diamond and graphite are both forms of carbon. Explain why diamond is very hard but graphite is soft.
    [3]
    (b)
    Explain why iodine has a much lower melting point than diamond, even though both contain only covalent bonds.
    [2]
    (c)
    Explain why magnesium oxide conducts electricity when molten but not when solid.
    [2]
    (d)
    Explain why copper is malleable.
    [1]
    • Diamond: each C atom covalently bonded to four others in a rigid 3D (tetrahedral) network
    • Graphite: layers in which each C is bonded to three others
    • The layers are held by weak (id-id / van der Waals') forces, so they slide over each other
    • Iodine is simple molecular: only weak id-id forces between I2 molecules are overcome on melting
    • Diamond is giant molecular: many strong covalent bonds must be broken
    • In the solid, the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice
    • When molten, the ions are free to move and carry charge
    • Layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking the metallic bonding (the delocalised electrons move with them)

    Every reaction transfers energy to or from its surroundings, because bonds are broken and made. This topic covers how to define, measure and calculate enthalpy changes, including those you can't measure directly, using Hess's law.

    Enthalpy changes

    The enthalpy change, ΔH, is the heat energy transferred in a reaction at constant pressure, in kJ mol−1.

    Exothermic: ΔH is negative

    Energy is transferred to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises. The products have less enthalpy than the reactants. Examples: combustion, neutralisation, most oxidation reactions.

    Endothermic: ΔH is positive

    Energy is taken in from the surroundings, so the temperature falls. The products have more enthalpy than the reactants. Examples: thermal decomposition of CaCO3, photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium nitrate.

    Reaction pathway diagrams

    A reaction pathway diagram (energy profile) shows the enthalpy of the reactants and products, and the energy barrier between them. The activation energy, EA, is the minimum energy needed for a reaction to happen (Topic 8). It is measured from the reactants up to the top of the barrier.

    Standard conditions and definitions

    Enthalpy changes depend on conditions, so they are quoted under standard conditions, shown by the symbol : a temperature of 298 K and a pressure of 101 kPa, with solutions at 1 mol dm−3, and every substance in its standard state (its normal physical state under those conditions).

    Enthalpy change of reaction, ΔHr
    The enthalpy change when the amounts of reactants shown in the equation react under standard conditions.
    Enthalpy change of formation, ΔHf
    The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions.
    Enthalpy change of combustion, ΔHc
    The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is burned completely in oxygen under standard conditions.
    Enthalpy change of neutralisation, ΔHneut
    The enthalpy change when one mole of water is formed by the reaction of an acid with an alkali under standard conditions.
    2C(s) + 3H2(g) + ½O2(g) → C2H5OH(l) ΔHf of ethanol: elements in their standard states, one mole of product
    C2H5OH(l) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l) ΔHc of ethanol: one mole of fuel, complete combustion
    ½H2SO4(aq) + NaOH(aq) → ½Na2SO4(aq) + H2O(l) ΔHneut: one mole of water. For any strong acid with a strong alkali it is about −57 kJ mol−1.
    Watch the details

    By definition, ΔHf of an element in its standard state is zero. Fractions such as ½O2 are fine in these equations, because the definition fixes one mole of the substance. Carbon's standard state is graphite, C(s).

    Bond energies

    Breaking a bond needs energy (endothermic). Making a bond releases energy (exothermic). The overall enthalpy change depends on the balance between the two:

    From bond energiesΔHr = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds made)Learn it

    Worked example: combustion of methane

    CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(g). Bond energies / kJ mol−1: C–H 410, O=O 496, C=O (in CO2) 805, O–H 460.

    1. Bonds broken: 4 C–H + 2 O=O = 4(410) + 2(496) = 2632 kJ
    2. Bonds made: 2 C=O + 4 O–H = 2(805) + 4(460) = 3450 kJ
    3. ΔH = 2632 − 3450

    ΔH = −818 kJ mol−1

    The experimental ΔHc of methane is −890 kJ mol−1. The answers differ because bond energies are averages taken over many compounds, and because the bond energy calculation is for gases, while under standard conditions water is a liquid (condensing releases more energy).

    Worked example: hydrogenation of ethene

    C2H4(g) + H2(g) → C2H6(g). Only the bonds that change need counting: break C=C (610) and H–H (436); make C–C (350) and two new C–H (2 × 410).

    ΔH = (610 + 436) − (350 + 820) = 1046 − 1170 = −124 kJ mol−1

    Measuring enthalpy changes

    In calorimetry, the reaction heats (or cools) a known mass of water or solution, and you measure the temperature change.

    Energy transferredq = mcΔTLearn it
    Enthalpy change per moleΔH = −mcΔTnLearn it

    m is the mass of the liquid being heated (for dilute solutions, take 1 cm3 = 1 g), c is 4.18 J g−1 K−1, ΔT is the temperature change, and n is the amount of the limiting reagent (or of water formed, for neutralisation). The minus sign makes ΔH negative when the temperature rises.

    Worked example: enthalpy change of neutralisation

    25.0 cm3 of 2.00 mol dm−3 HCl is mixed with 25.0 cm3 of 2.00 mol dm−3 NaOH in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises by 13.5 K.

    1. q = mcΔT = 50.0 × 4.18 × 13.5 = 2822 J
    2. n(H2O) = n(HCl) = 2.00 × 0.0250 = 0.0500 mol
    3. ΔH = −2822/0.0500 = −56 400 J mol−1

    ΔHneut = −56.4 kJ mol−1

    Worked example: enthalpy change of combustion with a spirit burner

    Burning 0.580 g of ethanol (C2H5OH, Mr 46.0) raises the temperature of 200 g of water in a copper can by 18.0 K.

    1. q = 200 × 4.18 × 18.0 = 15 048 J = 15.05 kJ
    2. n(ethanol) = 0.580 / 46.0 = 0.01261 mol
    3. ΔHc = −15.05/0.01261

    ΔHc = −1190 kJ mol−1 (3 s.f.). The data book value is −1367 kJ mol−1.

    The experimental value is less exothermic mainly because of heat losses to the surroundings (heating the air and the can), and also incomplete combustion (soot forms) and evaporation of ethanol from the wick.

    Correcting for heat loss

    In Paper 3 you may record the temperature every minute before and after mixing. Extrapolating the cooling line back to the time of mixing gives the maximum temperature the mixture would have reached with no heat loss.

    Hess's law

    Hess's law
    The total enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided the starting and finishing conditions are the same.

    Hess's law lets you calculate enthalpy changes that can't be measured directly, such as the enthalpy of formation of ethanol (you can't make ethanol by mixing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen). Draw a cycle with the reaction you want along the top and an alternative route through known enthalpy changes.

    Using enthalpy changes of formation

    Both reactants and products can be made from the same elements, so the arrows go up from the elements:

    From formation dataΔHr = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants)Learn it

    Worked example

    Calculate ΔH for CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g). ΔHf / kJ mol−1: CaCO3 −1207, CaO −635, CO2 −394.

    ΔH = (−635 + (−394)) − (−1207) = +178 kJ mol−1

    Using enthalpy changes of combustion

    Both reactants and products burn to give the same combustion products, so the arrows go down to the combustion products:

    From combustion dataΔHr = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΣΔHc(products)Learn it

    Worked example: enthalpy change of formation of ethanol

    ΔHc / kJ mol−1: C(s) −394, H2(g) −286, C2H5OH(l) −1367.

    1. Route via combustion: ΔHf = 2ΔHc(C) + 3ΔHc(H2) − ΔHc(C2H5OH)
    2. = 2(−394) + 3(−286) − (−1367) = −788 − 858 + 1367

    ΔHf(ethanol) = −279 kJ mol−1

    Avoiding sign errors

    Write each step of the indirect route along the direction of its arrow. If you go against an arrow, change the sign of that value. Multiply each value by the number of moles in the equation.

    Questions

    Use c = 4.18 J g−1 K−1. Questions 1 to 4 are multiple choice. Questions 5 to 7 are structured.

    1Paper 1 style

    Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethanol?

    1. 2C(g) + 6H(g) + O(g) → C2H5OH(l)
    2. C2H5OH(l) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l)
    3. 2C(s) + 3H2(g) + ½O2(g) → C2H5OH(l)
    4. 4C(s) + 6H2(g) + O2(g) → 2C2H5OH(l)

    Formation uses the elements in their standard states (C(s), H2(g), O2(g)) and makes exactly one mole of the compound. D makes two moles; A uses gaseous atoms.

    2Paper 1 style

    Use the bond energies H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242 and H–Cl 431 kJ mol−1. What is ΔH for H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g)?

    1. −184 kJ mol−1
    2. +184 kJ mol−1
    3. −247 kJ mol−1
    4. +247 kJ mol−1

    Broken: 436 + 242 = 678. Made: 2 × 431 = 862. ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ mol−1. C and D forget that two H–Cl bonds form.

    3Paper 1 style

    ΔHc values / kJ mol−1: C(s) −394, H2(g) −286, CH4(g) −890. What is ΔHf of methane?

    1. +76 kJ mol−1
    2. −76 kJ mol−1
    3. −210 kJ mol−1
    4. −1570 kJ mol−1

    ΔHf = ΔHc(C) + 2ΔHc(H2) − ΔHc(CH4) = −394 + 2(−286) + 890 = −76 kJ mol−1.

    4Paper 1 style

    Which statement about the standard enthalpy change of formation of oxygen, O2(g), is correct?

    1. It is equal to the O=O bond energy.
    2. It is equal to half the O=O bond energy.
    3. It is negative because forming bonds releases energy.
    4. It is zero, because oxygen is an element in its standard state.

    Forming an element from itself in its standard state involves no change, so ΔHf = 0.

    5Paper 2 and 3 style

    A student adds 2.00 g of zinc powder (an excess) to 50.0 cm3 of 0.400 mol dm−3 copper(II) sulfate solution in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises from 20.5 °C to 40.0 °C.

    Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s)

    (a)
    Calculate the energy released.
    [1]
    (b)
    Calculate the enthalpy change of reaction, in kJ mol−1.
    [2]
    (c)
    The data book value is −217 kJ mol−1. Suggest two improvements to the method that would give a more accurate value.
    [2]
    • q = 50.0 × 4.18 × 19.5 = 4076 J (4.08 kJ)
    • n(CuSO4) = 0.400 × 0.0500 = 0.0200 mol (zinc is in excess, so copper(II) sulfate is limiting)
    • ΔH = −4.076 / 0.0200 = −204 kJ mol−1 (negative sign needed)
    • Insulate the cup / use a lid, to reduce heat loss
    • Record the temperature over time and extrapolate the cooling curve back to the time of mixing (allow: use a more precise thermometer)
    6Paper 2 style

    The enthalpy change for CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l) → CuSO4·5H2O(s) can't be measured directly. Instead, the enthalpy changes of solution are measured: anhydrous CuSO4(s) −66.5 kJ mol−1; hydrated CuSO4·5H2O(s) +11.5 kJ mol−1.

    (a)
    State Hess's law.
    [1]
    (b)
    Draw an energy cycle and use it to calculate ΔH for the hydration of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
    [2]
    (c)
    Suggest why this enthalpy change can't be measured directly.
    [1]
    • The enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route, provided the initial and final conditions are the same
    • Cycle: CuSO4(s) → CuSO4(aq) directly (−66.5), and CuSO4(s) → CuSO4·5H2O(s) → CuSO4(aq) (ΔH then +11.5)
    • ΔH = −66.5 − (+11.5) = −78.0 kJ mol−1
    • You can't add exactly 5 mol of water so that it all becomes water of crystallisation; the solid would dissolve or react too slowly / incompletely
    7Paper 2 style

    Propene reacts with hydrogen: CH2=CHCH3(g) + H2(g) → CH3CH2CH3(g).

    (a)
    Define bond energy.
    [1]
    (b)
    Use the bond energies C=C 610, C–C 350, C–H 410 and H–H 436 kJ mol−1 to calculate ΔH for this reaction.
    [2]
    (c)
    Sketch a labelled reaction pathway diagram for this reaction.
    [2]
    • The energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state
    • Broken: C=C + H–H = 610 + 436 = 1046; made: C–C + 2 C–H = 350 + 820 = 1170
    • ΔH = −124 kJ mol−1
    • Products drawn lower than reactants, with ΔH shown as a downward arrow labelled
    • Hump with EA shown from the reactant level to the peak; axes labelled enthalpy and progress of reaction

    Redox reactions transfer electrons. Oxidation numbers are the bookkeeping that tracks where the electrons go, and they let you name compounds, identify oxidising and reducing agents, and balance difficult equations.

    Oxidation numbers

    An oxidation number is the charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic. Work it out with these rules, in order:

    RuleExample
    An uncombined element is 0.Na, O2, Cl2, S8: all 0
    A simple ion: its charge.Fe3+ is +3; Cl− is −1
    The oxidation numbers in a compound add up to 0; in an ion, to the ion's charge.In SO42−: S + 4(−2) = −2
    Group 1 metals are +1, Group 2 are +2, aluminium is +3.In MgCl2, Mg is +2 and each Cl is −1
    Fluorine is always −1.In OF2, F is −1, so O is +2
    Hydrogen is +1, except in metal hydrides (e.g. NaH), where it is −1.In H2O, H is +1; in NaH, H is −1
    Oxygen is −2, except in peroxides (e.g. H2O2, −1) and in OF2 (+2).In CO2, O is −2, so C is +4
    Chlorine is −1, except when combined with O or F.In ClO3−, Cl is +5

    Worked examples

    SpeciesWorkingOxidation number
    Mn in MnO4−Mn + 4(−2) = −1+7
    Cr in Cr2O72−2Cr + 7(−2) = −2+6
    S in S2O32−2S + 3(−2) = −2+2 (average)
    N in NH4+N + 4(+1) = +1−3
    N in NO3−N + 3(−2) = −1+5
    V in VO2+V + 2(−2) = +1+5

    Roman numerals in names give the oxidation number of the element before them: iron(III) chloride FeCl3, potassium manganate(VII) KMnO4, potassium dichromate(VI) K2Cr2O7, sodium chlorate(I) NaClO, sodium chlorate(V) NaClO3.

    Redox

    TermIn terms of electronsIn terms of oxidation number
    Oxidationloss of electronsincrease in oxidation number
    Reductiongain of electronsdecrease in oxidation number
    Redoxa reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen together
    Oxidising agenta species that oxidises another species, and is itself reduced (it gains electrons)
    Reducing agenta species that reduces another species, and is itself oxidised (it loses electrons)
    Disproportionationa reaction in which the same element is both oxidised and reduced

    Remember "OIL RIG": Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

    Worked example: identifying what is oxidised

    2Fe3+(aq) + 2I−(aq) → 2Fe2+(aq) + I2(aq)

    • Fe: +3 → +2. Iron is reduced, so Fe3+ is the oxidising agent.
    • I: −1 → 0. Iodide is oxidised, so I− is the reducing agent.

    Disproportionation

    Cl2(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + NaClO(aq) + H2O(l) Cl goes from 0 to −1 (reduced) and from 0 to +1 (oxidised)
    2H2O2(aq) → 2H2O(l) + O2(g) O goes from −1 to −2 (reduced) and from −1 to 0 (oxidised)
    2Cu+(aq) → Cu(s) + Cu2+(aq) Cu goes from +1 to 0 and from +1 to +2

    Balancing redox equations

    Method 1: half-equations

    Balance each half separately, then add them so that the electrons cancel. In acidic solution, balance O atoms with H2O and H atoms with H+, then balance charge with electrons.

    Worked example: manganate(VII) and iron(II)

    1. Reduction: MnO4− → Mn2+. Add 4 H2O to balance O, then 8 H+ to balance H: MnO4− + 8H+ → Mn2+ + 4H2O. Charge on the left is +7 and on the right +2, so add 5 electrons on the left: MnO4− + 8H+ + 5e− → Mn2+ + 4H2O
    2. Oxidation: Fe2+ → Fe3+ + e−. Multiply by 5 so the electrons match.
    3. Add and cancel the electrons:

    MnO4−(aq) + 8H+(aq) + 5Fe2+(aq) → Mn2+(aq) + 4H2O(l) + 5Fe3+(aq)

    Method 2: changes in oxidation number

    The total increase in oxidation number must equal the total decrease.

    Worked example: copper and concentrated nitric acid

    Unbalanced: Cu + HNO3 → Cu(NO3)2 + NO2 + H2O

    1. Cu: 0 → +2, an increase of 2. N: +5 → +4 (in NO2), a decrease of 1.
    2. So 2 N atoms must be reduced for every Cu oxidised: Cu + … → … + 2NO2.
    3. Another 2 HNO3 provide the nitrate ions in Cu(NO3)2, so 4 HNO3 in total. Then balance H and O with water.

    Cu(s) + 4HNO3(aq) → Cu(NO3)2(aq) + 2NO2(g) + 2H2O(l)

    Topic 24 (A Level) builds on this with electrode potentials, which predict whether a redox reaction will happen.

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    What is the oxidation number of chromium in K2Cr2O7?

    1. +3
    2. +5
    3. +6
    4. +7

    2(+1) + 2Cr + 7(−2) = 0, so 2Cr = +12 and Cr = +6.

    2Paper 1 style

    Which reaction is a disproportionation?

    1. Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu
    2. 3Cl2 + 6OH− → 5Cl− + ClO3− + 3H2O
    3. 2Fe2+ + Cl2 → 2Fe3+ + 2Cl−
    4. CaCO3 → CaO + CO2

    In B, chlorine goes from 0 to −1 (in Cl−) and from 0 to +5 (in ClO3−): the same element is both reduced and oxidised. D is not a redox reaction at all.

    3Paper 1 style

    In the reaction SO2 + 2H2S → 3S + 2H2O, which statement is correct?

    1. SO2 is the oxidising agent.
    2. SO2 is oxidised.
    3. H2S gains electrons.
    4. The oxidation number of hydrogen changes.

    S in SO2 goes from +4 to 0 (reduced), so SO2 is the oxidising agent. S in H2S goes from −2 to 0 (oxidised, loses electrons). H stays at +1.

    4Paper 2 style

    Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) oxidises iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions. The dichromate(VI) ion is reduced to chromium(III) ions.

    (a)
    Construct the half-equation for the reduction of Cr2O72− to Cr3+ in acid.
    [2]
    (b)
    Hence write the overall ionic equation for the reaction.
    [1]
    (c)
    State the role of the Fe2+ ion in this reaction, and explain your answer in terms of electrons.
    [2]
    • Correct species: Cr2O72−, H+, Cr3+, H2O with 6 electrons
    • Cr2O72− + 14H+ + 6e− → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O
    • Cr2O72− + 14H+ + 6Fe2+ → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O + 6Fe3+
    • Reducing agent
    • It loses an electron (it is oxidised from +2 to +3), giving electrons to the dichromate(VI)
    5Paper 2 style

    When chlorine reacts with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide, sodium chloride and sodium chlorate(V) form.

    (a)
    Give the formula of sodium chlorate(V).
    [1]
    (b)
    Use oxidation numbers to construct a balanced equation for the reaction.
    [2]
    (c)
    Explain why this is a disproportionation reaction.
    [1]
    • NaClO3
    • Cl: 0 → −1 (decrease of 1) and 0 → +5 (increase of 5), so 5 Cl reduced for each 1 oxidised
    • 3Cl2 + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO3 + 3H2O
    • Chlorine is both oxidised (to +5) and reduced (to −1) in the same reaction

    Many reactions never go to completion: they reach a balance in which reactants and products are both present. This topic explains that balance, how to shift it, how to calculate equilibrium constants, and how acids and bases behave.

    Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium

    A reversible reaction can go in both directions: the products can react to re-form the reactants. It is shown with the symbol ⇌, for example N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g).

    Dynamic equilibrium
    The state in which the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.

    "Dynamic" means both reactions are still happening; there is just no overall change. Equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system, where nothing can enter or leave. In an open system, a gaseous product would escape and the reverse reaction couldn't keep up.

    Equilibrium is the same whichever side you start from: starting with only NH3 gives the same equilibrium mixture as starting with the equivalent amounts of N2 and H2 under the same conditions.

    Le Chatelier's principle

    Le Chatelier's principle
    If a change is made to a system at dynamic equilibrium, the position of equilibrium moves to minimise this change.
    ChangeEffect on the position of equilibriumEffect on K
    Increase the concentration of a reactantMoves to the right, using up some of the added reactantnone
    Remove a productMoves to the right, replacing some of the productnone
    Increase the pressure (gases)Moves towards the side with fewer gas molecules, reducing the pressure. No effect if both sides have the same number.none
    Increase the temperatureMoves in the endothermic direction, absorbing the extra heatchanges
    Decrease the temperatureMoves in the exothermic directionchanges
    Add a catalystNo change. It speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster.none
    Only temperature changes K

    A change in concentration or pressure moves the position of equilibrium, but the system then readjusts so that K has the same value. For an exothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature decreases K. For an endothermic forward reaction, it increases K.

    Equilibrium constants

    Kc, in terms of concentrations

    For a general reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD at equilibrium:

    Equilibrium constantKc = [C]c[D]d[A]a[B]bLearn it
