    Square brackets mean concentration at equilibrium in mol dm−3. Products go on top, and each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient. Work out the units from the expression: for N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, Kc = [NH3]2[N2][H2]3 has units (mol dm−3)2 / (mol dm−3)4 = mol−2 dm6.

    A large Kc means the equilibrium lies to the right (mostly products); a small one means it lies to the left.

    Worked example: calculating Kc

    1.00 mol of H2 and 1.00 mol of I2 are heated in a sealed 1.00 dm3 flask. At equilibrium, 1.56 mol of HI is present. H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)

    H2I2HI
    Start / mol1.001.000
    Change / mol−0.78−0.78+1.56
    Equilibrium / mol0.220.221.56
    Concentration / mol dm−30.220.221.56

    Use the equation's ratio for the change row: forming 1.56 mol HI uses 0.78 mol each of H2 and I2.

    Kc = 1.5620.22 × 0.22 = 50 (no units, because the powers cancel)

    Worked example: an esterification

    1.00 mol of ethanoic acid and 1.00 mol of ethanol reach equilibrium. 0.667 mol of ethyl ethanoate is then present. CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O

    At equilibrium: acid 0.333 mol, ethanol 0.333 mol, ester 0.667 mol, water 0.667 mol. The volume V cancels because there are equal numbers of moles on each side.

    Kc = 0.667 × 0.6670.333 × 0.333 = 4.0

    Kp, in terms of partial pressures

    Mole fraction
    The amount of one gas divided by the total amount of gas: xA = nAntotal
    Partial pressure
    The pressure that one gas in a mixture would exert if it occupied the container on its own: pA = xA × ptotal. The partial pressures add up to the total pressure.

    For gas-phase equilibria, Kp uses partial pressures in place of concentrations. For 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g): Kp = pSO32pSO22 × pO2, with units Pa−1 (or kPa−1).

    Worked example: calculating Kp

    An equilibrium mixture contains 0.20 mol SO2, 0.10 mol O2 and 1.70 mol SO3 at a total pressure of 200 kPa.

    1. Total amount = 2.00 mol. Mole fractions: SO2 0.10, O2 0.050, SO3 0.85.
    2. Partial pressures: SO2 20 kPa, O2 10 kPa, SO3 170 kPa.
    3. Kp = 1702202 × 10 = 28 9004000

    Kp = 7.2 kPa−1

    In both kinds of calculation, set up a table of start, change and equilibrium amounts. At AS Level you won't need to solve a quadratic equation.

    Equilibria in industry

    Industrial conditions are a compromise between a good yield (position of equilibrium), a good rate, and cost and safety.

    The Haber process

    N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g) ΔH = −92 kJ mol−1

    ConditionValue usedReasoning
    Temperatureabout 400 to 450 °CThe forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature gives a higher yield, but the rate would be too slow. This is a compromise.
    Pressureabout 20 MPa (200 atm)4 gas molecules become 2, so high pressure increases the yield and the rate. Higher pressures would cost too much to generate and contain safely.
    CatalystironIncreases the rate. It does not change the yield.
    Removing productammonia is cooled and liquefied; unreacted gases are recycledThe yield per pass is only about 15%, but recycling gives an overall conversion of about 98%.

    The Contact process

    2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g) ΔH = −197 kJ mol−1. The SO3 is then used to make sulfuric acid.

    ConditionValue usedReasoning
    Temperatureabout 450 °CA compromise between yield (favoured by low temperature) and rate.
    Pressurejust above atmospheric, 1 to 2 atm3 gas molecules become 2, so high pressure would increase the yield, but the conversion is already about 99% at low pressure, so the extra cost isn't worth it.
    Catalystvanadium(V) oxide, V2O5Increases the rate.

    Acids and bases

    Common acids and alkalis

    AcidFormulaAlkaliFormula
    hydrochloric acidHClsodium hydroxideNaOH
    sulfuric acidH2SO4potassium hydroxideKOH
    nitric acidHNO3ammoniaNH3
    ethanoic acidCH3COOHcalcium hydroxideCa(OH)2

    The Brønsted–Lowry theory

    Brønsted–Lowry acid
    A proton (H+) donor.
    Brønsted–Lowry base
    A proton (H+) acceptor.

    In HCl(g) + H2O(l) → H3O+(aq) + Cl−(aq), HCl donates a proton (acid) and water accepts it (base). In NH3(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ NH4+(aq) + OH−(aq), water donates a proton (acid) and ammonia accepts it (base). Water can act as either, depending on what it reacts with.

    Strong and weak acids and bases

    Strong

    Fully dissociated (ionised) in aqueous solution. HCl, H2SO4, HNO3, NaOH, KOH.

    HCl(aq) → H+(aq) + Cl−(aq)

    Weak

    Only partially dissociated in aqueous solution; most molecules stay intact. Ethanoic acid and ammonia.

    CH3COOH(aq) ⇌ CH3COO−(aq) + H+(aq)

    "Strong" and "weak" describe the extent of dissociation, not the concentration. A dilute solution of a strong acid can have a lower [H+] than a concentrated solution of a weak one.

    pH

    The pH scale measures acidity: pure water has a pH of 7, acidic solutions are below 7 and alkaline solutions are above 7. Each unit of pH is a factor of 10 in the concentration of H+ ions (the pH calculations are in Topic 25).

    Telling strong and weak acids apart

    Compare solutions of the same concentration, for example 0.1 mol dm−3 HCl and 0.1 mol dm−3 CH3COOH:

    TestStrong acid (HCl)Weak acid (CH3COOH)
    pH meter or universal indicatorlower pH (about 1)higher pH (about 3)
    Electrical conductivityhigher: more ionslower: fewer ions
    Reaction with magnesiumfaster fizzing: higher [H+]slower fizzing
    Total volume of H2 with excess Mgthe same: as H+ is used up, more CH3COOH dissociates, so both eventually release the same amount of H+

    Neutralisation and salts

    In every neutralisation between an acid and an alkali, H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(l). The other ions form a salt, for example KOH(aq) + HNO3(aq) → KNO3(aq) + H2O(l).

    pH titration curves

    A titration curve plots pH against the volume of alkali added. The shape depends on whether the acid and base are strong or weak. All four below use 25.0 cm3 of 0.100 mol dm−3 acid and 0.100 mol dm−3 base, so the equivalence point is at 25.0 cm3.

    TitrationpH at equivalenceSteep sectionSuitable indicator
    strong acid + strong base7about pH 3 to 11methyl orange or phenolphthalein
    weak acid + strong baseabove 7 (about 8.7)about pH 7 to 11phenolphthalein
    strong acid + weak basebelow 7 (about 5.3)about pH 3 to 7methyl orange
    weak acid + weak baseabout 7no steep sectionnone is suitable

    Choosing an indicator: its colour-change range must lie entirely within the steep (vertical) part of the curve. Then one drop of alkali at the end-point changes the pH right across the indicator's range.

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    For N2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), ΔH = +180 kJ mol−1. Which change increases the equilibrium yield of NO?

    1. increasing the pressure
    2. increasing the temperature
    3. adding a catalyst
    4. decreasing the temperature

    The forward reaction is endothermic, so a higher temperature moves the equilibrium to the right. There are 2 gas molecules on each side, so pressure has no effect, and a catalyst never changes the yield.

    2Paper 1 style

    What are the units of Kc for 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g)?

    1. no units
    2. mol dm−3
    3. mol−1 dm−3
    4. mol−1 dm3

    Kc = [SO3]2[SO2]2[O2], so the units are (mol dm−3)2 / (mol dm−3)3 = (mol dm−3)−1 = mol−1 dm3.

    3Paper 1 style

    In which reaction is water acting as a Brønsted–Lowry base?

    1. NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH−
    2. CO32− + H2O ⇌ HCO3− + OH−
    3. HNO3 + H2O → H3O+ + NO3−
    4. CH3COO− + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + OH−

    In C, water accepts a proton from HNO3 to become H3O+. In A, B and D, water donates a proton, so it is acting as an acid.

    4Paper 1 style

    Which indicator is suitable for titrating ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide?

    1. phenolphthalein, range pH 8.3 to 10.0
    2. methyl orange, range pH 3.1 to 4.4
    3. methyl red, range pH 4.4 to 6.2
    4. no indicator is suitable

    For a weak acid and a strong base, the steep section is at about pH 7 to 11, so phenolphthalein changes colour right at the end-point.

    5Paper 2 style

    Hydrogen is made by the reaction CH4(g) + H2O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H2(g), ΔH = +206 kJ mol−1.

    (a)
    State and explain the effect on the equilibrium yield of hydrogen of (i) increasing the temperature and (ii) increasing the pressure.
    [4]
    (b)
    Write the expression for Kp, and give its units.
    [2]
    (c)
    At equilibrium at a total pressure of 300 kPa, the mixture contains 0.40 mol CH4, 0.40 mol H2O, 0.30 mol CO and 0.90 mol H2. Calculate Kp.
    [3]
    • (i) Yield increases
    • The forward reaction is endothermic, so equilibrium moves right to absorb the added heat
    • (ii) Yield decreases
    • There are more gas molecules on the right (4) than the left (2), so equilibrium moves left to reduce the pressure
    • Kp = pCO × pH23pCH4 × pH2O
    • kPa2 (or Pa2)
    • Total = 2.00 mol; mole fractions CH4 0.20, H2O 0.20, CO 0.15, H2 0.45
    • Partial pressures: CH4 60, H2O 60, CO 45, H2 135 kPa
    • Kp = 45 × 1353 / (60 × 60) = 3.08 × 104 kPa2
    6Paper 2 style

    2.00 mol of PCl5 is heated in a sealed 4.00 dm3 container until it reaches equilibrium: PCl5(g) ⇌ PCl3(g) + Cl2(g). At equilibrium, 0.50 mol of Cl2 is present.

    (a)
    Explain what is meant by dynamic equilibrium.
    [2]
    (b)
    Calculate Kc, giving its units.
    [3]
    (c)
    State the effect on the value of Kc of adding more Cl2 at constant temperature.
    [1]
    • The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal
    • The concentrations of reactants and products stay constant (in a closed system)
    • Equilibrium amounts: PCl5 1.50 mol, PCl3 0.50 mol, Cl2 0.50 mol; concentrations 0.375, 0.125, 0.125 mol dm−3
    • Kc = 0.125 × 0.125 / 0.375 = 0.0417
    • mol dm−3
    • No change (only temperature changes Kc)

    Kinetics is about how fast reactions go. Collision theory and the Boltzmann distribution explain why concentration, pressure, temperature and catalysts change the rate.

    Rate of reaction

    Rate of reaction
    The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. Units: mol dm−3 s−1.

    Rates are measured by following a property that changes during the reaction: the volume of gas given off (gas syringe), the loss in mass as a gas escapes, a colour change (colorimeter), or by taking samples and titrating them.

    • The average rate over a period = change in concentration ÷ time taken.
    • The rate at a particular moment is the gradient of the tangent to the concentration–time curve at that time. The initial rate is the gradient at t = 0.

    Worked example

    The concentration of a reactant falls from 0.050 mol dm−3 to 0.030 mol dm−3 in the first 40 s. What is the average rate over this time?

    rate = (0.050 − 0.030) / 40 = 5.0 × 10−4 mol dm−3 s−1

    Collision theory

    For particles to react, they must collide, with at least the activation energy and in the right orientation.

    Activation energy, EA
    The minimum energy required for a collision to be effective.
    Effective collision
    A collision that results in a reaction.
    Non-effective collision
    A collision in which the particles bounce apart unchanged, because they have too little energy or the wrong orientation.

    The rate depends on the frequency of effective collisions: the number per second.

    Higher concentration

    More particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent, and so are effective collisions.

    Higher gas pressure

    The same as higher concentration: the gas particles are closer together.

    Larger surface area

    For a solid, more particles are exposed, so collisions with it are more frequent.

    Temperature and the Boltzmann distribution

    In a gas (or solution), particles have a range of energies. The Boltzmann distribution shows how many particles have each energy.

    Key features to show when you sketch the curve: it starts at the origin, has no particles with zero energy, rises to a peak (the most likely energy) and then falls towards the energy axis without touching or crossing it, because there is no maximum energy.

    Why a higher temperature increases the rate:

    1. Particles have more kinetic energy, so a much larger proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than EA. This is the main effect.
    2. Particles also move faster, so they collide more often. This is a much smaller effect.

    Together, these increase the frequency of effective collisions. For many reactions near room temperature, a rise of 10 °C roughly doubles the rate.

    Catalysts

    Catalyst
    A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up overall. It provides an alternative reaction pathway (a different mechanism) with a lower activation energy.

    With a lower EA, a greater proportion of particles have enough energy to react, so the frequency of effective collisions increases. A catalyst does not change ΔH, and it does not change the position of equilibrium.

    Homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts

    TypeMeaningExamples
    HomogeneousThe catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants.H+ ions in esterification (all in solution); Fe2+ in the reaction of I− with S2O82−; enzymes in solution
    HeterogeneousThe catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants, usually a solid with gaseous or dissolved reactants.iron in the Haber process; V2O5 in the Contact process; Pt, Pd and Rh in catalytic converters; nickel in hydrogenating alkenes

    How these catalysts work in detail (adsorption, and catalysts that change oxidation state) is covered in Topic 26.

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    Why does increasing the temperature increase the rate of a reaction?

    1. The activation energy decreases.
    2. The particles collide more often, and this is the main effect.
    3. A greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.
    4. The reaction becomes more exothermic.

    The main effect is that many more particles have at least EA. Collisions do become more frequent, but that is a much smaller effect. EA and ΔH don't change.

    2Paper 1 style

    What happens to the Boltzmann distribution curve of a gas when the temperature is increased?

    1. The peak moves to higher energy and becomes lower.
    2. The peak moves to higher energy and becomes higher.
    3. The peak stays at the same energy and becomes lower.
    4. The area under the curve increases.

    The particles spread out over a wider range of energies. The number of particles is unchanged, so the area stays the same and the peak must get lower.

    3Paper 1 style

    Which is an example of heterogeneous catalysis?

    1. H+(aq) catalysing the hydrolysis of an ester in solution
    2. Fe2+(aq) catalysing the reaction between I−(aq) and S2O82−(aq)
    3. an enzyme in solution catalysing a reaction in solution
    4. solid iron catalysing the reaction between gaseous nitrogen and hydrogen

    In D the catalyst (solid) is in a different phase from the reactants (gases). The others are all in solution.

    4Paper 2 style
    (a)
    Define activation energy.
    [1]
    (b)
    Sketch the Boltzmann distribution for a gas at temperature T1. On the same axes, sketch the curve at a higher temperature T2. Label the axes and mark EA.
    [3]
    (c)
    Use your sketch to explain why the rate of reaction is greater at T2.
    [2]
    • The minimum energy required for a collision to be effective / for a reaction to occur
    • Axes: number of molecules (with a given energy) against energy
    • T1 curve starts at the origin and does not touch or cross the energy axis at high energy
    • T2 curve has a lower peak, moved to the right, and is above T1 at high energies
    • More molecules have energy ≥ EA at T2 (larger area beyond EA)
    • So there are more effective / successful collisions per unit time
    5Paper 2 and 3 style

    Marble chips (calcium carbonate) react with excess hydrochloric acid: CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g).

    (a)
    Describe how you could follow the rate of this reaction.
    [2]
    (b)
    The experiment is repeated with the same mass of marble as a powder. Explain the effect on the rate.
    [2]
    (c)
    The experiment is repeated using hydrochloric acid of half the concentration (still in excess). Explain the effect on the rate, and state the effect on the total volume of gas produced.
    [3]
    • Collect the CO2 in a gas syringe (or measure mass loss on a balance)
    • Record the volume (or mass) at regular time intervals
    • The rate increases: a powder has a larger surface area
    • More particles are exposed, so collisions with acid particles are more frequent
    • The rate decreases
    • Fewer acid particles per unit volume, so less frequent (effective) collisions
    • The total volume of gas is the same, because the amount of marble (the limiting reagent) is the same

    Period 3 runs from sodium to argon. Across it, the structure changes from giant metallic to giant covalent to simple molecular, and the oxides and chlorides change from ionic and basic to covalent and acidic. Learning why lets you predict the chemistry of any element from its position.

    Physical properties across Period 3

    Atomic and ionic radius

    Atomic radius decreases from Na to Cl: the nuclear charge increases but the extra electrons go into the same (third) shell with similar shielding, so the outer electrons are pulled closer. For the ions, Na+ to Si4+ have lost their third shell and get smaller as nuclear charge rises; P3− to Cl− keep three shells, so they are much larger, and they also get smaller across the period. The values are in the table in Topic 1.

    Melting point

    ElementsStructureExplanation of melting point
    Na, Mg, Algiant metallicRises from Na to Al: the number of delocalised electrons per atom increases (1, 2, 3) and the ions get smaller and more highly charged, so the metallic bonding gets stronger.
    Sigiant covalent (like diamond)Highest: every atom is held by four strong covalent bonds, and very many must be broken.
    P4, S8, Cl2simple molecularLow: only weak id-id forces between molecules are overcome. S8 (128 electrons) > P4 (60) > Cl2 (34), because larger molecules have stronger id-id forces.
    Arsingle atomsLowest: very weak id-id forces between separate atoms (18 electrons).

    Electrical conductivity

    Na, Mg and Al are good conductors because of their delocalised electrons. Conductivity increases from Na to Al, as the number of delocalised electrons per atom increases. Silicon is a semiconductor: a poor conductor whose conductivity rises with temperature. Phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine and argon do not conduct, because all their electrons are held in covalent bonds or in single atoms.

    Reactions of the elements

    With oxygen

    ElementEquationObservations
    Na4Na(s) + O2(g) → 2Na2O(s)burns with a bright yellow-orange flame; white solid
    Mg2Mg(s) + O2(g) → 2MgO(s)burns with a brilliant white flame; white solid
    Al4Al(s) + 3O2(g) → 2Al2O3(s)a thin, protective oxide layer forms at once; the powder burns with white sparks; white solid
    SiSi(s) + O2(g) → SiO2(s)only on strong heating; white solid
    PP4(s) + 5O2(g) → P4O10(s)white phosphorus catches fire in air with a bright flame and dense white smoke
    SS(s) + O2(g) → SO2(g)burns with a blue flame; colourless, choking gas. SO2 is oxidised further to SO3 only with a catalyst (Topic 7).

    With chlorine

    ElementEquationProduct
    Na2Na(s) + Cl2(g) → 2NaCl(s)white ionic solid; bright yellow-orange flame
    MgMg(s) + Cl2(g) → MgCl2(s)white ionic solid
    Al2Al(s) + 3Cl2(g) → 2AlCl3(s)pale yellow / white solid that sublimes; covalent, forms Al2Cl6
    SiSi(s) + 2Cl2(g) → SiCl4(l)colourless covalent liquid
    P2P(s) + 5Cl2(g) → 2PCl5(s)pale yellow covalent solid (with excess chlorine; PCl3, a liquid, with limited chlorine)

    Sodium and magnesium with water

    2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g) vigorous: sodium floats, melts into a ball, fizzes and moves about. The solution is strongly alkaline, pH 13 to 14.
    Mg(s) + 2H2O(l) → Mg(OH)2(aq) + H2(g) very slow with cold water: a few bubbles over days. The solution is weakly alkaline, about pH 9 to 10, because Mg(OH)2 is only slightly soluble.
    Mg(s) + H2O(g) → MgO(s) + H2(g) with steam: magnesium burns with a bright white glow.

    Oxidation numbers of the oxides and chlorides

    OxideNa2OMgOAl2O3SiO2P4O10SO2 / SO3
    Oxidation number+1+2+3+4+5+4 / +6
    ChlorideNaClMgCl2AlCl3SiCl4PCl5
    Oxidation number+1+2+3+4+5

    The maximum oxidation number equals the number of outer-shell electrons, because in the highest oxide or chloride the element uses all of its outer electrons in bonding. In the chlorides it stops at +5 for phosphorus, because there isn't room around a sulfur atom for six chlorine atoms.

    The oxides: acid–base behaviour

    OxideBondingWith waterpHNature
    Na2OionicNa2O + H2O → 2NaOH13–14basic
    MgOionicMgO + H2O → Mg(OH)2 (slightly soluble)about 9–10basic
    Al2O3ionic, with some covalent characterinsoluble7amphoteric
    SiO2giant covalentinsoluble7acidic
    P4O10simple molecular covalentP4O10 + 6H2O → 4H3PO4about 2acidic
    SO2simple molecular covalentSO2 + H2O → H2SO3about 2–3acidic
    SO3simple molecular covalentSO3 + H2O → H2SO4about 1acidic

    Reactions with acids and bases

    Na2O(s) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H2O(l) basic oxide with acid
    MgO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2O(l) basic oxide with acid
    Al2O3(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl3(aq) + 3H2O(l) amphoteric oxide reacting as a base
    Al2O3(s) + 2NaOH(aq) + 3H2O(l) → 2NaAl(OH)4(aq) amphoteric oxide reacting as an acid: sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate forms
    SiO2(s) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na2SiO3(aq) + H2O(l) acidic oxide; needs hot, concentrated NaOH. Sodium silicate forms.
    P4O10(s) + 12NaOH(aq) → 4Na3PO4(aq) + 6H2O(l) acidic oxide
    SO2(g) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na2SO3(aq) + H2O(l) and SO3(g) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na2SO4(aq) + H2O(l) acidic oxides

    The hydroxides follow the same pattern: NaOH and Mg(OH)2 are basic, and aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric:

    Al(OH)3(s) + 3HCl(aq) → AlCl3(aq) + 3H2O(l) and Al(OH)3(s) + NaOH(aq) → NaAl(OH)4(aq)

    Explaining the trend

    Across the period, the electronegativity of the element increases, so the difference from oxygen decreases. The bonding in the oxides changes from ionic (Na, Mg) to covalent (Si to S), with aluminium in between.

    • Ionic oxides contain O2− ions, which accept protons: O2− + H2O → 2OH−. So they are basic.
    • Covalent oxides of non-metals react with water to form acids, or react with bases. So they are acidic.
    • Aluminium oxide sits between the two and shows both behaviours: it is amphoteric.

    The chlorides with water

    ChlorideBondingWhat happens in waterpH
    NaClionicdissolves; the ions are surrounded by water molecules but don't react7
    MgCl2ionicdissolves, with very slight hydrolysisabout 6.5
    AlCl3covalentreacts (hydrolyses) to form an acidic solution; with a little water, steamy fumes of HClabout 3
    SiCl4covalenthydrolyses violently: white solid SiO2 and steamy fumes of HClabout 1–2
    PCl5covalenthydrolyses violently; steamy fumes of HClabout 1–2
    AlCl3(s) + 6H2O(l) → [Al(H2O)6]3+(aq) + 3Cl−(aq), then [Al(H2O)6]3+(aq) ⇌ [Al(H2O)5(OH)]2+(aq) + H+(aq) the small, highly charged Al3+ ion pulls electron density from a water ligand, which releases H+
    SiCl4(l) + 2H2O(l) → SiO2(s) + 4HCl(aq)
    PCl5(s) + 4H2O(l) → H3PO4(aq) + 5HCl(aq)

    Explaining the trend: ionic chlorides simply dissolve, giving neutral solutions. Covalent chlorides are hydrolysed by water to form HCl, so their solutions are strongly acidic. As with the oxides, the bonding changes from ionic to covalent across the period as electronegativity increases.

    Inferring bonding from properties

    A chloride or oxide with a high melting point that conducts when molten is ionic. One with a low melting point that reacts with water to give an acidic solution is covalent. Expect to be given data and asked to decide which.

    Periodicity of other elements

    The same patterns repeat in every period, so you can predict an element's properties from its position. For example, germanium (Group 14, Period 4) should be a semiconductor like silicon, form GeO2 and GeCl4, and its chloride should be hydrolysed by water. Use the explorer to compare electronegativity and first ionisation energy across the table.

    Worked example: identifying an unknown element

    Element X is in Period 3. Its oxide has a very high melting point and does not dissolve in water, but it does react with hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide. It does not react with acids. Its chloride is a liquid that fumes in moist air. Identify X.

    X is silicon. The oxide is giant covalent and acidic (SiO2); the chloride SiCl4 is a covalent liquid that hydrolyses to give HCl fumes. (Aluminium oxide would also react with acids.)

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    Which Period 3 element has the highest melting point?

    1. aluminium
    2. silicon
    3. phosphorus
    4. sulfur

    Silicon has a giant covalent structure, so many strong covalent bonds must be broken.

    2Paper 1 style

    Which oxide reacts with both hydrochloric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide?

    1. MgO
    2. SiO2
    3. Al2O3
    4. P4O10

    Aluminium oxide is amphoteric. MgO is basic only; SiO2 and P4O10 are acidic only.

    3Paper 1 style

    A Period 3 chloride is added to water. The solution has a pH of 7. Which chloride was it?

    1. AlCl3
    2. SiCl4
    3. PCl5
    4. NaCl

    Sodium chloride is ionic and dissolves without hydrolysis. The others are hydrolysed to give acidic solutions.

    4Paper 2 style
    (a)
    Explain why the melting point of aluminium is higher than that of sodium.
    [2]
    (b)
    Explain why the melting point of sulfur (S8) is higher than that of phosphorus (P4).
    [2]
    (c)
    Write equations to show the amphoteric nature of aluminium oxide.
    [2]
    (d)
    Write an equation for the reaction of silicon(IV) chloride with water, and state the approximate pH of the resulting mixture.
    [2]
    • Al has more delocalised electrons per atom (3 compared with 1) and a smaller ion with a higher charge
    • So the metallic bonding (attraction between ions and delocalised electrons) is stronger
    • Both are simple molecular, so id-id forces are overcome
    • S8 has more electrons than P4, so its id-id forces are stronger
    • Al2O3 + 6HCl → 2AlCl3 + 3H2O
    • Al2O3 + 2NaOH + 3H2O → 2NaAl(OH)4
    • SiCl4 + 2H2O → SiO2 + 4HCl
    • pH 1 to 2
    5Paper 2 style

    Sodium oxide and sulfur trioxide both react with water.

    (a)
    Write equations for both reactions and state the approximate pH of each solution.
    [3]
    (b)
    Explain, in terms of bonding, why the two oxides give solutions with such different pH values.
    [2]
    (c)
    Write an equation for the reaction of sulfur trioxide with sodium hydroxide.
    [1]
    • Na2O + H2O → 2NaOH
    • SO3 + H2O → H2SO4
    • Na2O: pH 13–14; SO3: pH 0–1
    • Na2O is ionic: its oxide ions react with water to form hydroxide ions
    • SO3 is covalent (simple molecular): it reacts with water to form an acid that releases H+
    • SO3 + 2NaOH → Na2SO4 + H2O

    The Group 2 metals, magnesium to barium, all form 2+ ions and get more reactive down the group. Their compounds show clear trends in solubility and thermal stability, which come up often in Paper 1.

    The elements

    MgCaSrBa
    Electronic configuration[Ne] 3s2[Ar] 4s2[Kr] 5s2[Xe] 6s2
    Flame colournone (bright white when burning)brick redcrimson redapple green

    Reactivity increases down the group. Each atom reacts by losing its two outer electrons to form an M2+ ion. Down the group, the atoms get larger and the outer electrons are more shielded, so the first and second ionisation energies decrease. The electrons are lost more easily.

    Reactions of the metals

    ReactantGeneral equationNotes
    oxygen2M(s) + O2(g) → 2MO(s)burn with the flame colours above to give white oxides; faster down the group
    cold waterM(s) + 2H2O(l) → M(OH)2(aq) + H2(g)Mg reacts extremely slowly; Ca fizzes steadily, giving a cloudy white suspension of Ca(OH)2; Sr and Ba react faster still
    steamMg(s) + H2O(g) → MgO(s) + H2(g)magnesium burns with a bright white flame
    dilute hydrochloric acidM(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MCl2(aq) + H2(g)all fizz; faster down the group; the chlorides are soluble
    dilute sulfuric acidM(s) + H2SO4(aq) → MSO4 + H2(g)Mg reacts fully. With Ca, Sr and Ba the reaction quickly slows and stops, because an insoluble sulfate coating forms on the metal

    Reactions of the compounds

    CompoundReactionEquation
    oxideswith waterMO(s) + H2O(l) → M(OH)2; CaO reacts vigorously and gives out heat (making "slaked lime")
    oxideswith dilute acidMO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MCl2(aq) + H2O(l)
    hydroxideswith dilute acidM(OH)2 + 2HCl(aq) → MCl2(aq) + 2H2O(l)
    carbonateswith dilute acidMCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g); with sulfuric acid, the reaction of CaCO3, SrCO3 and BaCO3 soon stops (insoluble sulfate coating)
    carbonateswith waterinsoluble; no reaction

    The oxides and hydroxides are bases. Solutions of the hydroxides are alkaline, and the pH increases down the group because the hydroxides get more soluble.

    Thermal decomposition

    MCO3(s) → MO(s) + CO2(g) carbonates decompose on heating to the oxide and carbon dioxide
    2M(NO3)2(s) → 2MO(s) + 4NO2(g) + O2(g) nitrates decompose to the oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide and oxygen

    Thermal stability increases down the group: you need a higher temperature to decompose BaCO3 than MgCO3. (The explanation, in terms of how much the cation polarises the large carbonate or nitrate ion, is an A Level topic: see Topic 27.)

    Solubility trends

    Hydroxides: more soluble down the group

    Mg(OH)2 is only sparingly soluble; Ba(OH)2 is quite soluble. So limewater, Ca(OH)2(aq), is only weakly alkaline, while barium hydroxide solution is strongly alkaline.

    Sulfates: less soluble down the group

    MgSO4 is soluble; BaSO4 is insoluble. Adding acidified barium chloride solution to a solution containing sulfate ions gives a white precipitate: Ba2+(aq) + SO42−(aq) → BaSO4(s).

    Some uses follow from these properties: calcium hydroxide is used to neutralise acidic soil, magnesium hydroxide is used in indigestion remedies, and insoluble barium sulfate can be swallowed safely for X-ray images of the gut.

    Making predictions

    Use the trends to predict beryllium or radium chemistry, or unfamiliar compounds. For example, radium should react with water even more vigorously than barium, and radium sulfate should be even less soluble.

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    Which statement about the Group 2 elements, from magnesium to barium, is correct?

    1. The solubility of the hydroxides increases.
    2. The solubility of the sulfates increases.
    3. The thermal stability of the carbonates decreases.
    4. The first ionisation energy increases.

    Hydroxides become more soluble down the group. Sulfates become less soluble, carbonates become more stable and first ionisation energy decreases.

    2Paper 1 style

    What are the products when calcium nitrate is heated strongly?

    1. Ca(NO2)2 and O2
    2. CaO and NO2 only
    3. CaO, NO2 and O2
    4. Ca, N2 and O2

    2Ca(NO3)2 → 2CaO + 4NO2 + O2. (Group 1 nitrates other than lithium form the nitrite and oxygen instead.)

    3Paper 1 style

    Barium reacts with dilute sulfuric acid, but the reaction stops very soon. Why?

    1. Barium is less reactive than magnesium.
    2. The acid is used up.
    3. Hydrogen gas forms a layer over the metal.
    4. Insoluble barium sulfate coats the metal.

    BaSO4 is insoluble, so it forms a layer on the barium that stops the acid reaching the metal.

    4Paper 2 style
    (a)
    Write an equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of strontium with water.
    [2]
    (b)
    Explain why strontium reacts with water more vigorously than calcium.
    [2]
    (c)
    The solution formed in (a) is tested with universal indicator. Suggest its pH, compared with the solution formed by calcium. Explain your answer.
    [2]
    (d)
    Describe a test to show that a solution contains sulfate ions. Give the observation and an ionic equation.
    [3]
    • Sr + 2H2O → Sr(OH)2 + H2
    • State symbols: Sr(s), H2O(l), Sr(OH)2(aq), H2(g)
    • Sr atoms are larger / outer electrons more shielded and further from the nucleus
    • So the (first and second) ionisation energies are lower and electrons are lost more easily
    • Higher pH (about 13 compared with about 12)
    • Sr(OH)2 is more soluble, so the concentration of OH− is higher
    • Add dilute HCl (or HNO3) then barium chloride (or barium nitrate) solution
    • White precipitate
    • Ba2+(aq) + SO42−(aq) → BaSO4(s)

    The halogens are reactive non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules. Down the group they become less volatile, weaker oxidising agents and more strongly coloured, while their halide ions become stronger reducing agents. These trends explain a set of classic test-tube reactions.

    Physical properties

    Chlorine, Cl2Bromine, Br2Iodine, I2
    State at room temperaturegasliquidsolid
    Appearancepale yellow-green gasred-brown liquid, orange-brown vapourgrey-black shiny solid, purple vapour
    In watervery pale green (almost colourless)orange to yellowbrown (dissolves only slightly, better in KI solution)
    In a non-polar solvent such as hexanevery pale greenorange-redpurple / violet
    Boiling point / °C−3459184
    Bond energy, X–X / kJ mol−1242193151

    Volatility decreases down the group

    The halogens are simple molecular. Down the group, the molecules have more electrons, so the instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces between them get stronger. More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so boiling points rise and volatility falls.

    Bond strength decreases down the group

    The atoms get larger, so the bonding pair of electrons is further from the two nuclei and is attracted less strongly. (Fluorine, F–F 158 kJ mol−1, is an exception: its atoms are so small that the lone pairs on the two atoms repel each other.)

    The halogens as oxidising agents

    A halogen reacts by gaining an electron: X2 + 2e− → 2X−. So halogens are oxidising agents. Oxidising power decreases down the group: chlorine is the strongest and iodine the weakest of the three.

    Explanation: down the group the atoms get larger and the outer shell is more shielded, so there is less attraction between the nucleus and an incoming electron.

    Displacement reactions

    A halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from a solution of its halide ions.

    Halogen added ↓ / halide ion →Cl−(aq)Br−(aq)I−(aq)
    Cl2(aq)–yellow-orange solution: Br2 formsbrown solution: I2 forms
    Br2(aq)no reaction–brown solution: I2 forms
    I2(aq)no reactionno reaction–
    Cl2(aq) + 2Br−(aq) → 2Cl−(aq) + Br2(aq)
    Cl2(aq) + 2I−(aq) → 2Cl−(aq) + I2(aq)
    Br2(aq) + 2I−(aq) → 2Br−(aq) + I2(aq)

    Bromine and iodine solutions can look similar. Shaking with hexane makes it clear: bromine gives an orange-red upper layer, iodine a purple one.

    Reactions with hydrogen

    All the halogens react with hydrogen to form hydrogen halides, H2(g) + X2 → 2HX(g), but reactivity falls sharply down the group:

    HalogenReaction with hydrogen
    fluorineexplosive, even in the cold and dark
    chlorineexplosive in sunlight (or a flame); slow in the dark
    bromineneeds heating (about 300 °C) with a platinum catalyst; not explosive
    iodineslow and incomplete even when heated with a catalyst; the reaction is reversible

    Thermal stability of the hydrogen halides

    Down the group the hydrogen halides become less stable to heat. Hydrogen chloride does not decompose at ordinary temperatures, hydrogen bromide decomposes slightly on strong heating, and a hot glass rod plunged into hydrogen iodide produces purple fumes of iodine: 2HI(g) → H2(g) + I2(g).

    Explanation: the H–X bond energy decreases (H–Cl 431, H–Br 366, H–I 299 kJ mol−1), because the bond gets longer as the halogen atom gets larger. A weaker bond is broken more easily.

    Reactions of the halide ions

    Halide ions as reducing agents

    A halide ion acts as a reducing agent by losing an electron: 2X− → X2 + 2e−. Reducing power increases down the group: iodide is the strongest reducing agent. Down the group, the ions get larger and the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are lost more easily.

    Testing with silver nitrate and ammonia

    Acidify the solution with dilute nitric acid (to remove carbonate ions, which would also give a precipitate), then add aqueous silver nitrate. Then test the precipitate with aqueous ammonia.

    HalideWith AgNO3(aq)Add dilute NH3(aq)Add concentrated NH3(aq)
    chloridewhite precipitate, AgCldissolvesdissolves
    bromidecream precipitate, AgBrdoes not dissolvedissolves
    iodideyellow precipitate, AgIdoes not dissolvedoes not dissolve
    Ag+(aq) + X−(aq) → AgX(s) the ionic equation for all three precipitates
    AgCl(s) + 2NH3(aq) → [Ag(NH3)2]+(aq) + Cl−(aq) the precipitate dissolves because a soluble complex ion forms

    The precipitates get less soluble from AgCl to AgI, so it takes more concentrated ammonia to dissolve them, and AgI doesn't dissolve at all.

    Reactions with concentrated sulfuric acid

    Adding concentrated sulfuric acid to a solid halide first gives the hydrogen halide (an acid–base reaction). Bromide and iodide are strong enough reducing agents to go on and reduce the sulfuric acid; chloride is not.

    HalideEquationsObservationsS oxidation number
    NaClNaCl + H2SO4 → NaHSO4 + HClsteamy white fumes of HClstays +6 (no redox)
    NaBrNaBr + H2SO4 → NaHSO4 + HBr
    2HBr + H2SO4 → Br2 + SO2 + 2H2O    		steamy fumes of HBr, and orange-brown vapour of Br2; colourless, choking SO2+6 → +4
    NaINaI + H2SO4 → NaHSO4 + HI
    2HI + H2SO4 → I2 + SO2 + 2H2O
    6HI + H2SO4 → 3I2 + S + 4H2O
    8HI + H2SO4 → 4I2 + H2S + 4H2O    		some steamy fumes, purple vapour and black solid of I2, yellow solid sulfur, and a smell of rotten eggs (H2S)+6 → +4, 0 and −2

    The further the sulfur is reduced, the stronger the reducing agent. Iodide reduces sulfur all the way from +6 to −2.

    The reactions of chlorine

    With sodium hydroxide: disproportionation

    Cl2(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + NaClO(aq) + H2O(l) cold, dilute NaOH. Cl: 0 → −1 (in NaCl) and 0 → +1 (in sodium chlorate(I), NaClO). This solution is household bleach.
    3Cl2(aq) + 6NaOH(aq) → 5NaCl(aq) + NaClO3(aq) + 3H2O(l) hot, concentrated NaOH. Cl: 0 → −1 and 0 → +5 (in sodium chlorate(V), NaClO3).

    Both are disproportionation reactions: chlorine is oxidised and reduced at the same time.

    Chlorine in water purification

    Chlorine is added to drinking water to kill bacteria. It reacts with the water (another disproportionation):

    Cl2(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ HCl(aq) + HOCl(aq) chloric(I) acid, HOCl, forms; Cl: 0 → −1 and +1
    HOCl(aq) ⇌ H+(aq) + ClO−(aq) HOCl is a weak acid, so it partly dissociates to chlorate(I) ions

    Both HOCl and ClO− are strong oxidising agents that kill bacteria. They are the active agents in the water.

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    Why does the boiling point of the halogens increase from chlorine to iodine?

    1. The X–X bond energy increases.
    2. The molecules become more polar.
    3. Hydrogen bonding between molecules increases.
    4. Instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces increase.

    More electrons per molecule means stronger id-id forces. The X–X bond energy actually decreases, and boiling doesn't break these bonds anyway.

    2Paper 1 style

    A white precipitate forms when silver nitrate is added to an acidified solution of X. The precipitate dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia. What is X?

    1. sodium bromide
    2. sodium chloride
    3. sodium iodide
    4. sodium nitrate

    Silver chloride is white and dissolves in dilute ammonia. AgBr is cream and AgI is yellow; sodium nitrate gives no precipitate.

    3Paper 1 style

    Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium iodide. Which product shows that sulfur has been reduced to an oxidation number of −2?

    1. SO2
    2. S
    3. H2S
    4. NaHSO4

    In H2S, S is −2. In SO2 it is +4, in S it is 0, and in NaHSO4 it is still +6.

    4Paper 1 style

    What is the oxidation number of chlorine in the chlorine-containing product (other than NaCl) of the reaction between chlorine and hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide?

    1. +5
    2. +1
    3. +3
    4. +7

    Hot, concentrated NaOH gives sodium chlorate(V), NaClO3: Na + Cl + 3(−2) = 0, so Cl = +5. Cold, dilute NaOH gives NaClO, with Cl at +1.

    5Paper 2 style
    (a)
    Chlorine water is added to aqueous potassium bromide. Describe what you would see, and write an ionic equation.
    [2]
    (b)
    Explain why chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine.
    [2]
    (c)
    A hot glass rod is placed in a jar of hydrogen iodide. Purple fumes are seen. Explain this observation, using bond energies H–Cl 431 and H–I 299 kJ mol−1 to compare HI with HCl.
    [2]
    • Colourless solution turns orange / yellow-orange
    • Cl2 + 2Br− → 2Cl− + Br2
    • Chlorine atoms are smaller / the outer shell is closer to the nucleus and less shielded
    • So there is a stronger attraction for an electron being gained
    • HI decomposes to hydrogen and (purple) iodine vapour: 2HI → H2 + I2
    • The H–I bond is much weaker than H–Cl (299 compared with 431), so HI is less thermally stable
    6Paper 2 style
    (a)
    Concentrated sulfuric acid is added separately to solid sodium chloride and to solid sodium bromide. Describe what you would see in each case, and write equations for the reactions with sodium bromide.
    [4]
    (b)
    Explain the difference between the two reactions in terms of the reducing power of the halide ions.
    [2]
    (c)
    Chlorine is used to treat drinking water. Write an equation for the reaction of chlorine with water and name the species that kill bacteria.
    [2]
    • NaCl: steamy (misty) white fumes only
    • NaBr: steamy fumes and orange-brown vapour (bromine)
    • NaBr + H2SO4 → NaHSO4 + HBr
    • 2HBr + H2SO4 → Br2 + SO2 + 2H2O
    • Bromide is a stronger reducing agent than chloride
    • Bromide (HBr) reduces S from +6 to +4; chloride is too weak to reduce the sulfuric acid
    • Cl2 + H2O ⇌ HCl + HOCl
    • HOCl and ClO−

    Nitrogen makes up 78% of the air but is remarkably unreactive. Its compounds, though, matter a great deal: ammonia is a base and a fertiliser, and oxides of nitrogen from engines cause smog and acid rain, helped along by sulfur dioxide.

    The lack of reactivity of nitrogen

    Nitrogen, N2, is unreactive for two reasons:

    • The N≡N triple bond is very strong (944 kJ mol−1), so a lot of energy is needed to break it: reactions have a very high activation energy.
    • The molecule is non-polar: both atoms are identical, so there are no δ+ or δ− sites to attract electrophiles or nucleophiles.

    Ammonia and the ammonium ion

    Ammonia, NH3, is a weak Brønsted–Lowry base: the lone pair on nitrogen accepts a proton.

    NH3(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ NH4+(aq) + OH−(aq) aqueous ammonia is weakly alkaline (about pH 11)
    NH3(aq) + H+(aq) → NH4+(aq) with acids, forming ammonium salts, for example NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl

    The ammonium ion, NH4+, is tetrahedral (109.5°). The new N–H bond is a coordinate bond, but once formed all four bonds are identical (Topic 3).

    Displacing ammonia from ammonium salts

    Warming any ammonium salt with a stronger base, such as aqueous sodium hydroxide or calcium hydroxide, releases ammonia gas. This is an acid–base reaction: the hydroxide ion takes a proton from the ammonium ion.

    NH4Cl(s) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(l) + NH3(g)
    NH4+(aq) + OH−(aq) → NH3(g) + H2O(l) the ionic equation

    This is the test for ammonium ions: the gas turns damp red litmus paper blue. It is also why ammonium fertilisers should not be spread at the same time as lime (calcium hydroxide): ammonia would be lost.

    Oxides of nitrogen

    Nitrogen and oxygen in the air react only at very high temperatures:

    N2(g) + O2(g) → 2NO(g) nitrogen monoxide forms naturally in lightning, and in car engines and power stations, where fuel burns at high temperature
    2NO(g) + O2(g) → 2NO2(g) in the air, NO is oxidised to brown nitrogen dioxide

    Removing oxides of nitrogen from exhaust gases

    A catalytic converter in a car exhaust contains platinum, palladium and rhodium on a honeycomb support with a large surface area. It converts oxides of nitrogen and carbon monoxide into harmless gases:

    2CO(g) + 2NO(g) → 2CO2(g) + N2(g)

    How the metal surface catalyses this (adsorption of the gases, bond weakening, desorption of the products) is covered in Topic 26.

    Photochemical smog and PAN

    In sunny, still weather, oxides of nitrogen react with unburnt hydrocarbons from vehicle exhausts to form peroxyacetyl nitrate, PAN, CH3CO–O–O–NO2. PAN is a key part of photochemical smog: it irritates the eyes and lungs and damages plants. Sunlight starts the process by splitting NO2 into NO and oxygen atoms; the radicals formed react with the hydrocarbons, and the products combine with NO2.

    Acid rain

    Fossil fuels contain sulfur, which burns to sulfur dioxide. Oxides of nitrogen act as a catalyst for oxidising atmospheric sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide:

    SO2(g) + NO2(g) → SO3(g) + NO(g) NO2 oxidises SO2
    NO(g) + ½O2(g) → NO2(g) NO2 is regenerated, so it acts as a catalyst
    SO3(g) + H2O(l) → H2SO4(aq) sulfuric acid in rain

    Nitrogen dioxide also forms nitric acid directly: 4NO2(g) + O2(g) + 2H2O(l) → 4HNO3(aq).

    Acid rain damages buildings made of limestone and marble (CaCO3), corrodes metals, acidifies lakes so that fish die, and damages trees by leaching nutrients from the soil.

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    What is the role of nitrogen dioxide in the formation of acid rain from sulfur dioxide?

    1. It is a reducing agent.
    2. It is a catalyst.
    3. It is a product.
    4. It absorbs sunlight.

    NO2 oxidises SO2 to SO3 and is regenerated when NO reacts with oxygen, so it acts as a catalyst overall.

    2Paper 1 style

    Which statement explains why ammonia acts as a base?

    1. It has polar N–H bonds.
    2. It forms hydrogen bonds with water.
    3. Its nitrogen atom has a lone pair that can accept a proton.
    4. It dissolves to form NH4+ and H+ ions.

    A Brønsted–Lowry base accepts a proton, using the lone pair on nitrogen.

    3Paper 1 style

    Why is nitrogen gas, N2, very unreactive?

    1. N2 molecules are polar
    2. the N≡N triple bond has a very high bond energy
    3. nitrogen has a very high electronegativity
    4. nitrogen has a giant covalent structure

    The N≡N bond energy is 994 kJ mol−1, so a lot of energy is needed to break it. The molecule is also non-polar, so it doesn't attract electrophiles or nucleophiles.

    4Paper 1 style

    Nitrogen dioxide catalyses the oxidation of sulfur dioxide in the atmosphere. Which equation shows the step in which SO2 is oxidised?

    1. SO2 + NO2 → SO3 + NO
    2. 2NO + O2 → 2NO2
    3. SO3 + H2O → H2SO4
    4. 2SO2 + O2 → 2SO3

    NO2 oxidises SO2 and is reduced to NO. The NO is then reoxidised by oxygen (B), so NO2 is regenerated, which is why it is a catalyst. D is the overall equation.

    5Paper 1 style

    Which statement about the ammonium ion, NH4+, is correct?

    1. it is pyramidal, with bond angles of 107°
    2. it has a lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom
    3. ammonia is released when an ammonium salt is warmed with dilute acid
    4. it forms when ammonia accepts a proton, acting as a Brønsted–Lowry base

    NH3 uses its lone pair to form a dative bond to H+, so NH4+ is tetrahedral (109.5°) with no lone pair. Ammonia is released by warming with an alkali, not an acid.

    6Paper 2 style
    (a)
    Give two reasons why nitrogen gas is unreactive.
    [2]
    (b)
    Explain how nitrogen monoxide forms in a car engine, and write an equation for its removal in a catalytic converter.
    [3]
    (c)
    Describe, with equations, how nitrogen dioxide helps to convert sulfur dioxide into sulfuric acid in the atmosphere.
    [3]
    (d)
    Name the pollutant that forms when oxides of nitrogen react with unburnt hydrocarbons in sunlight.
    [1]
    • Strong N≡N triple bond (high bond energy)
    • The molecule is non-polar
    • The high temperature in the engine provides enough energy for N2 and O2 from the air to react
    • N2 + O2 → 2NO
    • 2CO + 2NO → 2CO2 + N2
    • SO2 + NO2 → SO3 + NO
    • NO + ½O2 → NO2, so NO2 is regenerated / acts as a catalyst
    • SO3 + H2O → H2SO4
    • PAN / peroxyacetyl nitrate

    Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Millions exist, but they fall into a few families, each defined by its functional group. This topic sets up the language you need for every organic topic: formulas, names, reaction types, mechanisms and isomers.

    Hydrocarbons and homologous series

    Hydrocarbon
    A compound containing carbon and hydrogen only.
    Alkane
    A saturated hydrocarbon, with only single bonds. General formula CnH2n+2 (for non-cyclic alkanes).
    Homologous series
    A family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which each member differs from the next by CH2. Members have similar chemical properties and a gradual trend in physical properties such as boiling point.
    Functional group
    The atom or group of atoms that gives a family of compounds its characteristic reactions.
    Saturated / unsaturated
    Saturated compounds have only single C–C bonds. Unsaturated compounds contain at least one C=C (or C≡C) multiple bond.

    Functional groups at AS Level

    FamilyFunctional groupName ending or prefixExample
    alkaneC–C, C–H only-anepropane, CH3CH2CH3
    alkeneC=C-enepropene, CH3CH=CH2
    halogenoalkaneC–X (X = F, Cl, Br, I)fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-bromoethane, CH3CH2Br

    Types of formula

    FormulaShowsButan-1-ol
    molecularthe number of each type of atomC4H10O
    empiricalthe simplest whole-number ratioC4H10O
    generalthe formula for a whole seriesCnH2n+1OH
    structuralthe arrangement of atoms, without drawing every bondCH3CH2CH2CH2OH
    displayedevery atom and every bondsee below
    skeletalthe carbon skeleton as zig-zag lines; C atoms at the corners and ends, H atoms on carbon not shown, functional groups drawn in fullsee below

    Naming organic compounds

    1. Find the longest carbon chain containing the functional group. Its length gives the stem: meth (1), eth (2), prop (3), but (4), pent (5), hex (6).
    2. Add the suffix for the main functional group (-ane, -ene, -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid, -nitrile, -amine).
    3. Number the chain so that the functional group (or the first branch) gets the lowest number.
    4. Add prefixes for branches and halogens in alphabetical order, with position numbers: methyl, ethyl, bromo, chloro. Use di-, tri- for repeats (these don't count for alphabetical order).
    StructureNameWhy
    CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH32-methylbutanelongest chain 4 C; methyl on C2
    CH2=CHCH2CH3but-1-eneC=C starts at C1
    CH3CHBrCH32-bromopropaneBr on the middle carbon
    CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3butan-2-olsecondary alcohol, OH on C2
    CH3CH2CHOpropanalthe aldehyde C is always C1, so no number is needed
    CH3COCH2CH3butanonethe C=O can only be at C2 in a 4-carbon ketone
    CH2ClCH2Cl1,2-dichloroethanetwo Cl atoms, one on each carbon
    (CH3)2C(OH)CH32-methylpropan-2-oltertiary alcohol
    CH3CH2CNpropanenitrilethe carbon of C≡N is counted in the chain

    Characteristic organic reactions

    How bonds break

    Homolytic fission
    A covalent bond breaks so that each atom takes one electron of the shared pair, forming two free radicals: Cl–Cl → Cl• + Cl•.
    Heterolytic fission
    A covalent bond breaks so that one atom takes both electrons, forming a positive ion and a negative ion: H–Br → H+ + Br−.

    Attacking species

    Nucleophile
    An electron-pair donor. It is attracted to a δ+ or positive carbon. Examples: OH−, CN−, NH3, H2O.
    Electrophile
    An electron-pair acceptor. It is attracted to an electron-rich region such as a C=C. Examples: H+, Br+ (from a polarised Br2), NO2+.
    Free radical
    A species with an unpaired electron, such as Cl• or CH3•.

    Types of reaction

    TypeWhat happensExample
    additiontwo molecules join to make oneC2H4 + Br2 → C2H4Br2
    substitutionone atom or group is replaced by anotherCH3CH2Br + OH− → CH3CH2OH + Br−
    eliminationa small molecule is removed from a larger one, often forming a C=CCH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O
    hydrolysisa compound is broken down by reaction with water (or OH− or H+)ester + water → acid + alcohol
    condensationtwo molecules join, losing a small molecule such as wateracid + alcohol → ester + water
    oxidationgain of O or loss of H, shown by [O]CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O
    reductiongain of H or loss of O, shown by [H]CH3CHO + 2[H] → CH3CH2OH

    Mechanisms and curly arrows

    A mechanism shows how a reaction happens, step by step. A curly arrow shows the movement of a pair of electrons. It must start from a lone pair or a bond, and point to where the electrons end up: an atom (forming a bond) or another atom (when a bond breaks). The four mechanisms at AS Level are:

    • free-radical substitution: alkanes with halogens (Topic 14)
    • electrophilic addition: alkenes (Topic 14)
    • nucleophilic substitution: halogenoalkanes (Topic 15)
    • nucleophilic addition: aldehydes and ketones (Topic 17)

    Shapes of organic molecules

    Carbon chains can be straight, branched or cyclic. The shape around each carbon depends on its bonds (Topic 3):

    Carbon atomHybridisationShape and angleExample
    four single bondssp3tetrahedral, 109.5°every C in an alkane
    one double bond (3 σ + 1 π)sp2trigonal planar, 120°the C atoms of C=C and C=O
    one triple bond (2 σ + 2 π)splinear, 180°the C of C≡N

    Atoms attached directly to a C=C double bond lie in the same plane as the two carbons: ethene is a planar molecule. Because the π bond prevents rotation about C=C, groups attached to each end are locked in place.

    Isomerism

    Structural isomers
    Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulas.
    Stereoisomers
    Compounds with the same structural formula but a different arrangement of atoms in space.

    Structural isomerism

    • Chain isomers have different carbon skeletons (straight or branched).
    • Positional isomers have the same functional group at different positions on the chain.
    • Functional group isomers have different functional groups, for example an aldehyde and a ketone, or an alcohol and an ether.

    Geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism

    Geometrical isomerism happens when there is restricted rotation about a C=C double bond (because of the π bond) and each carbon of the C=C has two different groups attached. In the cis isomer the two similar groups are on the same side; in the trans isomer they are on opposite sides.

    Optical isomerism

    A chiral centre is a carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups. A molecule with one chiral centre exists as two optical isomers (enantiomers): non-superimposable mirror images of each other, like a left and a right hand.

    When you draw optical isomers, show the chiral carbon with two bonds in the plane, one wedge and one hashed bond, and draw the second isomer as a reflection of the first.

    Worked example: how many isomers?

    Deduce all the isomers of C4H9Br.

    1. Straight chain: 1-bromobutane, CH3CH2CH2CH2Br, and 2-bromobutane, CH3CHBrCH2CH3.
    2. Branched chain: 1-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH3)2CHCH2Br, and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH3)3CBr.
    3. Check for chiral centres: in 2-bromobutane, C2 carries H, Br, CH3 and C2H5, so it has two optical isomers.

    4 structural isomers, 5 isomers in total including the pair of enantiomers.

    Alkanes are fuels: unreactive apart from burning and free-radical substitution. Alkenes, with their electron-rich C=C bond, take part in a wide range of addition reactions that make them the starting point for plastics, alcohols and many other chemicals.

    Alkanes

    Making alkanes

    • Hydrogenation of alkenes: C2H4(g) + H2(g) → C2H6(g), with a Pt or Ni catalyst, heat.
    • Cracking of long-chain alkanes: breaking them into shorter alkanes and alkenes, using high temperature and a catalyst (such as aluminium oxide or zeolites), for example C10H22 → C8H18 + C2H4. Cracking matches the supply of crude oil fractions to the demand for petrol and for alkenes.

    Why alkanes are unreactive

    The C–C and C–H bonds are strong, and they are non-polar (carbon and hydrogen have similar electronegativities, 2.55 and 2.20). So there are no δ+ or δ− sites to attract nucleophiles or electrophiles. Alkanes don't react with acids, alkalis or most oxidising agents.

    Combustion

    C8H18(l) + 12½O2(g) → 8CO2(g) + 9H2O(l) complete combustion, in plenty of oxygen
    C8H18(l) + 8½O2(g) → 8CO(g) + 9H2O(l) incomplete combustion, in limited oxygen, gives carbon monoxide (and soot, C)

    Environmental consequences of burning hydrocarbons

    PollutantSourceEffect
    carbon dioxidecomplete combustiongreenhouse gas, contributes to climate change
    carbon monoxideincomplete combustiontoxic: binds to haemoglobin and reduces oxygen transport
    soot (carbon particles)incomplete combustionbreathing problems; blackens buildings
    oxides of nitrogenN2 and O2 reacting in hot enginesacid rain, photochemical smog (Topic 12)
    unburnt hydrocarbonsincomplete combustionphotochemical smog
    sulfur dioxidesulfur impurities in fuelsacid rain

    Catalytic converters remove CO, NO and unburnt hydrocarbons: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO2 + N2.

    Free-radical substitution

    In ultraviolet light, alkanes react with chlorine or bromine. For example, C2H6 + Cl2 → C2H5Cl + HCl. The mechanism has three stages:

    StageEquationsWhat happens
    InitiationCl2 → 2Cl•UV light breaks the Cl–Cl bond by homolytic fission, forming two chlorine radicals. (Cl–Cl is the weakest bond present.)
    PropagationC2H6 + Cl• → C2H5• + HCl
    C2H5• + Cl2 → C2H5Cl + Cl•    		A radical reacts with a molecule to make a new radical. The second step regenerates Cl•, so this is a chain reaction: one radical can lead to thousands of product molecules.
    TerminationCl• + Cl• → Cl2
    C2H5• + Cl• → C2H5Cl
    C2H5• + C2H5• → C4H10    		Two radicals join and the chain stops. Notice that a little butane forms.

    The reaction gives a mixture: Cl• can also attack chloroethane, giving C2H4Cl2, C2H3Cl3 and so on. Using an excess of the alkane favours the monosubstituted product.

    Alkenes

    Making alkenes

    FromReagents and conditionsExample
    halogenoalkane (elimination of HX)NaOH in ethanol, heatCH3CH2Br + NaOH → CH2=CH2 + NaBr + H2O
    alcohol (dehydration)heated Al2O3 catalyst or concentrated H2SO4 or H3PO4, heatCH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O
    long-chain alkane (cracking)high temperature, catalystC10H22 → C8H18 + C2H4

    Reactions of alkenes

    The C=C bond is a region of high electron density (the π bond), and the π electrons are exposed above and below the plane of the molecule. So alkenes attract electrophiles and undergo addition reactions, in which the π bond breaks.

    ReagentConditionsProductExample
    hydrogenPt or Ni catalyst, heatalkaneCH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3CH3
    steamH3PO4 catalyst, about 300 °C, 6 MPaalcoholCH2=CH2 + H2O → CH3CH2OH
    hydrogen halide, HX(g)room temperaturehalogenoalkaneCH2=CH2 + HBr → CH3CH2Br
    halogen, X2room temperaturedihalogenoalkaneCH2=CH2 + Br2 → CH2BrCH2Br
    cold, dilute, acidified KMnO4room temperaturediol; purple → colourlessCH2=CH2 + [O] + H2O → HOCH2CH2OH
    hot, concentrated, acidified KMnO4heatthe C=C is broken (oxidative cleavage)see below
    itselfsee Topic 20addition polymernCH2=CH2 → (CH2CH2)n
    The test for an alkene

    Shake with aqueous bromine (bromine water). An alkene turns it from orange to colourless. Alkanes don't react, so the colour stays.

    Oxidative cleavage with hot, concentrated manganate(VII)

    Hot, concentrated, acidified KMnO4 breaks the C=C completely. What forms from each end depends on what is attached to that carbon:

    End of the C=CProduct
    =CH2CO2 and H2O
    =CHRa carboxylic acid, RCOOH (via the aldehyde)
    =CR2a ketone, R2C=O

    For example, but-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH3, gives two molecules of ethanoic acid; 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2, gives propanone and carbon dioxide. Working backwards from the products tells you where the double bond was.

    Mechanism: electrophilic addition

    Bromine and ethene. As a Br2 molecule approaches the electron-rich C=C, its electrons are repelled, inducing a dipole (Brδ+–Brδ−). The π electrons attack the δ+ bromine, the Br–Br bond breaks heterolytically, and a carbocation forms. The bromide ion then attacks the positive carbon.

    Hydrogen bromide and propene. H–Br is already polar. The π bond attacks the δ+ hydrogen. Two carbocations could form, and the more stable one is formed in greater amount.

    Markovnikov addition and carbocation stability

    Alkyl groups have a positive inductive effect: they push electron density towards a neighbouring positive carbon, spreading out its charge and stabilising it. So carbocation stability is:

    tertiary (R3C+) > secondary (R2CH+) > primary (RCH2+)

    With an unsymmetrical alkene, the major product comes from the more stable carbocation. In practice: the hydrogen adds to the carbon of the C=C that already has more hydrogen atoms (Markovnikov's rule). Propene + HBr gives mainly 2-bromopropane, with a little 1-bromopropane (from the primary carbocation).

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    Which equation is a propagation step in the reaction of methane with chlorine in UV light?

    1. Cl2 → 2Cl•
    2. CH4 + Cl• → CH3• + HCl
    3. CH3• + Cl• → CH3Cl
    4. CH4 + Cl• → CH3Cl + H•

    A propagation step uses one radical and makes another. A is initiation, C is termination, and D doesn't happen (an H radical is not formed).

    2Paper 1 style

    What is the major product of the reaction between 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2, and hydrogen bromide?

    1. 1-bromo-2-methylpropane
    2. 1-bromobutane
    3. 2-bromo-2-methylpropane
    4. 1,2-dibromo-2-methylpropane

    H adds to the CH2 end, forming the tertiary carbocation (CH3)3C+, which is the most stable. Br then adds to give (CH3)3CBr.

    3Paper 1 style

    2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH3)2C=CHCH3, is heated with concentrated, acidified potassium manganate(VII). What are the organic products?

    1. propanone and ethanoic acid
    2. propanone and ethanal
    3. propanoic acid and ethanoic acid
    4. butanone and methanoic acid

    The (CH3)2C= end becomes the ketone (CH3)2C=O (propanone). The =CHCH3 end becomes ethanoic acid, because aldehydes are oxidised further under these conditions.

    4Paper 1 style

    Which reagent and conditions convert ethene into ethane-1,2-diol?

    1. steam with a phosphoric acid catalyst
    2. aqueous sodium hydroxide, heat
    3. hot, concentrated, acidified KMnO4
    4. cold, dilute, acidified KMnO4

    Cold, dilute manganate(VII) adds two OH groups across the C=C. The hot, concentrated reagent would break the molecule apart.

    • Free-radical substitution
    • Initiation: Br2 → 2Br•
    • C2H6 + Br• → C2H5• + HBr
    • C2H5• + Br2 → C2H5Br + Br•
    • Termination, e.g. C2H5• + Br• → C2H5Br or 2Br• → Br2
    • Two ethyl radicals combine in a termination step: 2C2H5• → C4H10
    • Bromine radicals also substitute H atoms in bromoethane (further substitution), giving C2H4Br2 etc.
    • Use an excess of ethane
    6Paper 2 style

    Propene reacts with hydrogen bromide to form two products. The major product is 2-bromopropane.

    (a)

    (b)
