    [1]
    • Dipole on H–Br (Hδ+, Brδ−) and a curly arrow from the C=C to the H
    • Curly arrow from the H–Br bond to Br
    • Secondary carbocation, CH3C+HCH3, and Br− with a lone pair
    • Curly arrow from the lone pair on Br− to the positive carbon
    • The secondary carbocation is more stable than the primary one
    • Because of the positive inductive effect of two alkyl groups, which push electrons towards the positive carbon
    • Steam, H3PO4 catalyst (high temperature and pressure)

    The polar C–X bond makes halogenoalkanes useful starting materials: nucleophiles replace the halogen to make alcohols, nitriles and amines, while a base in ethanol removes HX to make alkenes. How fast they react depends on whether they are primary, secondary or tertiary, and on the halogen.

    Making halogenoalkanes

    FromReagents and conditionsExample
    alkaneCl2 or Br2, UV light (free-radical substitution)C2H6 + Cl2 → C2H5Cl + HCl
    alkeneHX(g) or X2, room temperature (electrophilic addition)CH2=CH2 + HBr → CH3CH2Br
    alcohol (substitution of OH)HX(g)CH3CH2OH + HBr → CH3CH2Br + H2O
    KCl (or KBr) and concentrated H2SO4 or H3PO4, which make HX in the flaskKBr + H2SO4 → KHSO4 + HBr, then as above
    PCl3 and heat3CH3CH2OH + PCl3 → 3CH3CH2Cl + H3PO3
    PCl5, room temperatureCH3CH2OH + PCl5 → CH3CH2Cl + POCl3 + HCl (steamy fumes of HCl: a test for OH)
    SOCl2CH3CH2OH + SOCl2 → CH3CH2Cl + SO2 + HCl (both by-products are gases, so the product is easy to separate)

    Primary, secondary and tertiary

    A halogenoalkane is classified by the number of alkyl groups attached to the carbon that carries the halogen: primary (one, e.g. 1-bromobutane), secondary (two, e.g. 2-bromobutane) or tertiary (three, e.g. 2-bromo-2-methylpropane).

    Nucleophilic substitution

    Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polar: Cδ+–Xδ−. A nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbon and replaces the halogen, which leaves as a halide ion.

    NucleophileReagents and conditionsProductEquation
    OH−NaOH(aq), heat under refluxalcoholCH3CH2Br + NaOH → CH3CH2OH + NaBr
    CN−KCN in ethanol, heat under refluxnitrile (one more carbon in the chain)CH3CH2Br + KCN → CH3CH2CN + KBr
    NH3NH3 in ethanol, heat in a sealed tube (under pressure)primary amineCH3CH2Br + 2NH3 → CH3CH2NH2 + NH4Br
    H2OAgNO3(aq) in ethanol, warmalcohol; the halide forms a silver halide precipitateCH3CH2Br + H2O → CH3CH2OH + H+ + Br−, then Ag+ + Br− → AgBr
    • Heating with ammonia uses an excess of ammonia, because the amine product is also a nucleophile and could react further with the halogenoalkane.
    • The reaction with KCN is useful in synthesis because it lengthens the carbon chain by one. The nitrile can then be hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid (Topic 19).

    Mechanisms: SN2 and SN1

    SN2 (substitution, nucleophilic, bimolecular) happens mainly with primary halogenoalkanes. It is one step: the nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbon from the side opposite the halogen as the C–X bond breaks. In the middle there is a transition state in which the carbon is partly bonded to both.

    SN1 (substitution, nucleophilic, unimolecular) happens mainly with tertiary halogenoalkanes. It is two steps: first the C–X bond breaks heterolytically to form a carbocation (slow), then the nucleophile attacks it (fast).

    Why tertiary favours SN1

    The tertiary carbocation is stabilised by the positive inductive effect of three alkyl groups. Also, the three bulky groups get in the way of a nucleophile approaching the carbon (steric hindrance), which blocks SN2.

    Why primary favours SN2

    A primary carbocation would be very unstable (only one alkyl group), so SN1 is unlikely. The carbon is easy to reach, so SN2 is fast.

    Secondary halogenoalkanes react by a mixture of the two mechanisms.

    Elimination

    With NaOH in ethanol, heated, the hydroxide ion acts as a base rather than a nucleophile. It removes an H from the carbon next to the C–X, and HX is eliminated, forming an alkene:

    CH3CH2Br + NaOH → CH2=CH2 + NaBr + H2O bromoethane → ethene. 2-Bromobutane gives a mixture of but-1-ene and cis- and trans-but-2-ene.
    Same reagent, different product

    NaOH in water (aqueous) gives substitution → alcohol. NaOH in ethanol (ethanolic) gives elimination → alkene. Always state the solvent.

    Reactivity and the C–X bond

    Warming each halogenoalkane with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol shows how fast it hydrolyses, because the halide ions released form a precipitate.

    HalogenoalkanePrecipitateTime for precipitateC–X bond energy / kJ mol−1
    1-chlorobutanewhite AgClslowest (may need several minutes or more)C–Cl 340
    1-bromobutanecream AgBrmoderateC–Br 280
    1-iodobutaneyellow AgIfastestC–I 240

    The C–Cl bond is the most polar, so you might expect it to react fastest. In fact the bond strength decides the rate: the C–I bond is the weakest, so it breaks most easily and iodoalkanes are the most reactive. (C–F is so strong that fluoroalkanes hardly react at all.)

    The same test also identifies the halogen from the colour of the precipitate.

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    Which reagent and conditions convert 1-bromopropane into butanenitrile?

    1. HCN, room temperature
    2. KCN in water, room temperature
    3. KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux
    4. NH3 in ethanol, heat under pressure

    Cyanide ions in ethanol, heated, substitute for Br, adding one carbon: CH3CH2CH2Br + CN− → CH3CH2CH2CN + Br−, butanenitrile.

    2Paper 1 style

    Which halogenoalkane gives a precipitate most quickly when warmed with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol?

    1. 2-iodo-2-methylpropane
    2. 2-chloro-2-methylpropane
    3. 1-chlorobutane
    4. 1-bromobutane

    Iodo-compounds are fastest because C–I is the weakest bond, and tertiary halogenoalkanes react quickly through the stable tertiary carbocation.

    3Paper 1 style

    Which statement about the SN1 hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is correct?

    1. It takes place in one step.
    2. The hydroxide ion attacks the carbon at the same time as the C–Br bond breaks.
    3. A transition state with five groups around carbon is formed.
    4. The intermediate is stabilised by the inductive effect of three methyl groups.

    SN1 goes via a tertiary carbocation, which is stabilised by electron donation from the three methyl groups. A, B and C describe SN2.

    4Paper 2 style

    Bromoethane reacts with sodium hydroxide in two different ways, depending on the conditions.

    (a)
    Give the conditions and name the organic product for each reaction. Name the type of reaction in each case.
    [4]
    (b)
    Draw the mechanism of the substitution reaction. Show the transition state.
    [3]
    (c)
    Explain why 2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts with aqueous NaOH by a different mechanism.
    [2]
    • Aqueous NaOH, heat under reflux
    • Ethanol; nucleophilic substitution
    • NaOH in ethanol, heat
    • Ethene; elimination
    • Cδ+–Brδ− dipole and a curly arrow from a lone pair on OH− to the carbon
    • Curly arrow from the C–Br bond to Br
    • Transition state [HO···C···Br]− with partial bonds, then ethanol and Br−
    • It is tertiary: it forms a stable tertiary carbocation (SN1)
    • Three bulky methyl groups hinder attack by OH− on the carbon (so SN2 is blocked)

    Alcohols are the hub of AS organic chemistry: they are made from alkenes, halogenoalkanes, carbonyl compounds and esters, and they turn into halogenoalkanes, alkenes, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and esters. Whether an alcohol is primary, secondary or tertiary decides how it oxidises.

    Making alcohols

    FromReagents and conditionsExample
    alkenesteam, H3PO4 catalyst (electrophilic addition)CH2=CH2 + H2O → CH3CH2OH
    alkenecold, dilute, acidified KMnO4CH2=CH2 + [O] + H2O → HOCH2CH2OH
    halogenoalkaneNaOH(aq), heat (nucleophilic substitution)CH3CH2Br + OH− → CH3CH2OH + Br−
    aldehyde or ketoneNaBH4 or LiAlH4 (reduction)CH3COCH3 + 2[H] → CH3CH(OH)CH3
    carboxylic acidLiAlH4 (reduction)CH3COOH + 4[H] → CH3CH2OH + H2O
    esterdilute acid or dilute alkali, heat (hydrolysis)CH3COOCH2CH3 + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + CH3CH2OH

    Classifying alcohols

    An alcohol is primary if the carbon carrying the OH has one alkyl group (e.g. ethanol, CH3CH2OH), secondary if it has two (e.g. propan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH3) and tertiary if it has three (e.g. 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH3)3COH). Molecules with more than one OH group are classified one OH at a time: propane-1,2-diol, CH3CH(OH)CH2OH, has one primary and one secondary OH.

    Reactions of alcohols

    ReactionReagents and conditionsExample
    combustionburn in oxygenC2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O
    substitution → halogenoalkaneHX, KX + conc. H2SO4, PCl3 + heat, PCl5 or SOCl2 (see Topic 15)C2H5OH + PCl5 → C2H5Cl + POCl3 + HCl
    with sodiumNa(s), room temperature2C2H5OH + 2Na → 2C2H5O−Na+ + H2; fizzing, less vigorous than sodium with water. Sodium ethoxide forms.
    oxidationacidified K2Cr2O7 or acidified KMnO4, heatsee below
    dehydration → alkeneheated Al2O3 or conc. H2SO4 or H3PO4, heatCH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O
    esterificationcarboxylic acid, conc. H2SO4 catalyst, warmCH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O

    Oxidation

    The usual oxidising agent is potassium dichromate(VI) acidified with dilute sulfuric acid. When it oxidises an alcohol, its colour changes from orange (Cr2O72−) to green (Cr3+). Acidified manganate(VII) also works (purple to colourless).

    AlcoholProductConditionsColour change with Cr2O72−/H+
    primaryaldehyde: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2Oheat and distil off the aldehyde as it forms (it has a lower boiling point than the alcohol), so it isn't oxidised furtherorange → green
    primarycarboxylic acid: CH3CH2OH + 2[O] → CH3COOH + H2Oexcess oxidising agent, heat under reflux, so the aldehyde can't escape and is oxidised furtherorange → green
    secondaryketone: CH3CH(OH)CH3 + [O] → CH3COCH3 + H2Oheat (under reflux or with distillation)orange → green
    tertiaryno reactionheatstays orange

    Tertiary alcohols are not oxidised because the carbon carrying the OH has no hydrogen atom to lose. This colour change is a test that distinguishes tertiary alcohols from primary and secondary ones.

    Distillation

    The vapour leaves the flask, is cooled in a condenser and collected. Used to remove a volatile product (an aldehyde) as soon as it forms.

    Reflux

    A vertical condenser returns the vapour to the flask, so the mixture can be heated for a long time without losing volatile substances. Used to make the reaction go to completion.

    The tri-iodomethane (iodoform) test

    Warm the compound with alkaline aqueous iodine (iodine and NaOH). A pale yellow precipitate of tri-iodomethane, CHI3 (with an antiseptic smell), shows that the compound contains the group CH3CH(OH)–. The rest of the molecule ends up as a carboxylate ion, RCO2−.

    Positive: ethanol (the only primary alcohol to give it), propan-2-ol, butan-2-ol. Negative: methanol, propan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Ethanal and methyl ketones (CH3CO–) also give a positive result (Topic 17), because the iodine first oxidises CH3CH(OH)– to CH3CO–.

    Acidity: why alcohols are weaker acids than water

    Alcohols can lose the H of the OH group, as their reaction with sodium shows, but they are even weaker acids than water. The alkyl group has a positive inductive effect: it pushes electron density onto the oxygen of the alkoxide ion, RO−. This intensifies the negative charge, making RO− less stable than OH− and more likely to take back a proton.

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    Which alcohol gives a positive result with both acidified potassium dichromate(VI) and alkaline aqueous iodine?

    1. propan-1-ol
    2. butan-2-ol
    3. 2-methylpropan-2-ol
    4. methanol

    Butan-2-ol is secondary (oxidised: orange to green) and contains CH3CH(OH)– (iodoform positive). Propan-1-ol and methanol lack the CH3CH(OH)– group; 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary.

    2Paper 1 style

    Which conditions convert propan-1-ol into propanal?

    1. acidified K2Cr2O7, heat and distil the product off immediately
    2. acidified K2Cr2O7 in excess, heat under reflux
    3. NaBH4
    4. concentrated H2SO4, heat

    Distilling the aldehyde off as it forms stops it being oxidised further to propanoic acid (which is what B gives). D would dehydrate the alcohol to propene.

    3Paper 1 style

    Which alcohol gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine and is oxidised to a ketone by acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?

    1. ethanol
    2. propan-2-ol
    3. 2-methylpropan-2-ol
    4. propan-1-ol

    The tri-iodomethane test needs a CH3CH(OH)– group. Propan-2-ol has one and is a secondary alcohol, so it oxidises to propanone. Ethanol gives the test but oxidises to ethanal and ethanoic acid.

    4Paper 1 style

    Butan-2-ol is heated with concentrated phosphoric acid. How many different alkenes, including stereoisomers, could form?

    1. 1
    2. 2
    3. 3
    4. 4

    Water can be lost towards C1, giving but-1-ene, or towards C3, giving but-2-ene, which exists as cis and trans isomers: 3 alkenes.

    5Quick check

    Which reagent reacts with ethanol to give hydrogen gas?

    1. sodium
    2. sodium hydroxide
    3. sodium carbonate
    4. sodium chloride

    2C2H5OH + 2Na → 2C2H5ONa + H2. Alcohols are too weakly acidic to react with NaOH or with carbonates.

    6Paper 2 and 3 style

    Three isomeric alcohols have the formula C4H10O: butan-1-ol (A), butan-2-ol (B) and 2-methylpropan-2-ol (C).

    (a)
    Classify each as primary, secondary or tertiary.
    [1]
    (b)
    Each is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Describe what you would see, and give the structural formula of any organic product formed under reflux.
    [4]
    (c)
    Which of A, B and C gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine? Explain.
    [2]
    (d)
    Write an equation for the reaction of B with sodium.
    [1]
    • A primary, B secondary, C tertiary
    • A and B: orange to green; C: stays orange
    • A gives butanoic acid, CH3CH2CH2COOH
    • B gives butanone, CH3COCH2CH3
    • C: no reaction, because there is no H on the carbon bearing the OH
    • B
    • It contains the CH3CH(OH)– group
    • 2CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 + 2Na → 2CH3CH(O−Na+)CH2CH3 + H2

    Aldehydes and ketones both contain the C=O carbonyl group. They are made by oxidising alcohols, reduced back to alcohols, and attacked by nucleophiles. A set of simple test-tube tests identifies them and tells them apart.

    Structure and naming

    In an aldehyde the C=O is at the end of the chain, with an H attached: –CHO (e.g. ethanal, CH3CHO; propanal, CH3CH2CHO). In a ketone the C=O is within the chain, with two carbon groups attached: C–CO–C (e.g. propanone, CH3COCH3; butanone, CH3COCH2CH3).

    The C=O bond is polar: Cδ+=Oδ−. The δ+ carbon attracts nucleophiles.

    Making aldehydes and ketones

    ProductFromReagents and conditions
    aldehydeprimary alcoholacidified K2Cr2O7 (or KMnO4), heat, distil the aldehyde off
    ketonesecondary alcoholacidified K2Cr2O7 (or KMnO4), heat (with distillation)

    Reactions

    Reduction to alcohols

    Reducing agents: NaBH4 (sodium tetrahydridoborate, in water or ethanol) or LiAlH4 (lithium tetrahydridoaluminate, in dry ether).

    CH3CHO + 2[H] → CH3CH2OH aldehydes give primary alcohols
    CH3COCH3 + 2[H] → CH3CH(OH)CH3 ketones give secondary alcohols

    Addition of hydrogen cyanide

    With HCN, a KCN catalyst, and heat, aldehydes and ketones form hydroxynitriles, adding a carbon to the chain:

    CH3CHO + HCN → CH3CH(OH)CN ethanal → 2-hydroxypropanenitrile
    CH3COCH3 + HCN → (CH3)2C(OH)CN propanone → 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile

    Mechanism: nucleophilic addition

    The KCN provides cyanide ions, the nucleophile. CN− attacks the δ+ carbon of C=O, and the π electrons move onto the oxygen. The negatively charged oxygen in the intermediate then takes a proton from an HCN molecule, which regenerates CN−. That is why KCN acts as a catalyst.

    The product from ethanal has a chiral centre. The C=O group is planar, so CN− is equally likely to attack from above or below: the product is a 50 : 50 mixture of the two optical isomers (a racemic mixture, Topic 29).

    Tests for carbonyl compounds

    TestReagent and methodAldehydeKetone
    any C=O2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH)orange (or yellow-orange) precipitate with both. The melting point of the purified precipitate can identify the compound.
    Tollens'ammoniacal silver nitrate, [Ag(NH3)2]+, warmsilver mirror (or grey-black precipitate): Ag+ reduced to Agno change
    Fehling'sFehling's solution (Cu2+ complex in alkali), warmblue solution → brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide, Cu2Ostays blue
    dichromateacidified K2Cr2O7, warmorange → greenstays orange
    tri-iodomethanealkaline I2(aq), warmpale yellow precipitate of CHI3 for ethanal and any methyl ketone, CH3CO– (e.g. propanone, butanone)

    Aldehydes are distinguished from ketones because aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids (they still have an H on the carbonyl carbon). Ketones are not, so they don't reduce Tollens', Fehling's or dichromate.

    RCHO + [O] → RCOOH in Tollens' (alkaline) the acid forms as RCOO−

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    A compound gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH and a yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine, but does not react with Tollens' reagent. What could it be?

    1. ethanal
    2. propanal
    3. butanone
    4. pentan-3-one

    2,4-DNPH: a carbonyl. No silver mirror: a ketone. Iodoform positive: a methyl ketone, CH3CO–. Butanone fits; pentan-3-one is not a methyl ketone.

    2Paper 1 style

    What is the product when propanone reacts with HCN in the presence of KCN?

    1. CH3CH2CH2CN
    2. (CH3)2C(OH)CN
    3. CH3COCH2CN
    4. (CH3)2CHCN

    CN adds to the carbonyl carbon and H adds to the oxygen, giving 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile.

    3Paper 1 style

    Which reagent gives an orange precipitate with both propanal and propanone?

    1. Tollens' reagent
    2. Fehling's solution
    3. 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine
    4. acidified potassium dichromate(VI)

    2,4-DNPH reacts with the C=O group of any aldehyde or ketone. Tollens', Fehling's and dichromate(VI) react only with the aldehyde.

    4Paper 1 style

    Hydrogen cyanide, with a little KCN, reacts with ethanal. Why is the product, 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, optically inactive?

    1. the product has no chiral centre
    2. the CN− ion attacks the planar C=O group equally from either side, giving a racemic mixture
    3. the reaction goes by an SN1 mechanism
    4. the product is rapidly hydrolysed

    The product does have a chiral carbon. Because the carbonyl group is planar, attack from above and below is equally likely, so equal amounts of the two enantiomers form and their effects on plane-polarised light cancel.

    5Quick check

    What forms when butanone is reduced by NaBH4?

    1. butanal
    2. butan-1-ol
    3. butanoic acid
    4. butan-2-ol

    Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols: CH3COCH2CH3 + 2[H] → CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3.

    6Paper 2 style

    Butanal and butanone are isomers with formula C4H8O.

    (a)
    Describe a chemical test that gives a positive result for both compounds, and one that distinguishes them. Give the observations.
    [3]
    (b)
    Name the product formed when butanone is reduced with NaBH4, and classify it.
    [2]
    (c)
    Describe the mechanism of the reaction between butanal and HCN, with KCN as catalyst. Explain why KCN is described as a catalyst.
    [4]
    • 2,4-DNPH: orange precipitate with both
    • Tollens' reagent, warm (or Fehling's, or acidified dichromate)
    • Butanal gives a silver mirror (brick-red precipitate / orange to green); butanone: no change
    • Butan-2-ol
    • Secondary alcohol
    • Dipole on C=O, and a curly arrow from the lone pair on C of CN− to the carbonyl C
    • Curly arrow from the C=O π bond to O, giving the alkoxide intermediate
    • Curly arrow from O− to H of HCN, and from the H–C bond to C, giving CH3CH2CH2CH(OH)CN
    • CN− is used in the first step and regenerated in the second

    Carboxylic acids contain the –COOH group. They are weak acids, so they show all the typical reactions of acids, and they react with alcohols to make esters, the compounds behind many fruity smells and flavours.

    Carboxylic acids

    The functional group is the carboxyl group, –COOH. Names end in -oic acid: methanoic acid HCOOH, ethanoic acid CH3COOH, propanoic acid CH3CH2COOH. They are weak acids: CH3COOH(aq) ⇌ CH3COO−(aq) + H+(aq).

    Making carboxylic acids

    FromReagents and conditionsExample
    primary alcohol or aldehydeacidified K2Cr2O7 or KMnO4, heat under refluxCH3CH2OH + 2[O] → CH3COOH + H2O
    nitriledilute acid, heat under refluxCH3CH2CN + 2H2O + H+ → CH3CH2COOH + NH4+
    nitriledilute alkali, heat under reflux, then acidifyCH3CH2CN + OH− + H2O → CH3CH2COO− + NH3, then CH3CH2COO− + H+ → CH3CH2COOH
    esterdilute acid or alkali, heat (then acidify if alkali was used)CH3COOC2H5 + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + C2H5OH

    Reactions of carboxylic acids

    ReactantProductsExample
    reactive metalsalt + hydrogen2CH3COOH + Mg → (CH3COO)2Mg + H2
    alkalisalt + water (neutralisation)CH3COOH + NaOH → CH3COONa + H2O
    carbonatesalt + water + carbon dioxide2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 → 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2
    alcoholester + water (conc. H2SO4 catalyst, warm)CH3COOH + CH3OH ⇌ CH3COOCH3 + H2O
    LiAlH4primary alcohol (reduction)CH3COOH + 4[H] → CH3CH2OH + H2O

    Fizzing with a carbonate or hydrogencarbonate is the test for a carboxylic acid: alcohols and phenols don't do this. The salts are named as -oates: sodium ethanoate, magnesium ethanoate.

    Esters

    Naming esters

    An ester is named from the alcohol part first (as an alkyl group) and then the acid part (as -oate). Ethanoic acid + methanol gives methyl ethanoate, CH3COOCH3. Propanoic acid + ethanol gives ethyl propanoate, CH3CH2COOCH2CH3.

    Making esters (esterification)

    Warm a carboxylic acid with an alcohol and a few drops of concentrated H2SO4 as a catalyst. This is a condensation reaction (water is lost) and it is reversible:

    CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O ethanoic acid + ethanol ⇌ ethyl ethanoate + water

    Hydrolysis of esters

    With dilute acid, heat under reflux

    The reverse of esterification. It is reversible, so it does not go to completion: CH3COOC2H5 + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + C2H5OH

    With dilute alkali (NaOH), heat under reflux

    Goes to completion, because the acid is converted into its salt, which doesn't react with the alcohol: CH3COOC2H5 + NaOH → CH3COONa + C2H5OH. Add acid afterwards to obtain the carboxylic acid.

    Esters have sweet, fruity smells, so they are used in flavourings and perfumes. They are also good solvents (ethyl ethanoate is used in nail varnish remover and glues).

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    What is the name of CH3CH2COOCH3?

    1. ethyl ethanoate
    2. propyl methanoate
    3. ethyl methanoate
    4. methyl propanoate

    The acid part, CH3CH2COO–, comes from propanoic acid; the alcohol part, –CH3, from methanol: methyl propanoate.

    2Paper 1 style

    Which reagent distinguishes ethanoic acid from ethanol?

    1. aqueous sodium carbonate
    2. sodium metal
    3. PCl5
    4. concentrated sulfuric acid

    Only the acid fizzes with sodium carbonate (giving CO2). Both compounds react with Na and with PCl5, because both have an OH group.

    3Paper 1 style

    Which substances react with ethanoic acid to produce a gas?
    1 sodium carbonate
    2 magnesium
    3 sodium hydroxide

    1. 1, 2 and 3
    2. 1 and 2 only
    3. 2 and 3 only
    4. 1 only

    Sodium carbonate gives CO2 and magnesium gives H2. Sodium hydroxide neutralises the acid, but no gas forms.

    4Paper 1 style

    Ethyl propanoate is heated under reflux with excess NaOH(aq). Which pair of products forms?

    1. propanoic acid and ethanol
    2. sodium ethanoate and propan-1-ol
    3. sodium propanoate and ethanol
    4. ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol

    Alkaline hydrolysis gives the salt of the acid part (propanoate) and the alcohol part (ethanol): CH3CH2COOC2H5 + NaOH → CH3CH2COONa + C2H5OH.

    5Paper 2 style

    Propyl ethanoate is used as a flavouring.

    (a)
    Give the structural formulas of the acid and the alcohol needed to make it, and the conditions.
    [3]
    (b)
    Write an equation for the hydrolysis of propyl ethanoate with aqueous sodium hydroxide, and explain why alkaline hydrolysis goes to completion but acid hydrolysis does not.
    [3]
    (c)
    Ethanoic acid can be made from ethanenitrile. Give the reagents and conditions, and write an equation.
    [2]
    • CH3COOH
    • CH3CH2CH2OH
    • Concentrated H2SO4 catalyst, warm
    • CH3COOCH2CH2CH3 + NaOH → CH3COONa + CH3CH2CH2OH
    • Acid hydrolysis is reversible / an equilibrium
    • In alkali the carboxylic acid is removed as its salt (carboxylate ion), which can't react with the alcohol
    • Dilute HCl (or H2SO4), heat under reflux
    • CH3CN + 2H2O + H+ → CH3COOH + NH4+

    At AS Level you need to know how to make primary amines, nitriles and hydroxynitriles, and how to turn nitriles into carboxylic acids. Nitriles are especially useful because making them adds a carbon atom to the chain.

    Primary amines

    A primary amine has an –NH2 group attached to a carbon chain, for example ethylamine, CH3CH2NH2. It forms when a halogenoalkane is heated with ammonia in ethanol, in a sealed tube (under pressure):

    CH3CH2Br + 2NH3 → CH3CH2NH2 + NH4Br

    An excess of ammonia is used. The amine product has a lone pair on N, so it is itself a nucleophile and could react with more halogenoalkane to form secondary and tertiary amines. (Classifying amines and their basicity come at A Level, Topic 34.)

    Nitriles

    Nitriles contain the –C≡N group. They are named from the total number of carbon atoms, including the carbon of C≡N: CH3CN is ethanenitrile and CH3CH2CN is propanenitrile.

    MakingReagents and conditionsExample
    nitrile from a halogenoalkaneKCN in ethanol, heat under refluxCH3CH2Br + KCN → CH3CH2CN + KBr
    hydroxynitrile from an aldehyde or ketoneHCN, KCN catalyst, heatCH3CHO + HCN → CH3CH(OH)CN

    Hydrolysis of nitriles

    Heating a nitrile under reflux with a dilute acid or a dilute alkali hydrolyses the –C≡N to –COOH:

    CH3CH2CN + 2H2O + H+ → CH3CH2COOH + NH4+ with dilute acid, e.g. HCl(aq): the carboxylic acid forms directly
    CH3CH2CN + H2O + OH− → CH3CH2COO− + NH3 with dilute alkali, e.g. NaOH(aq): the carboxylate salt forms, and ammonia is given off. Then acidify to obtain the acid.

    Worked example: a two-step synthesis

    How can propanoic acid be made from bromoethane?

    1. Bromoethane → propanenitrile: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux. The chain grows from 2 to 3 carbons.
    2. Propanenitrile → propanoic acid: dilute HCl, heat under reflux.

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    Which compound is formed when 2-hydroxypropanenitrile is heated under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid?

    1. propanoic acid
    2. 2-hydroxypropanoic acid
    3. propan-2-ol
    4. 2-aminopropanoic acid

    Only the C≡N is hydrolysed, to COOH. The OH group is unchanged: CH3CH(OH)COOH, 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid).

    2Paper 1 style

    Ethylamine is made by heating bromoethane with ammonia in ethanol in a sealed tube. Why is excess ammonia used?

    1. ammonia is a catalyst
    2. to reduce further substitution, which would give secondary and tertiary amines
    3. to make the reaction go by an SN1 mechanism
    4. to dissolve the bromoethane

    Ethylamine is itself a nucleophile and can attack more bromoethane. A large excess of NH3 makes it much more likely that bromoethane meets an ammonia molecule instead.

    3Paper 1 style

    1-bromopropane is heated under reflux with KCN in ethanol. The organic product is then heated with dilute hydrochloric acid. What is the final organic product?

    1. propanoic acid
    2. propan-1-amine
    3. propanenitrile
    4. butanoic acid

    CN− replaces Br, giving butanenitrile, CH3CH2CH2CN (4 carbons). Acid hydrolysis turns –CN into –COOH: butanoic acid.

    4Paper 2 style
    (a)
    Give the reagents and conditions to convert 1-bromopropane into propylamine, and explain why one reagent is used in excess.
    [3]
    (b)
    Suggest a two-step synthesis of butanoic acid from 1-bromopropane. Give the reagents, conditions and intermediate.
    [3]
    • Ammonia in ethanol
    • Heat in a sealed tube / under pressure
    • Excess ammonia, to stop the amine product reacting further (forming secondary / tertiary amines)
    • Step 1: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux
    • Intermediate: butanenitrile, CH3CH2CH2CN
    • Step 2: dilute acid (HCl), heat under reflux

    Alkenes join together in long chains to form addition polymers: poly(ethene) for bags and bottles, poly(chloroethene) for window frames and pipes. You need to draw repeat units, work back to the monomer, and explain why these plastics are hard to dispose of.

    Addition polymerisation

    In addition polymerisation, many small unsaturated molecules (monomers) join together to form one very long molecule (a polymer). The π bond of each C=C opens up and the monomers link through new C–C single bonds. No other product is formed.

    nCH2=CHCl → (CH2–CHCl)n chloroethene → poly(chloroethene)

    Finding the monomer from a polymer

    Find the repeating pattern of two carbons along the main chain, draw one repeat unit, and put a C=C between those two carbons.

    Disposal of poly(alkene)s

    • Non-biodegradable: poly(alkene)s are chemically inert, like alkanes. Their C–C and C–H bonds are strong and non-polar, so microorganisms can't break them down, and they last for centuries in landfill or the sea.
    • Harmful combustion products: burning them releases energy but can produce carbon monoxide (incomplete combustion), and burning PVC releases hydrogen chloride, which is toxic and causes acid rain. Other toxic chlorinated compounds can also form.
    • Recycling and the development of degradable polymers (Topic 35) help reduce these problems.

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    What is the repeat unit of the polymer formed from but-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH3?

    1. –CH2–CH2–CH2–CH2–
    2. –CH2–CH(C2H5)–
    3. –CH(CH3)–CH(CH3)–
    4. –CH2–CH(CH3)–CH2–

    The two carbons of the C=C form the main chain; each still carries its methyl group.

    2Paper 1 style

    Which is the repeat unit of poly(propene)?

    1. –CH2–CH2–CH2–
    2. –CH2–CH(CH3)–
    3. –CH(CH3)–CH(CH3)–
    4. –CH2=C(CH3)–

    Propene is CH2=CHCH3. The C=C opens and the CH3 becomes a side group on every other carbon. No C=C bonds remain in the polymer.

    3Paper 1 style

    A polymer has the repeat unit –CH2–CHCl–. What is its monomer?

    1. chloroethane
    2. 1,2-dichloroethene
    3. chloroethene
    4. ethene

    The monomer has the same atoms with a C=C bond: CH2=CHCl, chloroethene. The polymer is PVC.

    4Quick check

    Why are poly(alkene)s difficult to dispose of?

    1. they are chemically inert, so they are non-biodegradable, and burning some of them releases toxic gases
    2. they contain reactive C=C bonds
    3. they are soluble in water
    4. they are ionic, so they have very high melting points

    Poly(alkene)s are saturated, with strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds, so microorganisms can't break them down. Burning PVC releases HCl.

    5Paper 2 style

    Poly(tetrafluoroethene), PTFE, is made from tetrafluoroethene, CF2=CF2.

    (a)
    Draw the repeat unit of PTFE.
    [1]
    (b)
    Explain why poly(alkene)s such as poly(ethene) are not biodegradable.
    [2]
    (c)
    Suggest why burning waste PVC is a particular problem.
    [1]
    • –CF2–CF2– drawn with C–C single bond, four F atoms and continuation bonds through brackets
    • They are saturated / have strong C–C and C–H bonds
    • The bonds are non-polar, so they are unreactive and can't be broken down by microorganisms (enzymes)
    • It produces toxic hydrogen chloride (which also causes acid rain)

    Synthesis questions ask you to plan a route from one compound to another using the reactions in Topics 13 to 20, or to identify the functional groups in an unfamiliar molecule and predict how it reacts. The key is knowing which reagent turns each functional group into which other.

    The AS reaction map

    Choose a functional group to see every way to make it and everything it can be turned into, with reagents and conditions.

    Planning a route

    1. Compare the start and target: has the number of carbons changed? Which functional groups are lost and which are gained?
    2. Need an extra carbon? Use a cyanide: halogenoalkane + KCN, or aldehyde/ketone + HCN. Then hydrolyse or reduce the nitrile.
    3. Work backwards from the target: what can make it? Can that be made from the starting material?
    4. Give full conditions for each step: reagent, solvent, catalyst, temperature (heat, reflux, distil, UV light).

    Worked example 1

    Suggest how to make ethanoic acid from ethene in two steps.

    1. Ethene → ethanol: steam, H3PO4 catalyst
    2. Ethanol → ethanoic acid: acidified K2Cr2O7, heat under reflux

    Worked example 2

    Suggest a three-step route from propene to 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile, (CH3)2C(OH)CN.

    1. Propene → propan-2-ol: steam, H3PO4 catalyst (OH goes on the middle carbon, Markovnikov)
    2. Propan-2-ol → propanone: acidified K2Cr2O7, heat
    3. Propanone → product: HCN with KCN catalyst

    Worked example 3: a molecule with several groups

    Predict what happens when HOCH2CH2CHO (3-hydroxypropanal) reacts with (a) excess acidified dichromate under reflux, (b) NaBH4, (c) Tollens' reagent.

    1. Both the primary OH and the CHO are oxidised to COOH: HOOCCH2COOH (propanedioic acid).
    2. Only the CHO is reduced: HOCH2CH2CH2OH (propane-1,3-diol).
    3. Silver mirror; the CHO is oxidised (to –COO−); the OH is unchanged.

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    Which two-step route converts ethene into ethanoic acid?

    1. steam with H3PO4 catalyst; then acidified K2Cr2O7, heat under reflux
    2. HBr; then KCN in ethanol
    3. H2 with Ni; then Cl2 in UV light
    4. cold, dilute, acidified KMnO4; then NaOH(aq)

    Hydration gives ethanol, and refluxing with excess acidified dichromate(VI) oxidises it fully to ethanoic acid. Route B gives propanenitrile; route D gives a diol.

    2Paper 1 style

    Which is the best way to convert bromoethane into propanoic acid?

    1. NaOH(aq); then acidified K2Cr2O7 under reflux
    2. KCN in ethanol; then heat with dilute HCl
    3. excess NH3 in ethanol; then dilute HCl
    4. NaOH in ethanol; then steam with H3PO4

    Propanoic acid has 3 carbons and bromoethane 2, so a carbon must be added: substitution by CN−, then hydrolysis of the nitrile. Route A gives ethanoic acid.

    3Paper 1 style

    A compound decolourises bromine water and fizzes with sodium carbonate solution. Which could it be?

    1. CH3CH2COOH
    2. CH2=CHCH2OH
    3. CH2=CHCOOH
    4. CH3COOCH=CH2

    Decolourising bromine water shows a C=C bond; fizzing with a carbonate shows a carboxylic acid. Only propenoic acid has both.

    4Paper 2 style
    (a)
    Suggest a three-step synthesis of propanoic acid from ethene. Give reagents and conditions for each step, and name the intermediates.
    [4]
    (b)
    The compound CH2=CHCH2OH is treated with (i) bromine dissolved in hexane and (ii) acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heated under reflux. Give the structural formula of each product.
    [2]
    • Ethene + HBr (room temperature) → bromoethane
    • Bromoethane + KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux → propanenitrile
    • Propanenitrile + dilute HCl, heat under reflux → propanoic acid
    • Intermediates named: bromoethane and propanenitrile
    • (i) CH2BrCHBrCH2OH
    • (ii) CH2=CHCOOH

    Going through ethanol doesn't help here: the chain must gain a carbon, and only the cyanide step does that.

    Infrared spectroscopy tells you which functional groups a molecule contains. Mass spectrometry tells you its relative molecular mass, how many carbon atoms it has, whether it contains chlorine or bromine, and which fragments it breaks into. Together they can identify an unknown compound.

    Infrared spectroscopy

    Covalent bonds vibrate (stretch and bend). Each type of bond absorbs infrared radiation at a characteristic frequency, quoted as a wavenumber in cm−1. An IR spectrum plots transmittance against wavenumber; each absorption shows as a dip (often called a peak).

    BondFound inWavenumber / cm−1Appearance
    C–Oalcohols, carboxylic acids, esters1040–1300strong
    C=Calkenes1500–1680weak to medium
    C=Oaldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, amides1640–1750strong, sharp
    C≡Nnitriles2200–2250medium, sharp
    C–Halkanes, alkenes, arenes2850–3100strong
    O–Hcarboxylic acids (hydrogen bonded)2500–3000very broad
    O–Halcohols, phenols (hydrogen bonded)3200–3600broad
    N–Hamines, amides3300–3500medium

    In the exam, use the ranges printed in the Data Booklet; they are close to these. The region below about 1500 cm−1 is the fingerprint region: it has many overlapping absorptions that are unique to each compound, so it can be matched against a database.

    Reading a spectrum

    Start above 1500 cm−1. Is there a strong C=O near 1700? A broad O–H? If both, it's a carboxylic acid; C=O without O–H suggests an aldehyde, ketone or ester. Then use other evidence (tests, mass spectrum) to decide.

    Mass spectrometry

    In a mass spectrometer, molecules are ionised and the positive ions are separated by their mass-to-charge ratio, m/e. (You don't need to know how the instrument works.) The spectrum plots relative abundance against m/e. Most ions have a charge of 1+, so m/e equals the mass of the ion.

    Elements: isotopes and relative atomic mass

    For an element, each peak is one isotope, and its height gives the isotope's relative abundance.

    Worked example

    Use the spectrum of neon to calculate its relative atomic mass.

    Ar = (20 × 90.48 + 21 × 0.27 + 22 × 9.25) ÷ 100 = 20.19, so 20.2

    Compounds: the molecular ion and fragments

    • The molecular ion, M+, is the whole molecule with one electron removed. Its m/e (the last major peak) gives the relative molecular mass.
    • Molecular ions can break apart (fragment). Only the charged fragment is detected: M+ → X+ + Y•.
    • The tallest peak is the base peak, the most abundant ion, given 100%.
    m/e15172931434577
    Possible fragmentCH3+OH+C2H5+ or CHO+CH2OH+C3H7+ or CH3CO+COOH+C6H5+

    The [M+1] peak: counting carbon atoms

    About 1.1% of carbon atoms are 13C. So a small peak appears one unit above the molecular ion, and its height depends on the number of carbon atoms, n:

    Number of carbon atomsn = 100 × abundance of [M + 1]+1.1 × abundance of M+Learn it

    Worked example

    A compound has its M+ peak at m/e 72 with a relative abundance of 40.0, and an [M+1]+ peak with an abundance of 1.76.

    1. n = 100 × 1.761.1 × 40.0 = 4.0, so 4 carbon atoms.
    2. 4 C account for 48 of the 72 mass units. The remaining 24 could be H8O (8 + 16 = 24), giving C4H8O: for example, butanone or butanal.

    The [M+2] peak: chlorine and bromine

    HalogenIsotopesPattern
    one Cl atom35Cl : 37Cl ≈ 3 : 1M+ and [M+2]+ peaks in the ratio 3 : 1
    one Br atom79Br : 81Br ≈ 1 : 1M+ and [M+2]+ peaks of about equal height

    Questions

    1Paper 1 style

    The IR spectrum of a compound has a strong absorption at 1715 cm−1 and no broad absorption above 2500 cm−1. Which compound could it be?

    1. propan-1-ol
    2. butanone
    3. propanoic acid
    4. but-1-ene

    1715 cm−1 is C=O. No O–H rules out the alcohol and the acid. Butanone has C=O and no O–H.

    2Paper 1 style

    The mass spectrum of a compound has a molecular ion peak at m/e 78 and a peak at m/e 80 of one third of its height. What does the compound contain?

    1. one bromine atom
    2. two chlorine atoms
    3. one chlorine atom
    4. one bromine and one chlorine atom

    M : M+2 = 3 : 1 is the pattern for one chlorine atom. (The compound could be 2-chloropropane, C3H7Cl, Mr 78 with 35Cl.)

    3Paper 1 style

    The infrared spectrum of a compound has a very broad absorption from 2500 to 3000 cm−1 and a strong, sharp absorption at 1710 cm−1. Which compound could it be?

    1. ethanol
    2. propanone
    3. propanoic acid
    4. ethyl ethanoate

    The very broad band at 2500–3000 cm−1 is the O–H of a carboxylic acid, and 1710 cm−1 is C=O. Ethanol has no C=O; propanone and the ester have no O–H.

    4Paper 1 style

    The mass spectrum of a compound has two molecular-ion peaks, at m/e 94 and 96, of almost equal height. What is the compound?

    1. CH3Cl
    2. CH3Br
    3. CH2Cl2
    4. C2H5Br

    Equal M and M+2 peaks mean one bromine atom. CH379Br has M = 12 + 3 + 79 = 94; C2H5Br would be at 108 and 110.

    5Paper 2 style

    Compound Q contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. Its mass spectrum has the M+ peak at m/e 60 (abundance 24.0) and an [M+1]+ peak (abundance 0.53). Its IR spectrum has a very broad absorption from 2500 to 3000 cm−1 and a strong absorption at 1710 cm−1.

    (a)
    Calculate the number of carbon atoms in Q.
    [1]
    (b)
    Identify the bonds responsible for the two IR absorptions.
    [2]
    (c)
    Deduce the structural formula of Q.
    [1]
    (d)
    Suggest the formula of the fragment responsible for a peak at m/e 45, and write an equation for its formation from the molecular ion.
    [2]
    • n = 100 × 0.53 / (1.1 × 24.0) = 2.0, so 2 carbon atoms
    • 2500–3000 broad: O–H in a carboxylic acid
    • 1710: C=O
    • CH3COOH (ethanoic acid, Mr 60)
    • COOH+
    • CH3COOH+ → COOH+ + CH3•

    A Level Chemistry, built on AS

    Notes for all 15 A Level topics of the Cambridge 9701 syllabus, from Born–Haber cycles to NMR spectroscopy. Each topic has worked examples, diagrams, interactive tools and Paper 4 style questions with mark schemes. A Level questions often expect AS knowledge too, so revise both.

    Paper 4: A Level Structured Questions

    2 h100 marks38.5% of A Level

    Structured questions on the A Level topics; knowledge of the AS topics is assumed.

    Paper 5: Planning, Analysis and Evaluation

    1 h 15 min30 marks11.5% of A Level

    Planning an experiment, processing data, drawing graphs, and evaluating results and errors. May use unfamiliar contexts.

    Papers 1, 2 and 3 (the AS papers) make up the other 50% of the A Level.

    Topics

    Paper 5 skills

    Paper 5 has no practical work, but it tests the thinking behind practical work. Expect to:

    • Plan: identify the independent, dependent and control variables; describe a method with specific apparatus and quantities; explain how to make it fair and safe (with a hazard and a precaution).
    • Process data: calculate means, rates, ln values or reciprocals; give answers to a sensible number of significant figures.
    • Draw and read graphs: choose scales that use at least half the grid, plot accurately, draw a best-fit line, calculate a gradient using a large triangle, and identify anomalous points.
    • Evaluate: calculate percentage uncertainties (uncertainty ÷ reading × 100), compare them, decide whether the data support a conclusion, and suggest improvements.
    About the questions

    The questions here are written in the style of 9701 papers and test the same skills. They are not copies of official papers. For genuine past papers and mark schemes, use the Cambridge School Support Hub or ask your teacher.

    A Level energetics answers two big questions. Why do ionic compounds form, and why do some dissolve? (Lattice and hydration energies.) And will a reaction happen at all? (Entropy and Gibbs free energy.)

    New enthalpy terms

    Enthalpy change of atomisation, ΔHat
    The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state under standard conditions. Always positive. For example Na(s) → Na(g) and ½Cl2(g) → Cl(g).
    Lattice energy, ΔHlatt
    The enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions under standard conditions. Always negative (exothermic). For example Na+(g) + Cl−(g) → NaCl(s).
    First electron affinity, EA1
    The enthalpy change when one electron is added to each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms, to form one mole of gaseous 1− ions. For example Cl(g) + e− → Cl−(g), −349 kJ mol−1.
    Second electron affinity, EA2
    The enthalpy change when one electron is added to each ion in one mole of gaseous 1− ions, to form one mole of gaseous 2− ions. For example O−(g) + e− → O2−(g), +798 kJ mol−1.

    Electron affinity

    First electron affinities are usually exothermic: the incoming electron is attracted by the nucleus. The same factors as for ionisation energy apply: nuclear charge, distance from the nucleus and shielding. Second electron affinities are always endothermic, because the electron is being added to a negative ion, which repels it.

    Group 17FClBrIGroup 16OS
    EA1 / kJ mol−1−328−349−325−295EA1 / kJ mol−1−141−200
    • Down a group, EA1 becomes less exothermic: the atoms are larger and the outer shell more shielded, so the incoming electron is attracted less.
    • Fluorine and oxygen are exceptions: they are less exothermic than chlorine and sulfur. Their atoms are so small that the outer electrons are crowded together, and they repel the incoming electron strongly.
    • Group 17 vs Group 16: the halogens have more exothermic EA1 values, because they have a larger nuclear charge for the same shell.

    Born–Haber cycles

    Lattice energy can't be measured directly, so it is calculated with a Hess's law cycle, the Born–Haber cycle. One route forms the ionic solid directly from its elements (ΔHf). The other goes through gaseous atoms and then gaseous ions.

    From the cycleΔHf = ΔHat(metal) + ΣIE + ΔHat(non-metal) + ΣEA + ΔHlattLearn it

    Worked example: sodium chloride

    −411 = 107 + 496 + 122 + (−349) + ΔHlatt

    ΔHlatt = −411 − 376 = −787 kJ mol−1

    Worked example: magnesium oxide

    Data / kJ mol−1: ΔHf(MgO) −602; ΔHat(Mg) +148; IE1(Mg) +736; IE2(Mg) +1450; ΔHat(O) +249; EA1(O) −141; EA2(O) +798.

    1. Sum of the steps to the gaseous ions: 148 + 736 + 1450 + 249 − 141 + 798 = +3240
    2. ΔHlatt = −602 − 3240

    ΔHlatt(MgO) = −3842 kJ mol−1

    Note that both ionisation energies and both electron affinities are needed for 2+ and 2− ions. For MgCl2 or CaF2, the atomisation and electron affinity of the halogen must each be multiplied by 2.

    What makes a lattice energy large?

    CompoundNaClKClNaFMgCl2CaOMgO
    Lattice energy / kJ mol−1 (typical values)−787−711−918−2526−3401−3791
    • Larger ionic charge → much more exothermic lattice energy: the attraction between ions is stronger. MgO (2+, 2−) is about five times NaCl (1+, 1−).
    • Smaller ionic radius → more exothermic: the ions get closer together. NaCl > KCl (K+ is larger) and NaF > NaCl (F− is smaller); MgO > CaO.

    Experimental lattice energies (from Born–Haber cycles) can differ slightly from values calculated for a perfectly ionic model, but that comparison isn't assessed.

    Enthalpies of solution and hydration

    Enthalpy change of hydration, ΔHhyd
    The enthalpy change when one mole of a specified gaseous ion dissolves in enough water to form an infinitely dilute solution. Always exothermic. For example Na+(g) → Na+(aq).
    Enthalpy change of solution, ΔHsol
    The enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic solid dissolves in enough water to form an infinitely dilute solution. Can be exothermic or endothermic. For example NaCl(s) → Na+(aq) + Cl−(aq).
    Solution cycleΔHsol = −ΔHlatt + ΣΔHhydLearn it

    Worked example

    ΔHlatt(NaCl) = −787; ΔHhyd(Na+) = −406; ΔHhyd(Cl−) = −378 kJ mol−1.

    ΔHsol = +787 + (−406) + (−378) = +3 kJ mol−1: very slightly endothermic, which is why salt dissolving barely changes the temperature.

    Size of hydration enthalpies: smaller ions with larger charges attract the polar water molecules more strongly (δ− oxygen towards cations, δ+ hydrogen towards anions), so their hydration enthalpies are more exothermic. For example ΔHhyd: Li+ −519, Na+ −406, K+ −322 kJ mol−1, and 2+ ions are much more exothermic still.

    Entropy

    Entropy, S
    The number of possible arrangements of the particles and their energy in a given system. Units: J K−1 mol−1.

    The more ways the particles and their energy can be arranged, the more disordered the system and the higher its entropy. Systems tend to move towards higher entropy. Every substance above 0 K has a positive entropy.

    Predicting the sign of ΔS

    ChangeΔSReason
    melting, boiling, dissolving a solidpositiveparticles become freer to move, with more ways to arrange them: S(solid) < S(liquid) ≪ S(gas)
    freezing, condensing, precipitationnegativethe reverse
    increasing temperaturepositiveparticles have more energy, spread over more energy levels
    more moles of gas formed, e.g. CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g)positivegases have much higher entropy than solids or liquids
    fewer moles of gas, e.g. N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g)negative4 mol of gas become 2
    Entropy changeΔS = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants)Learn it

    Worked example

    S / J K−1 mol−1: CaCO3(s) 92.9, CaO(s) 39.7, CO2(g) 213.6.

    ΔS = (39.7 + 213.6) − 92.9 = +160.4 J K−1 mol−1. Positive, as expected, because a gas forms.

    Gibbs free energy

    Gibbs free energy changeΔG = ΔH − TΔSLearn it

    A reaction is feasible (it can happen spontaneously) when ΔG is negative. When ΔG = 0, the system is at the borderline (equilibrium).

    Watch the units

    ΔH is in kJ mol−1 but ΔS is in J K−1 mol−1. Divide ΔS by 1000 before using it, and use T in kelvin.

    Worked example: when does calcium carbonate decompose?

    For CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g), ΔH = +178 kJ mol−1 and ΔS = +160.4 J K−1 mol−1.

    1. At 298 K: ΔG = 178 − 298 × 0.1604 = +130 kJ mol−1. Positive, so not feasible at room temperature.
    2. It becomes feasible when ΔG ≤ 0, that is when T ≥ ΔH / ΔS = 178 / 0.1604

    T = 1110 K (about 837 °C). Limestone kilns run above this temperature.

    The effect of temperature on feasibility

    ΔHΔSΔG = ΔH − TΔSFeasible?
    negativepositivealways negativeat all temperatures
    positivenegativealways positivenever
    negativenegativenegative at low Tbelow T = ΔH/ΔS
    positivepositivenegative at high Tabove T = ΔH/ΔS

    Feasible doesn't mean fast. A negative ΔG says a reaction can happen, not how quickly. Diamond turning into graphite has a negative ΔG at room temperature, but the activation energy is so high that it never happens noticeably. Such systems are kinetically stable.

    Questions

    1Quick check

    Which ionic compound has the most exothermic lattice energy?

    1. NaCl
    2. MgO
    3. KBr
    4. CaO

    MgO has 2+ and 2− ions (high charge) and the small Mg2+ ion (smaller than Ca2+).

    2Quick check

    For a reaction, ΔH = −50 kJ mol−1 and ΔS = −100 J K−1 mol−1. Above which temperature does it stop being feasible?

    1. 0.5 K
    2. 200 K
    3. 500 K
    4. 5000 K

    T = ΔH/ΔS = −50 / −0.100 = 500 K. Below this, ΔG is negative.

    3Quick check

    Which change has the most negative entropy change, ΔS?

    1. H2O(l) → H2O(g)
    2. CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g)
    3. N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g)
    4. 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(l)

    In D three moles of gas become liquid (ΔS about −327 J K−1 mol−1), a bigger loss of disorder than four moles of gas becoming two in C (−199 J K−1 mol−1). A and B increase entropy.

    4Quick check

    The ions in magnesium oxide and in sodium fluoride all have the electron configuration of neon. Why is the lattice energy of MgO much more exothermic than that of NaF?

    1. Mg2+ and O2− have twice the charges of Na+ and F−
    2. Mg2+ and O2− are larger ions
    3. magnesium has a higher first ionisation energy than sodium
    4. oxygen is more electronegative than fluorine

    Lattice energy depends on the charges and radii of the ions. The radii are similar, but doubling both charges makes the attraction about four times stronger.

    5Quick check

    Which ion has the most exothermic enthalpy change of hydration?

    1. K+
    2. Na+
    3. Li+
    4. Mg2+

    Mg2+ has the highest charge and a small radius, so it attracts the δ− oxygen atoms of water molecules most strongly.

    6Paper 4 style

    Data / kJ mol−1: ΔHf(CaCl2(s)) −796; ΔHat(Ca) +178; IE1(Ca) +590; IE2(Ca) +1145; ΔHat(Cl) +122; EA1(Cl) −349.

    (a)
    Define lattice energy.
    [2]
    (b)
    Construct a Born–Haber cycle and calculate the lattice energy of calcium chloride.
    [3]
    (c)
    Suggest, with a reason, whether the lattice energy of CaBr2 is more or less exothermic than that of CaCl2.
    [2]
    • Enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound is formed
    • …from its gaseous ions (under standard conditions)
    • Correct cycle, with 2 × atomisation of Cl and 2 × EA of Cl
    • Sum to gaseous ions: 178 + 590 + 1145 + 2(122) + 2(−349) = +1459
    • ΔHlatt = −796 − 1459 = −2255 kJ mol−1
    • Less exothermic
    • Br− has a larger ionic radius than Cl−, so the ions are further apart and attract less strongly
    7Paper 4 style

    Ammonia is made by N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol−1. Standard entropies / J K−1 mol−1: N2 192, H2 131, NH3 193.

    (a)
    Explain why the entropy change for this reaction is negative, without calculation.
    [1]
    (b)
    Calculate ΔS.
    [1]
    (c)
    Calculate ΔG at 298 K and state whether the reaction is feasible.
    [2]
    (d)
    Calculate the temperature above which the reaction is no longer feasible. Suggest why the Haber process still runs at about 700 K.
    [3]
    • 4 mol of gas become 2 mol of gas, so there are fewer ways of arranging the particles
    • ΔS = 2(193) − [192 + 3(131)] = 386 − 585 = −199 J K−1 mol−1
    • ΔG = −92 − 298 × (−0.199) = −32.7 kJ mol−1
    • Negative, so feasible
    • T = 92 / 0.199 = 462 K
    • Above this, the equilibrium yield is low (ΔG positive means K < 1) but the rate is much faster
    • The high pressure and removal of ammonia push the equilibrium to the right, so a useful yield is still obtained

    Electrolysis uses electricity to drive a redox reaction; an electrochemical cell uses a redox reaction to produce electricity. Standard electrode potentials link the two, and predict which redox reactions can happen.

    Electrolysis

    In electrolysis, a direct current passes through an electrolyte (a molten or dissolved ionic compound). Positive ions move to the cathode (negative electrode), where they gain electrons (reduction). Negative ions move to the anode (positive electrode), where they lose electrons (oxidation).

    Predicting the products

    Molten compounds give the metal at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode: molten lead(II) bromide gives lead and bromine.

    Aqueous solutions also contain water, which can be reduced or oxidised instead. The product depends on the electrode potentials and on concentration:

    At the cathode

    If the metal ion has a more positive E⦵ than hydrogen (such as Cu2+, Ag+), the metal forms: Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu. Otherwise (Na, K, Mg, Al…) hydrogen forms instead: 2H2O + 2e− → H2 + 2OH− (or 2H+ + 2e− → H2 in acid).

    At an inert anode

    Iodide, bromide and concentrated chloride ions give the halogen: 2Cl− → Cl2 + 2e−. Otherwise (sulfate, nitrate, dilute chloride) oxygen forms: 4OH− → O2 + 2H2O + 4e− or 2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e−.

    ElectrolyteCathode productAnode product (inert electrodes)
    concentrated NaCl(aq)hydrogenchlorine
    dilute NaCl(aq)hydrogenmainly oxygen (some chlorine)
    CuSO4(aq)copperoxygen
    dilute H2SO4(aq)hydrogenoxygen (in a 2 : 1 volume ratio)
    KI(aq)hydrogeniodine
    CuSO4(aq) with copper electrodescopperthe copper anode dissolves: Cu → Cu2+ + 2e−

    Why concentration matters: E⦵(Cl2/Cl−) = +1.36 V and E⦵(O2/H2O) = +1.23 V are close. A high concentration of Cl− makes the Cl2/Cl− electrode potential less positive (see the Nernst equation below), so chloride is oxidised more easily than water.

    Quantitative electrolysis

    ChargeQ = ItLearn it
    Faraday constantF = LeLearn it
    Moles of electronsn(e−) = QFLearn it

    The Faraday constant is the charge on one mole of electrons: 6.02 × 1023 × 1.60 × 10−19 = 9.63 × 104 C mol−1 (the Data Booklet gives 9.65 × 104). Use the half-equation to link moles of electrons to moles of product.

    Worked example

    Copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed with a current of 0.500 A for 30.0 minutes. Calculate the mass of copper deposited and the volume of oxygen released (room conditions).

    1. Q = It = 0.500 × 30.0 × 60 = 900 C
    2. n(e−) = 900/96 500 = 9.33 × 10−3 mol
    3. Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu: n(Cu) = 4.66 × 10−3 mol, mass = 4.66 × 10−3 × 63.5 = 0.296 g
    4. 2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e−: n(O2) = 9.33 × 10−3 ÷ 4 = 2.33 × 10−3 mol, volume = 2.33 × 10−3 × 24.0 = 0.0560 dm3

    0.296 g of copper and 56.0 cm3 of oxygen

    Determining the Avogadro constant by electrolysis

    1. Weigh a clean, dry copper cathode. Set up a circuit with copper electrodes in copper(II) sulfate solution, an ammeter and a variable resistor to keep the current constant.
    2. Pass a measured current for a measured time.
    3. Remove the cathode, rinse it with water then propanone, dry and reweigh.
    4. Calculate Q = It, and moles of electrons = 2 × moles of copper. Then F = Q ÷ moles of electrons, and L = F ÷ e.

    Worked example

    A current of 0.200 A for 40.0 min increases the mass of the cathode by 0.158 g.

    1. Q = 0.200 × 2400 = 480 C
    2. n(Cu) = 0.158 / 63.5 = 2.49 × 10−3 mol, so n(e−) = 4.98 × 10−3 mol
    3. charge per mole of electrons = 480 / 4.98 × 10−3 = 9.65 × 104 C mol−1

    L = 9.65 × 104 / 1.60 × 10−19 = 6.03 × 1023 mol−1

    Standard electrode potentials

    Standard electrode potential, E⦵
    The electrode potential of a half-cell measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode, under standard conditions: 298 K, 1.00 mol dm−3 solutions, gases at 101 kPa.
    Standard cell potential, E⦵cell
    The potential difference between two half-cells under standard conditions.

    Electrode potentials are always written for the reduction half-equation, for example Cu2+(aq) + 2e− ⇌ Cu(s), E⦵ = +0.34 V.

    The standard hydrogen electrode

    The reference electrode is hydrogen gas at 101 kPa bubbling over a platinum electrode coated in platinum black, dipping into a solution with [H+] = 1.00 mol dm−3 (such as 1.00 mol dm−3 HCl), at 298 K. Its potential is defined as exactly 0.00 V.

    Measuring electrode potentials

    • A metal in contact with its ions (such as Cu in 1.00 mol dm−3 Cu2+): connect to the standard hydrogen electrode with a salt bridge and a high-resistance voltmeter.
    • Ions of the same element in two oxidation states (such as Fe3+/Fe2+): use a solution containing both ions at 1.00 mol dm−3, with an inert platinum electrode to carry the electrons.
    • A non-metal (such as Cl2/Cl−): bubble the gas at 101 kPa over a platinum electrode in a 1.00 mol dm−3 solution of its ions.

    The salt bridge (filter paper soaked in aqueous KNO3) completes the circuit by letting ions move between the half-cells, without the solutions mixing. A high-resistance voltmeter draws almost no current, so it measures the maximum potential difference.

    Half-equationE⦵ / VHalf-equationE⦵ / V
    Li+ + e− ⇌ Li−3.04Cu2+ + 2e− ⇌ Cu+0.34
    Mg2+ + 2e− ⇌ Mg−2.38I2 + 2e− ⇌ 2I−+0.54
    Zn2+ + 2e− ⇌ Zn−0.76Fe3+ + e− ⇌ Fe2++0.77
    Fe2+ + 2e− ⇌ Fe−0.44Ag+ + e− ⇌ Ag+0.80
    Pb2+ + 2e− ⇌ Pb−0.13Br2 + 2e− ⇌ 2Br−+1.07
    2H+ + 2e− ⇌ H20.00Cr2O72− + 14H+ + 6e− ⇌ 2Cr3+ + 7H2O+1.33
    Sn4+ + 2e− ⇌ Sn2++0.15Cl2 + 2e− ⇌ 2Cl−+1.36
    O2 + 4H+ + 4e− ⇌ 2H2O+1.23MnO4− + 8H+ + 5e− ⇌ Mn2+ + 4H2O+1.52
    • The more positive the E⦵, the more easily the species on the left is reduced, so the stronger the oxidising agent on the left. MnO4−/H+ and Cl2 are strong oxidising agents.
    • The more negative the E⦵, the more easily the species on the right is oxidised, so the stronger the reducing agent on the right. Li, Mg and Zn are strong reducing agents.

    Electrochemical cells

    Cell potentialEcell = E(positive electrode) − E(negative electrode)Learn it
    • The half-cell with the more positive E⦵ is the positive electrode; reduction happens there.
    • The half-cell with the more negative E⦵ is the negative electrode; oxidation happens there.
    • Electrons flow through the external circuit from negative to positive.

    Predicting feasibility

    A redox reaction is feasible if E⦵cell for it is positive. To check a reaction, find the half-equation for the species being reduced and the one for the species being oxidised; E⦵cell = E⦵(reduced) − E⦵(oxidised).

    Worked example: will iron(III) ions oxidise iodide ions?

    1. Reduction: Fe3+ + e− → Fe2+, +0.77 V. Oxidation: 2I− → I2 + 2e−, which is the reverse of +0.54 V.
    2. E⦵cell = 0.77 − 0.54 = +0.23 V, positive, so the reaction is feasible.
    3. Combine the half-equations so the electrons cancel (double the iron one):

    2Fe3+(aq) + 2I−(aq) → 2Fe2+(aq) + I2(aq), E⦵cell = +0.23 V

    Limitations: a positive E⦵cell means a reaction can happen, but it may be too slow to notice (high activation energy), and the conditions may not be standard (different concentrations or temperature change E).

    The effect of concentration: the Nernst equation

    By Le Chatelier's principle, increasing the concentration of the oxidised species (on the left of the half-equation) pushes the equilibrium to the right, making E more positive. Decreasing it makes E less positive.

    Nernst equation (298 K)E = E + 0.059zlog [oxidised species][reduced species]Learn it

    z is the number of electrons in the half-equation. Solid metals are left out of the expression (their "concentration" is constant).

    Worked examples

    1. Cu2+/Cu with [Cu2+] = 0.010 mol dm−3: E = 0.34 + 0.0592log (0.010) = 0.34 − 0.059 = +0.28 V
    2. Fe3+/Fe2+ with [Fe3+] = 0.10 and [Fe2+] = 1.0 mol dm−3: E = 0.77 + 0.059log 0.101.0 = 0.77 − 0.059 = +0.71 V

    Linking Ecell to Gibbs free energy

    Free energy from a cellΔG = −nFEcellLearn it

    n is the number of moles of electrons transferred in the equation. A positive E⦵cell gives a negative ΔG, consistent with a feasible reaction. For the zinc–copper cell: ΔG = −2 × 96 500 × 1.10 = −212 000 J mol−1 = −212 kJ mol−1.

    Questions

    1Quick check

    Which species is the strongest reducing agent? Use the table above.

    1. Cl−
    2. Fe2+
    3. Cu
    4. Zn

    The strongest reducing agent is on the right of the half-equation with the most negative E⦵: Zn (−0.76 V).

    2Quick check

    A silver half-cell is connected to a magnesium half-cell under standard conditions. What is E⦵cell?

    1. 1.58 V
    2. 3.18 V
    3. −3.18 V
    4. 0.80 V

    E⦵cell = 0.80 − (−2.38) = 3.18 V. Silver is the positive electrode.

    3Quick check

    What mass of aluminium is produced when 0.30 mol of electrons passes through molten aluminium oxide? (Ar: Al, 27.0)

    1. 0.90 g
    2. 2.7 g
    3. 8.1 g
    4. 27 g

    Al3+ + 3e− → Al: 0.30 mol of electrons gives 0.10 mol of Al, which is 0.10 × 27.0 = 2.7 g.

    4Quick check

    E⦵ values: Fe3+/Fe2+ +0.77 V; I2/I− +0.54 V; Cu2+/Cu +0.34 V; Br2/Br− +1.07 V; Zn2+/Zn −0.76 V. Which species can oxidise Fe2+ to Fe3+ under standard conditions?

    1. I2
    2. Cu2+
    3. Br2
    4. Zn2+

    The oxidising agent needs a more positive E⦵ than +0.77 V. Only Br2/Br− qualifies: E⦵cell = 1.07 − 0.77 = +0.30 V.

    5Quick check

    The concentration of Cu2+(aq) in a Cu2+/Cu half-cell is lowered from 1.00 to 0.010 mol dm−3. What happens to the electrode potential?

    1. it becomes less positive, by about 0.06 V
    2. it becomes more positive, by about 0.06 V
    3. it becomes less positive, by about 0.12 V
    4. it doesn't change

    E = E⦵ + (0.059/2) log[Cu2+] = 0.34 + 0.0295 × (−2) = 0.28 V, a fall of 0.059 V.

    6Paper 4 style

    [3]
    (b)
    A cell is made from a Br2/Br− half-cell and an Fe3+/Fe2+ half-cell. Calculate E⦵cell, state which electrode is positive, and write the overall equation for the cell reaction.
    [3]
    (c)

    [2]
    (d)
    Calculate ΔG⦵ for the cell reaction in (b).
    [2]
    • Hydrogen gas at 101 kPa (1 atm)
    • Platinum (platinised / coated with platinum black) electrode
    • 1.00 mol dm−3 H+(aq), at 298 K
    • E⦵cell = 1.07 − 0.77 = +0.30 V
    • The Br2/Br− electrode is positive
    • Br2 + 2Fe2+ → 2Br− + 2Fe3+
    • E = 0.77 + 0.059 log(0.050/0.50)
