    7Paper 4 style

    Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes.

    (a)
    Write half-equations for the reactions at the anode and cathode.
    [2]
    (b)
    Explain why chlorine, not oxygen, is the main product at the anode.
    [2]
    (c)
    A current of 2.50 A is passed for 1.00 hour. Calculate the volume of chlorine produced at room conditions.
    [3]
    • Anode: 2Cl− → Cl2 + 2e−
    • Cathode: 2H2O + 2e− → H2 + 2OH−
    • E⦵ values for Cl2/Cl− (+1.36) and O2/H2O (+1.23) are close
    • The high concentration of Cl− makes its electrode potential less positive, so Cl− is oxidised in preference
    • Q = 2.50 × 3600 = 9000 C
    • n(e−) = 9000 / 96 500 = 0.0933 mol; n(Cl2) = 0.0466 mol
    • V = 0.0466 × 24.0 = 1.12 dm3

    This topic makes acid–base chemistry quantitative: calculating pH for strong and weak acids, designing buffers that resist pH change, and using solubility products and partition coefficients to describe how solutes distribute themselves.

    Conjugate acids and bases

    When a Brønsted–Lowry acid donates a proton, what is left can accept a proton back: it is the conjugate base of that acid. Every acid–base reaction has two conjugate pairs.

    CH3COOH + H2O ⇌ CH3COO− + H3O+ acid 1 (CH3COOH) and its conjugate base 1 (CH3COO−); base 2 (H2O) and its conjugate acid 2 (H3O+)
    NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH− base 1 (NH3) and its conjugate acid (NH4+); acid 2 (H2O) and its conjugate base (OH−)

    A conjugate pair differs by exactly one H+. The stronger an acid, the weaker its conjugate base.

    pH, Kw and strong acids and bases

    pHpH = −log [H+], so [H+] = 10−pHLearn it
    Ionic product of waterKw = [H+][OH−] = 1.00 × 10−14 mol2 dm−6 (298 K)Kw in Data Booklet

    Water ionises slightly: H2O ⇌ H+ + OH−. In pure water at 298 K, [H+] = [OH−] = 1.00 × 10−7 mol dm−3, so pH = 7.00. (The ionisation is endothermic, so at higher temperatures Kw is larger and neutral water has a pH below 7.)

    SolutionWorkingpH
    0.0200 mol dm−3 HCl (strong, monoprotic)[H+] = 0.0200; pH = −log 0.02001.70
    0.0500 mol dm−3 NaOH (strong base)[OH−] = 0.0500; [H+] = 1.00 × 10−14 / 0.0500 = 2.00 × 10−1312.70
    0.0500 mol dm−3 Ba(OH)2two OH− per formula: [OH−] = 0.100; [H+] = 1.00 × 10−1313.00

    Weak acids: Ka and pKa

    For a weak acid HA ⇌ H+ + A−:

    Acid dissociation constantKa = [H+][A−][HA]Learn it
    pKapKa = −log KaLearn it

    The larger Ka (the smaller pKa), the stronger the acid. Ethanoic acid has Ka = 1.74 × 10−5 mol dm−3 (pKa 4.76).

    pH of a weak acid

    Two approximations make the calculation simple: (1) [H+] = [A−], because water's own ionisation is negligible; (2) [HA] at equilibrium ≈ the initial concentration c, because so little dissociates. Then Ka = [H+]2c, so:

    Weak acid[H+] = √Ka × cLearn it

    Worked example

    Calculate the pH of 0.100 mol dm−3 ethanoic acid. Ka = 1.74 × 10−5 mol dm−3.

    [H+] = √(1.74 × 10−5 × 0.100) = 1.32 × 10−3 mol dm−3; pH = 2.88

    Worked example: finding Ka from pH

    A 0.0500 mol dm−3 solution of a weak acid has pH 3.10. Find Ka.

    [H+] = 10−3.10 = 7.94 × 10−4; Ka = (7.94 × 10−4)2 / 0.0500 = 1.26 × 10−5 mol dm−3

    Buffer solutions

    Buffer solution
    A solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added.

    An acidic buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (a salt of the acid), both in large amounts, for example ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate. It can also be made by partly neutralising a weak acid with a strong base. (A basic buffer uses a weak base and its salt, such as ammonia and ammonium chloride.)

    In the ethanoic acid / sodium ethanoate buffer there is a large reservoir of both CH3COOH and CH3COO−:

    CH3COOH ⇌ CH3COO− + H+
    • Adding a little acid (H+): the added H+ reacts with the large amount of CH3COO−: CH3COO− + H+ → CH3COOH. The ratio [CH3COOH]/[CH3COO−] hardly changes, so [H+] and the pH hardly change.
    • Adding a little alkali (OH−): the OH− reacts with the large amount of CH3COOH: CH3COOH + OH− → CH3COO− + H2O. Again the ratio barely changes.
    Buffer pH[H+] = Ka × [HA][A−]Learn it

    Worked example 1

    A buffer contains 0.100 mol dm−3 ethanoic acid and 0.200 mol dm−3 sodium ethanoate. Ka = 1.74 × 10−5.

    [H+] = 1.74 × 10−5 × 0.100 / 0.200 = 8.70 × 10−6; pH = 5.06

    Worked example 2: by partial neutralisation

    25.0 cm3 of 0.200 mol dm−3 NaOH is added to 50.0 cm3 of 0.200 mol dm−3 ethanoic acid.

    1. n(acid) = 0.0100 mol; n(NaOH) = 0.00500 mol, which converts 0.00500 mol of acid into ethanoate.
    2. Left: 0.00500 mol CH3COOH and 0.00500 mol CH3COO−, in the same volume, so the ratio is 1.

    [H+] = Ka, so pH = pKa = 4.76. (This is the half-neutralisation point on a titration curve.)

    Buffers in the body

    Blood must stay at pH 7.35 to 7.45. The main buffer is carbonic acid / hydrogencarbonate: H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−, where H2CO3 comes from dissolved carbon dioxide (CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3). Extra acid is removed by HCO3− + H+ → H2CO3; the H2CO3 breaks down to CO2, which is breathed out. Extra alkali is removed by H2CO3 + OH− → HCO3− + H2O. Buffers are also used in shampoos, food, fermentation and to calibrate pH meters.

    The pH titration curves from Topic 7 are now fully explained: the flat region for a weak acid is a buffer region, with pH = pKa at half-neutralisation. Try changing the acid and base in the titration simulator below.

    Solubility product, Ksp

    For a sparingly soluble salt in equilibrium with its saturated solution, such as AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag+(aq) + Cl−(aq):

    Solubility product, Ksp
    The product of the concentrations of the ions in a saturated solution of a sparingly soluble salt, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the equation, at a given temperature. The solid is not included.
    SaltEquilibriumKsp expressionUnits
    AgClAgCl(s) ⇌ Ag+ + Cl−[Ag+][Cl−]mol2 dm−6
    CaF2CaF2(s) ⇌ Ca2+ + 2F−[Ca2+][F−]2mol3 dm−9
    Ag2CrO4Ag2CrO4(s) ⇌ 2Ag+ + CrO42−[Ag+]2[CrO42−]mol3 dm−9

    Worked example 1: Ksp from solubility

    The solubility of silver chloride is 1.30 × 10−5 mol dm−3.

    Ksp = (1.30 × 10−5)2 = 1.69 × 10−10 mol2 dm−6

    Worked example 2: solubility from Ksp

    Ksp(CaF2) = 3.90 × 10−11 mol3 dm−9. If the solubility is s, then [Ca2+] = s and [F−] = 2s, so Ksp = s(2s)2 = 4s3.

    s = ∛(3.90 × 10−11 / 4) = 2.14 × 10−4 mol dm−3

    The common ion effect

    A sparingly soluble salt is less soluble in a solution that already contains one of its ions. Adding the common ion pushes the equilibrium to the left, so more solid forms, until the ion product again equals Ksp.

    Worked example

    What is the solubility of AgCl (Ksp 1.69 × 10−10) in 0.100 mol dm−3 NaCl?

    [Cl−] ≈ 0.100 (the AgCl adds very little), so [Ag+] = 1.69 × 10−10 / 0.100 = 1.69 × 10−9 mol dm−3. That's nearly 10 000 times less than in pure water.

    A precipitate forms whenever mixing two solutions makes the ion product exceed Ksp.

    Partition coefficients

    Partition coefficient, Kpc
    The ratio of the concentrations of a solute in two immiscible solvents when it has reached equilibrium, at a given temperature (the solute is in the same physical state in both solvents).
    Partition coefficientKpc = [X in solvent 1][X in solvent 2]Learn it

    The value depends on the relative polarities: a non-polar solute (such as iodine) is much more soluble in a non-polar organic solvent than in water, so Kpc(organic/water) is large. A polar solute that can hydrogen bond with water (such as ammonia or ethanoic acid) has a smaller value.

    Worked example: solvent extraction

    Kpc for a compound Y between ether and water is 4.0. 100 cm3 of an aqueous solution contains 2.00 g of Y. How much Y is extracted by shaking with 50 cm3 of ether?

    1. Let x g go into the ether: x/50(2.00 − x)/100 = 4.0
    2. So 2x = 4.0(2.00 − x), giving x = 1.33 g (67% extracted).

    Two separate extractions with 25 cm3 of ether each remove 1.00 g then 0.50 g: 1.50 g in total (75%). Several small extractions are more efficient than one large one.

    Questions

    1Quick check

    What is the pH of 0.0010 mol dm−3 potassium hydroxide at 298 K?

    1. 3.0
    2. 10.0
    3. 11.0
    4. 14.0

    [OH−] = 1.0 × 10−3, so [H+] = 1.0 × 10−14 / 1.0 × 10−3 = 1.0 × 10−11, pH 11.0.

    2Quick check

    Which pair is a conjugate acid–base pair?

    1. H2SO4 and HSO4−
    2. H3O+ and OH−
    3. NH4+ and NH2−
    4. HCl and Cl2

    A conjugate pair differs by one H+. H3O+ and OH− differ by two; so do NH4+ and NH2−.

    3Quick check

    Which mixture is a buffer solution?

    1. HCl(aq) and NaCl(aq)
    2. NaOH(aq) and NaCl(aq)
    3. CH3COOH(aq) and CH3COONa(aq)
    4. NH3(aq) and excess HCl(aq)

    A buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid), both in reasonable amounts. With excess HCl, all the NH3 becomes NH4+, leaving no weak base.

    4Quick check

    What are the expression for the solubility product of silver chromate(VI), Ag2CrO4, and its units?

    1. [Ag+][CrO42−]; mol2 dm−6
    2. [Ag+]2[CrO42−]; mol3 dm−9
    3. [Ag+]2[CrO42−] / [Ag2CrO4]; no units
    4. 2[Ag+][CrO42−]; mol2 dm−6

    Ag2CrO4(s) ⇌ 2Ag+(aq) + CrO42−(aq). The solid isn't included, and three concentration terms give mol3 dm−9.

    5Quick check

    Solute X has a partition coefficient Kpc = [X]hexane / [X]water = 4.0. 100 cm3 of water containing 0.50 g of X is shaken with 100 cm3 of hexane. What mass of X stays in the water?

    1. 0.10 g
    2. 0.125 g
    3. 0.25 g
    4. 0.40 g

    Let x g stay in the water: ((0.50 − x)/100) ÷ (x/100) = 4.0, so 0.50 − x = 4.0x and x = 0.10 g.

    6Paper 4 style

    Propanoic acid, CH3CH2COOH, is a weak acid with Ka = 1.35 × 10−5 mol dm−3.

    (a)
    Write the expression for Ka of propanoic acid.
    [1]
    (b)
    Calculate the pH of 0.150 mol dm−3 propanoic acid.
    [2]
    (c)
    A buffer is made by adding 0.0300 mol of sodium propanoate to 200 cm3 of the 0.150 mol dm−3 acid. Calculate its pH.
    [2]
    (d)
    Explain, with an equation, how this buffer resists a decrease in pH when a small amount of acid is added.
    [2]
    • Ka = [CH3CH2COO−][H+][CH3CH2COOH]
    • [H+] = √(1.35 × 10−5 × 0.150) = 1.42 × 10−3
    • pH = 2.85
    • n(acid) = 0.0300 mol, n(salt) = 0.0300 mol, so the ratio is 1 and [H+] = Ka
    • pH = −log(1.35 × 10−5) = 4.87
    • CH3CH2COO− + H+ → CH3CH2COOH
    • There is a large reservoir of the conjugate base, so the ratio [HA]/[A−] (and so [H+]) changes very little
    7Paper 4 style

    Lead(II) iodide, PbI2, is sparingly soluble. Its solubility at 298 K is 1.52 × 10−3 mol dm−3.

    (a)
    Write the expression for Ksp of PbI2 and calculate its value, with units.
    [3]
    (b)
    Calculate the solubility of PbI2 in 0.100 mol dm−3 potassium iodide. Explain the difference from (a).
    [3]
    • Ksp = [Pb2+][I−]2
    • = (1.52 × 10−3)(3.04 × 10−3)2 = 1.40 × 10−8
    • mol3 dm−9
    • [Pb2+] = 1.40 × 10−8 / (0.100)2
    • = 1.40 × 10−6 mol dm−3
    • Common ion effect: the I− from KI shifts the equilibrium to the left, so less PbI2 dissolves

    A rate equation tells you exactly how the rate depends on each concentration. Finding it from experimental data, then working backwards to a mechanism, is one of the main Paper 4 and Paper 5 skills.

    Rate equations

    For a reaction A + B → products, experiments give a rate equation of the form:

    Rate equationrate = k[A]m[B]nLearn it
    Order of reaction with respect to a reactant
    The power to which the concentration of that reactant is raised in the rate equation (here m for A, n for B). In this course it is 0, 1 or 2.
    Overall order
    The sum of the individual orders, m + n.
    Rate constant, k
    The constant of proportionality in the rate equation. It is constant at a given temperature, and increases as the temperature increases.
    Half-life, t½
    The time taken for the concentration of a reactant to fall to half its initial value.
    Rate-determining step
    The slowest step in a multi-step reaction mechanism; it limits the overall rate.
    Intermediate
    A species formed in one step of a mechanism and used up in a later step. It does not appear in the overall equation.

    Orders can't be found from the balanced equation; they must be measured. The units of k depend on the overall order:

    Overall order0123
    Units of kmol dm−3 s−1s−1dm3 mol−1 s−1dm6 mol−2 s−1

    Finding orders from graphs

    Order in AConcentration–time graphRate–concentration graphHalf-life
    0straight line sloping downhorizontal line: rate doesn't depend on [A]decreases as [A] falls
    1curve with a constant half-lifestraight line through the originconstant, whatever the starting concentration
    2steeper curve that levels out more; half-life gets longerupward curve (rate ∝ [A]2)increases as [A] falls

    To get rates from a concentration–time graph, draw tangents at several points and find their gradients. The initial rate is the gradient at t = 0.

    First-order reactions and half-life

    For a first-order reaction the half-life is independent of concentration: going from 1.00 to 0.50, 0.50 to 0.25 or 0.25 to 0.125 mol dm−3 all take the same time. This is a quick test for first order. Radioactive decay is also first order.

    First-order half-lifek = 0.693t1/2Learn it

    Worked example

    The decomposition of a compound is first order with a half-life of 120 s. Find k, and the fraction left after 360 s.

    k = 0.693 / 120 = 5.78 × 10−3 s−1. 360 s is 3 half-lives, so (½)3 = 1/8 remains.

    Finding orders from initial rates

    Run the reaction several times, changing the concentration of one reactant at a time, and measure the initial rate each time. Compare pairs of experiments in which only one concentration changes.

    Worked example

    Experiment[A] / mol dm−3[B] / mol dm−3Initial rate / mol dm−3 s−1
    10.100.102.0 × 10−4
    20.200.108.0 × 10−4
    30.100.306.0 × 10−4
    1. Experiments 1 and 2: [A] doubles, rate × 4 = 22, so second order in A.
    2. Experiments 1 and 3: [B] × 3, rate × 3, so first order in B.
    3. Rate = k[A]2[B]; overall third order.
    4. From experiment 1: k = 2.0 × 10−4 / (0.102 × 0.10) = 0.20

    k = 0.20 dm6 mol−2 s−1

    Rate equations and mechanisms

    The rate equation contains only the species that take part in (or before) the rate-determining step, in the numbers that appear in that step. Species that react only after the slow step are zero order.

    Example 1: nucleophilic substitution

    • 2-bromo-2-methylpropane + OH−: rate = k[(CH3)3CBr]. Only the halogenoalkane is in the slow step (forming the carbocation): SN1.
    • Bromoethane + OH−: rate = k[CH3CH2Br][OH−]. Both are in the single step: SN2.

    Example 2: proposing a mechanism

    For NO2(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO2(g), rate = k[NO2]2. CO is zero order, so it isn't in the slow step, and two NO2 molecules are.

    1. Step 1 (slow): NO2 + NO2 → NO3 + NO
    2. Step 2 (fast): NO3 + CO → NO2 + CO2

    The steps add up to the overall equation, and NO3 is an intermediate.

    Example 3: a catalyst in the rate equation

    For the acid-catalysed iodination of propanone, CH3COCH3 + I2 → CH3COCH2I + HI, rate = k[CH3COCH3][H+]. Iodine is zero order, so it reacts after the slow step, and H+ is a catalyst: it appears in the rate equation but not in the overall equation.

    Temperature and the rate constant

    Increasing the temperature increases k, and so the rate, because a greater proportion of molecules have energy at least equal to EA (Topic 8). The orders don't change.

    Catalysts in more detail

    Heterogeneous catalysis

    The catalyst is a solid; the reactants are gases or in solution. It works in three stages:

    1. Adsorption: reactant molecules form weak bonds to active sites on the catalyst surface. This weakens bonds within the reactants and holds them close together in a favourable orientation.
    2. Reaction on the surface, with a lower activation energy.
    3. Desorption: the product molecules break away from the surface, freeing the sites.

    Examples: iron in the Haber process (N2 and H2 are adsorbed and their bonds weakened); platinum, palladium and rhodium in catalytic converters (CO and NO are adsorbed and react to form CO2 and N2). A good catalyst adsorbs strongly enough to weaken bonds, but not so strongly that the products can't desorb.

    Homogeneous catalysis

    The catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants. It is used up in one step and regenerated in a later step, usually by changing oxidation state.

    Iron ions and the iodide–peroxodisulfate reaction

    S2O82−(aq) + 2I−(aq) → 2SO42−(aq) + I2(aq) is slow, because both reactants are negative ions that repel each other, giving a high activation energy. Fe2+ catalyses it:

    S2O82− + 2Fe2+ → 2SO42− + 2Fe3+
    2Fe3+ + 2I− → 2Fe2+ + I2

    Each step is between oppositely charged ions, so the activation energy is lower. Fe3+ works equally well, starting with the second step. Both steps are feasible: E⦵(S2O82−/SO42−) = +2.01 V > +0.77 V > +0.54 V (Topic 24).

    Oxides of nitrogen and atmospheric sulfur dioxide

    SO2 + NO2 → SO3 + NO
    NO + ½O2 → NO2

    NO2 is regenerated, so it catalyses the oxidation of SO2 to SO3, which forms acid rain (Topic 12).

    Questions

    1Quick check

    The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[X][Y]2. What are the units of k?

    1. dm3 mol−1 s−1
    2. dm6 mol−2 s−1
    3. mol2 dm−6 s−1
    4. s−1

    Third order overall: k = rate / concentration3 = (mol dm−3 s−1) / (mol dm−3)3 = dm6 mol−2 s−1.

    2Quick check

    A reaction is first order. Its concentration falls from 0.80 to 0.20 mol dm−3 in 50 s. What is its half-life?

    1. 25 s
    2. 50 s
    3. 12.5 s
    4. 100 s

    0.80 → 0.40 → 0.20 is two half-lives in 50 s, so t½ = 25 s.

    3Quick check

    For the reaction A + B → C, rate = k[A][B]2. What are the units of k?

    1. s−1
    2. dm3 mol−1 s−1
    3. mol dm−3 s−1
    4. dm6 mol−2 s−1

    k = rate / ([A][B]2) = mol dm−3 s−1 ÷ (mol dm−3)3 = dm6 mol−2 s−1.

    4Quick check

    Which statement about a heterogeneous catalyst, such as iron in the Haber process, is correct?

    1. it is in the same phase as the reactants
    2. reactants are adsorbed onto its surface, which weakens their bonds
    3. it is used up and must be replaced
    4. it increases the equilibrium yield of ammonia

    Adsorption onto active sites weakens bonds and holds molecules close together; the products then desorb. A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so the equilibrium yield doesn't change.

    5Quick check

    The half-life of a first-order reaction is 20 s. What fraction of the reactant remains after 60 s?

    1. 1/3
    2. 1/6
    3. 1/8
    4. 1/4

    60 s is three half-lives: ½ × ½ × ½ = 1/8.

    6Paper 4 style

    Hydrogen peroxide reacts with iodide ions in acid: H2O2 + 2I− + 2H+ → I2 + 2H2O. Initial rates were measured:

    Experiment[H2O2][I−][H+]Initial rate / mol dm−3 s−1
    10.0100.0100.101.75 × 10−6
    20.0300.0100.105.25 × 10−6
    30.0300.0200.101.05 × 10−5
    40.0300.0200.201.05 × 10−5
    (a)
    Deduce the order with respect to each reactant. Explain your reasoning.
    [3]
    (b)
    Write the rate equation and calculate the rate constant, with units.
    [3]
    (c)
    Suggest the species involved in the rate-determining step.
    [1]
    • H2O2: first order: experiments 1 and 2, concentration × 3, rate × 3
    • I−: first order: experiments 2 and 3, concentration × 2, rate × 2
    • H+: zero order: experiments 3 and 4, rate unchanged
    • rate = k[H2O2][I−]
    • k = 1.75 × 10−6 / (0.010 × 0.010) = 0.0175
    • dm3 mol−1 s−1
    • One H2O2 and one I− (the acid reacts in a later, fast step)
    7Paper 4 style
    (a)
    Explain the difference between homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysis.
    [1]
    (b)
    Describe how iron catalyses the reaction between nitrogen and hydrogen in the Haber process.
    [3]
    (c)
    Explain, with equations, how Fe3+ ions catalyse the reaction between peroxodisulfate and iodide ions, and why the uncatalysed reaction is slow.
    [3]
    • Homogeneous: catalyst in the same phase as the reactants; heterogeneous: different phase
    • N2 and H2 are adsorbed onto the iron surface (active sites)
    • Bonds in the reactants are weakened and the molecules are held close together, so they react
    • The ammonia molecules desorb from the surface
    • 2Fe3+ + 2I− → 2Fe2+ + I2
    • 2Fe2+ + S2O82− → 2Fe3+ + 2SO42−
    • Uncatalysed: both reactant ions are negative and repel each other, so the activation energy is high

    At AS Level you learned the trends in Group 2. At A Level you explain two of them: why the nitrates and carbonates get more stable down the group, and why the hydroxides get more soluble while the sulfates get less soluble.

    Thermal stability of the nitrates and carbonates

    On heating, MCO3 → MO + CO2 and 2M(NO3)2 → 2MO + 4NO2 + O2. The temperature needed increases down the group.

    1. The cation M2+ attracts the electron cloud of the large carbonate (or nitrate) anion, polarising it: electron density is pulled towards the cation.
    2. This distortion weakens the C–O bonds in the carbonate ion (N–O in nitrate), making it easier to break them and release CO2 (or NO2 and O2).
    3. Down the group, the cation has the same charge but a larger radius, so its charge density is lower. It polarises the anion less, so the compound is more stable and needs a higher temperature to decompose.

    Mg2+ is the smallest, most polarising ion, so magnesium carbonate decomposes most easily; barium carbonate needs the highest temperature.

    Solubility of the hydroxides and sulfates

    Whether a salt dissolves depends on the balance in the solution cycle (Topic 23): ΔHsol = −ΔHlatt + ΔHhyd(cation) + ΔHhyd(anion). The more exothermic (or less endothermic) ΔHsol, the more soluble the salt tends to be.

    Down the group, the cation gets larger, so both the lattice energy and the hydration enthalpy of the cation become less exothermic. Which change wins depends on the size of the anion:

    Sulfates: less soluble down the group

    The sulfate ion is large, so the inter-ionic distance (r+ + r−) is dominated by the anion and changes only a little as the cation grows. The lattice energy decreases only slightly. But the hydration enthalpy of the cation decreases a lot. So ΔHsol becomes more endothermic, and solubility falls.

    Hydroxides: more soluble down the group

    The hydroxide ion is small, so a larger cation increases the inter-ionic distance significantly. The lattice energy decreases more than the cation's hydration enthalpy. So ΔHsol becomes more exothermic (less endothermic), and solubility rises.

    (Entropy also plays a part in solubility, but the enthalpy argument above is what the syllabus asks for.)

    Questions

    1Quick check

    Which carbonate decomposes at the lowest temperature?

    1. MgCO3
    2. CaCO3
    3. SrCO3
    4. BaCO3

    Mg2+ is the smallest Group 2 ion, with the highest charge density, so it polarises (distorts) the carbonate ion's electron cloud the most and weakens a C–O bond.

    2Quick check

    How do the solubilities of the Group 2 sulfates and hydroxides change down the group?

    1. both increase
    2. both decrease
    3. sulfates decrease, hydroxides increase
    4. sulfates increase, hydroxides decrease

    Down the group both the lattice energy and the hydration enthalpy become less exothermic. For the sulfates the hydration enthalpy falls faster, so solubility decreases; for the hydroxides the lattice energy falls faster, so solubility increases.

    3Paper 4 style
    (a)
    Write an equation for the thermal decomposition of strontium nitrate.
    [1]
    (b)
    Explain why magnesium carbonate decomposes at a lower temperature than barium carbonate.
    [3]
    (c)
    Explain, in terms of enthalpy changes, why barium sulfate is less soluble than magnesium sulfate.
    [3]
    • 2Sr(NO3)2 → 2SrO + 4NO2 + O2
    • Mg2+ is smaller than Ba2+ (same charge), so it has a higher charge density
    • It polarises (distorts) the carbonate ion's electron cloud more
    • This weakens the C–O bonds, so less energy is needed to decompose it
    • The hydration enthalpy of Ba2+ is much less exothermic than that of Mg2+
    • The lattice energy changes only slightly, because the large sulfate ion dominates the inter-ionic distance
    • So ΔHsol is more endothermic for BaSO4, making it less soluble
    4Paper 4 style
    (a)
    Write an equation for the thermal decomposition of magnesium nitrate.
    [2]
    (b)
    Describe and explain the trend in the thermal stability of the Group 2 nitrates.
    [3]
    • Correct formulas: Mg(NO3)2, MgO, NO2, O2
    • Balanced: 2Mg(NO3)2 → 2MgO + 4NO2 + O2
    • Thermal stability increases down the group
    • The cation radius increases, so its charge density decreases
    • So the cation polarises (distorts) the nitrate ion's electron cloud less, and the N–O bonds are weakened less

    The first-row transition elements, titanium to copper, have partly filled 3d orbitals. That one feature explains their variable oxidation states, their catalytic activity, their complex ions and their colours.

    What is a transition element?

    Transition element
    A d-block element that forms one or more stable ions with incompletely filled d orbitals.
    ElementTiVCrMnFeCoNiCu
    Configuration (after [Ar])3d2 4s23d3 4s23d5 4s13d5 4s23d6 4s23d7 4s23d8 4s23d10 4s1
    Common oxidation states+2, +3, +4+2, +3, +4, +5+2, +3, +6+2, +4, +6, +7+2, +3+2, +3+2+1, +2

    Scandium and zinc are d-block elements but not transition elements: scandium's only ion, Sc3+, has an empty 3d sub-shell ([Ar]), and zinc's only ion, Zn2+, has a full one ([Ar] 3d10).

    Shapes of d orbitals

    Characteristic properties

    Compared with s-block metals, transition elements are dense, hard and have high melting points. Chemically, they have four characteristic properties:

    Variable oxidation states

    The 3d and 4s sub-shells are close in energy, so different numbers of electrons can be lost (or used in bonding) for similar amounts of energy. The highest state rises to +7 at manganese (all 4s and 3d electrons), then falls.

    Catalytic activity

    They can change oxidation state easily (passing electrons to and from reactants), and they have vacant, energetically accessible d orbitals to form dative bonds with reactant molecules (adsorption).

    Complex ion formation

    Vacant d orbitals that are energetically accessible accept lone pairs from ligands.

    Coloured compounds

    Partly filled d orbitals that are split in energy by ligands absorb visible light (section below).

    Vanadium shows variable oxidation states clearly: reducing an acidified solution of ammonium vanadate(V) with zinc changes the colour from yellow (VO2+, +5) to blue (VO2+, +4) to green (V3+, +3) to violet (V2+, +2).

    Complexes and ligands

    Ligand
    A molecule or ion with one or more lone pairs available to donate to a transition element ion, forming a dative covalent bond.
    Complex
    A molecule or ion formed by a central metal atom or ion surrounded by one or more ligands.
    Coordination number
    The number of dative bonds formed between the ligands and the central metal ion.
    TypeBonds to the metalExamples
    monodentate1H2O, NH3, Cl−, CN−
    bidentate21,2-diaminoethane, H2NCH2CH2NH2 ("en", through both N); ethanedioate, C2O42− (through two O)
    polydentateseveralEDTA4−, which bonds through six atoms (four O and two N), wrapping around the metal ion

    Shapes of complexes

    Working out the formula and charge: overall charge = charge on the metal ion + total charge of the ligands. For example: Fe3+ with six CN− gives [Fe(CN)6]3−; Co3+ with six NH3 gives [Co(NH3)6]3+; Ni2+ with three en gives [Ni(en)3]2+ (coordination number 6); Cr3+ with four H2O and two Cl− gives [Cr(H2O)4Cl2]+.

    Ligand exchange

    In ligand exchange, one ligand replaces another. If the new ligands are larger (like Cl−), fewer fit around the metal, so the coordination number and shape can change.

    Copper(II)

    Add to [Cu(H2O)6]2+ (blue)ObservationEquation
    NaOH(aq)pale blue precipitate[Cu(H2O)6]2+ + 2OH− → [Cu(OH)2(H2O)4] + 2H2O
    NH3(aq), a littlepale blue precipitate (ammonia acts as a base)as above
    NH3(aq), excessprecipitate dissolves to a deep blue solution[Cu(H2O)6]2+ + 4NH3 → [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ + 4H2O
    concentrated HClyellow-green (then yellow) solution; octahedral → tetrahedral[Cu(H2O)6]2+ + 4Cl− ⇌ [CuCl4]2− + 6H2O

    Cobalt(II)

    Add to [Co(H2O)6]2+ (pink)ObservationEquation
    NaOH(aq)blue precipitate, which turns pink on standing and darkens (brown) in air[Co(H2O)6]2+ + 2OH− → [Co(OH)2(H2O)4] + 2H2O
    NH3(aq), a littleblue precipitateas above
    NH3(aq), excessprecipitate dissolves to a pale brown (straw) solution, which darkens in air as Co(II) is oxidised to Co(III)[Co(H2O)6]2+ + 6NH3 → [Co(NH3)6]2+ + 6H2O
    concentrated HClblue solution; octahedral → tetrahedral[Co(H2O)6]2+ + 4Cl− ⇌ [CoCl4]2− + 6H2O

    The reactions with HCl are reversible: adding water moves the equilibrium back to the aqua complex.

    Redox chemistry

    Use E⦵ values (Topic 24) to predict whether a transition-metal redox reaction is feasible. For example:

    • Acidified manganate(VII) can oxidise chloride ions (E⦵cell = 1.52 − 1.36 = +0.16 V), so manganate(VII) titrations are acidified with sulfuric acid, not hydrochloric acid.
    • Dichromate(VI) cannot oxidise chloride ions under standard conditions (1.33 − 1.36 = −0.03 V), so it can be used with HCl.

    Redox titrations

    (a) Manganate(VII) and iron(II)

    MnO4− + 8H+ + 5Fe2+ → Mn2+ + 4H2O + 5Fe3+ no indicator needed: the end point is the first permanent pale pink colour (excess MnO4−)

    25.0 cm3 of an iron(II) solution needs 21.60 cm3 of 0.0200 mol dm−3 KMnO4.

    1. n(MnO4−) = 0.0200 × 0.02160 = 4.32 × 10−4 mol
    2. n(Fe2+) = 5 × 4.32 × 10−4 = 2.16 × 10−3 mol

    [Fe2+] = 2.16 × 10−3 / 0.0250 = 0.0864 mol dm−3

    (b) Manganate(VII) and ethanedioate

    2MnO4− + 16H+ + 5C2O42− → 2Mn2+ + 8H2O + 10CO2 warm the flask to about 60 °C; the reaction speeds up as Mn2+ forms, because Mn2+ catalyses it (autocatalysis)

    What volume of 0.0200 mol dm−3 KMnO4 reacts with 0.150 g of sodium ethanedioate, Na2C2O4 (Mr 134.0)?

    n(C2O42−) = 1.12 × 10−3 mol; n(MnO4−) = 2/5 × that = 4.48 × 10−4 mol; volume = 4.48 × 10−4 / 0.0200 = 0.0224 dm3 = 22.4 cm3

    (c) Copper(II) and iodide

    2Cu2+ + 4I− → 2CuI + I2 white precipitate of copper(I) iodide, coloured brown by the iodine
    I2 + 2S2O32− → 2I− + S4O62− the iodine is titrated with sodium thiosulfate; starch is added near the end point (blue-black → colourless)

    Overall, 2 mol Cu2+ give 1 mol I2, which reacts with 2 mol S2O32−: so n(Cu2+) = n(S2O32−). If 25.0 cm3 of copper(II) solution needs 20.40 cm3 of 0.100 mol dm−3 thiosulfate:

    n(Cu2+) = 2.04 × 10−3 mol, so [Cu2+] = 0.0816 mol dm−3

    Why complexes are coloured

    Degenerate orbitals
    Orbitals of the same energy. In an isolated ion, all five 3d orbitals are degenerate.
    Non-degenerate orbitals
    Orbitals of different energy. Ligands split the d orbitals into two non-degenerate sets.
    1. When white light passes through the solution, an electron in a lower d orbital absorbs a photon and is promoted to a higher d orbital.
    2. The frequency of light absorbed depends on the energy gap: ΔE = hf. This is in the visible region.
    3. The colour we see is the complementary colour: the light that is transmitted. [Cu(H2O)6]2+ absorbs mainly red/orange light, so it looks blue.

    If the d sub-shell is empty (d0, such as Sc3+ and Ti4+) or full (d10, such as Zn2+ and Cu+), no d–d transition is possible, so the compounds are colourless (white solids).

    Different ligands, different colours: ligands split the d orbitals by different amounts. NH3 causes a larger splitting than H2O, so [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ absorbs a higher frequency (shorter wavelength) than [Cu(H2O)6]2+, and looks a deeper blue. Changing the oxidation state or the coordination number (shape) also changes ΔE and the colour.

    Stereoisomerism in complexes

    Geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism

    Cisplatin works by binding to DNA in cancer cells (the two Cl ligands are replaced by N atoms of the DNA bases), which stops the cells dividing. The trans isomer cannot do this.

    Optical isomerism

    Complexes with two or three bidentate ligands can be chiral. [Ni(en)3]2+ exists as two non-superimposable mirror images. [Ni(en)2(H2O)2]2+ has a trans isomer (not chiral) and a cis isomer that exists as a pair of enantiomers: three stereoisomers in total.

    Polarity: a complex is non-polar if its shape makes the bond dipoles cancel, as in trans-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]. The cis isomer is polar.

    Stability constants

    Stability constant, Kstab
    The equilibrium constant for the formation of a complex ion in a solvent from its constituent ions or molecules.

    For [Cu(H2O)6]2+ + 4NH3 ⇌ [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ + 4H2O, the concentration of water is effectively constant, so it is left out:

    Stability constantKstab = [[Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+][Cu2+][NH3]4Learn it

    (Here [Cu2+] means the hexaaqua ion.) The units are mol−4 dm12. Values are often quoted as lg Kstab:

    Complex[CuCl4]2−[Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+[Cu(EDTA)]2−
    lg Kstab5.613.118.8

    A larger Kstab means a more stable complex. Ligand exchange tends to go towards the complex with the larger Kstab: adding ammonia to [CuCl4]2− forms the ammine complex, and adding EDTA to either forms [Cu(EDTA)]2−. Polydentate ligands form very stable complexes partly because one ligand replaces several water molecules, increasing the number of particles and so the entropy.

    Worked example

    In a solution, [NH3] = 0.100 mol dm−3 and lg Kstab = 13.1. Find the ratio [complex] : [Cu2+].

    ratio = Kstab × [NH3]4 = 1013.1 × 10−4 = 1.3 × 109: essentially all the copper is in the ammine complex.

    Questions

    1Quick check

    Which ion is colourless in aqueous solution?

    1. Cu2+
    2. Fe3+
    3. Zn2+
    4. Ni2+

    Zn2+ is 3d10: with a full d sub-shell, no d–d transitions can happen.

    2Quick check

    What is the coordination number of nickel in [Ni(en)2(H2O)2]2+?

    1. 2
    2. 3
    3. 4
    4. 6

    Each en forms two dative bonds (4 in total) and each water forms one (2 more): 6.

    3Quick check

    What is the oxidation state of cobalt in [CoCl4]2−, and what is the shape of the complex?

    1. +2, square planar
    2. +2, tetrahedral
    3. +4, tetrahedral
    4. −2, octahedral

    x + 4(−1) = −2, so x = +2. The large chloride ligands give four-coordinate, tetrahedral complexes such as [CoCl4]2− and [CuCl4]2−.

    4Quick check

    Why is [Cu(H2O)6]2+ coloured?

    1. Cu2+ has a full 3d sub-shell
    2. the water ligands absorb visible light
    3. electrons move from the 4s to the 3d orbitals
    4. the ligands split the 3d orbitals, and an electron absorbs visible light to move to a higher d orbital

    Cu2+ is 3d9, so there is space in the higher-energy d orbitals. The gap ΔE matches visible light; red-orange light is absorbed and the complementary colour, blue, is seen.

    5Quick check

    Which ligand is bidentate?

    1. ethane-1,2-diamine, H2NCH2CH2NH2
    2. ammonia, NH3
    3. cyanide, CN−
    4. EDTA4−

    Ethane-1,2-diamine has two N atoms, each with a lone pair, so it forms two dative bonds to the metal ion. EDTA4− is hexadentate; NH3 and CN− are monodentate.

    6Paper 4 style

    [2]

    [4]

    • Complex: a central metal atom or ion surrounded by (dative-bonded) ligands

    • Dissolves in excess to give a deep blue solution

    • Ligands split the 3d orbitals into two non-degenerate sets

    • The complementary colour (the light not absorbed) is seen

    7Paper 4 style

    An iron tablet weighing 0.650 g is dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid, and all the iron is present as Fe2+. The solution needs 18.50 cm3 of 0.0200 mol dm−3 KMnO4 to reach the end point.

    (a)
    Write the ionic equation for the reaction.
    [1]
    (b)
    Calculate the percentage by mass of iron in the tablet.
    [3]
    (c)
    Explain why hydrochloric acid is not used to acidify the solution. Use E⦵ values: MnO4−/Mn2+ +1.52 V, Cl2/Cl− +1.36 V.
    [2]
    • MnO4− + 8H+ + 5Fe2+ → Mn2+ + 4H2O + 5Fe3+
    • n(MnO4−) = 0.0200 × 0.01850 = 3.70 × 10−4 mol
    • n(Fe) = 5 × 3.70 × 10−4 = 1.85 × 10−3 mol; mass = 1.85 × 10−3 × 55.8 = 0.103 g
    • % Fe = 0.103 / 0.650 × 100 = 15.9%

    • So more KMnO4 would be used and the titre would be too high

    A Level organic chemistry adds aromatic compounds (built on the benzene ring), acyl chlorides, amides and amino acids. This topic covers their names, the special bonding in benzene, and why optical isomers matter so much for medicines.

    New functional groups

    FamilyFunctional groupExample
    arenebenzene ring, C6H5– (phenyl)methylbenzene, C6H5CH3
    halogenoarenehalogen on a benzene ringchlorobenzene, C6H5Cl
    phenol–OH directly on a benzene ringphenol, C6H5OH
    acyl chloride–COClethanoyl chloride, CH3COCl
    amide–CONH2, –CONHRethanamide, CH3CONH2; N-methylethanamide, CH3CONHCH3
    secondary amine–NH–dimethylamine, (CH3)2NH
    amino acid–NH2 and –COOH on the same molecule2-aminopropanoic acid (alanine), CH3CH(NH2)COOH
    aromatic amine–NH2 on a benzene ringphenylamine, C6H5NH2

    Naming aromatic compounds

    Number the ring carbons from the carbon carrying the main functional group (C1), going the way that gives the lowest numbers to the other substituents.

    Esters and amides are named from both parts and can have up to six carbons in each: for example propyl butanoate, or N-ethylpropanamide (CH3CH2CONHCH2CH3), where "N-ethyl" means the ethyl group is on the nitrogen.

    New reaction types

    Electrophilic substitution
    An electrophile replaces an atom (usually H) on an aromatic ring. This is how arenes react (Topic 30).
    Addition–elimination
    A nucleophile adds to a C=O group, then a small molecule (such as HCl) is eliminated. This is how acyl chlorides react (Topic 33).

    The structure of benzene

    • Benzene, C6H6, is a planar regular hexagon. Each carbon is sp2 hybridised, forming three σ bonds (to two carbons and one hydrogen) at 120°.
    • Each carbon has one remaining p orbital, at right angles to the plane of the ring. The six p orbitals overlap sideways all the way round, forming a delocalised π system above and below the plane, containing six electrons.
    • All six C–C bonds are the same length, 0.139 nm: between a C–C single bond (0.154 nm) and a C=C double bond (0.134 nm).

    Evidence for delocalisation: hydrogenating cyclohexene releases 120 kJ mol−1, so a structure with three C=C bonds would release about 3 × 120 = 360 kJ mol−1. Benzene releases only 208 kJ mol−1, so it is about 152 kJ mol−1 more stable than expected. This extra stability is the delocalisation energy. It also explains why benzene does not decolourise bromine water: addition would destroy the delocalised system.

    Optical isomerism in more depth

    A pair of enantiomers (optical isomers) has identical physical and chemical properties, with two exceptions:

    • Plane-polarised light: each enantiomer rotates the plane of polarisation by the same angle, but in opposite directions. A compound that rotates plane-polarised light is optically active.
    • Biological activity: enzymes and receptors in the body are themselves chiral, so the two enantiomers can fit them differently and have different effects.
    Racemic mixture
    A 50 : 50 mixture of two enantiomers. It is not optically active, because the rotations cancel out.

    Reactions that make a new chiral centre from a planar starting material (such as HCN adding to an aldehyde, or an SN1 reaction through a planar carbocation) give a racemic mixture, because attack from either side is equally likely.

    Chirality and drugs

    • Often only one enantiomer of a drug is active. The other may be inactive, or even harmful. The best-known example is thalidomide in the 1950s and 1960s: one enantiomer is a sedative, while the other caused severe birth defects.
    • Synthesis in the lab usually gives a racemic mixture. Separating the enantiomers is difficult and expensive, and half the product is wasted.
    • Using chiral catalysts (or enzymes) makes only the required enantiomer. This means smaller doses, fewer side effects and less waste.

    Questions

    1Quick check

    Which statement about the bonding in benzene is correct?

    1. It contains three C=C and three C–C bonds.
    2. Each carbon atom uses three sp2 orbitals in σ bonds and one p orbital in the delocalised π system.
    3. The bond angles are 109.5°.
    4. The π electrons are located between alternate pairs of carbon atoms.

    The six p electrons are delocalised around the whole ring; all bonds are equal and the angles are 120°.

    2Quick check

    How many chiral centres are there in 2,3-dibromobutane, CH3CHBrCHBrCH3?

    1. 0
    2. 1
    3. 2
    4. 3

    C2 and C3 each have four different groups attached: H, Br, CH3 and the rest of the molecule.

    3Quick check

    What is the bond angle around each carbon atom in benzene, and how is each carbon hybridised?

    1. 109.5°, sp3
    2. 120°, sp2
    3. 180°, sp
    4. 90°, sp2

    Each carbon forms three σ bonds (two C–C, one C–H) in a plane at 120°. The remaining p orbital overlaps sideways with its neighbours to form the delocalised π system.

    4Paper 4 style

    The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −120 kJ mol−1, and of benzene is −208 kJ mol−1.

    (a)
    Use these data to explain what they show about the stability of benzene.
    [2]
    (b)
    Describe the bonding in benzene in terms of orbital overlap.
    [3]
    (c)
    A drug is made as a racemic mixture. Explain what is meant by a racemic mixture, and give two reasons why manufacturers try to produce a single enantiomer.
    [3]
    • Expected for three C=C: 3 × −120 = −360 kJ mol−1
    • Benzene releases 152 kJ mol−1 less, so it is more stable (because of delocalisation)
    • Each C is sp2 hybridised, forming σ bonds to two C and one H
    • The remaining p orbital on each C overlaps sideways with p orbitals on both neighbours
    • Forming a delocalised π system (ring of electron density) above and below the plane
    • A 50 : 50 mixture of two enantiomers (optically inactive)
    • Only one enantiomer may be active, so the dose can be halved / less waste
    • The other enantiomer may cause harmful side effects

    Benzene and methylbenzene are electron-rich but very stable. They react with electrophiles, but by substitution rather than addition, so that the delocalised ring survives. Groups already on the ring decide where the next substituent goes.

    Reactions of benzene and methylbenzene

    ReactionReagents and conditionsProduct from benzene
    halogenation (ring)Cl2 or Br2 with AlCl3 or AlBr3 (or Fe) catalyst, room temperature, no lightchlorobenzene or bromobenzene + HCl/HBr
    nitrationconcentrated HNO3 and concentrated H2SO4, 25–60 °Cnitrobenzene, C6H5NO2 + H2O
    Friedel–Crafts alkylationCH3Cl (a chloroalkane) and AlCl3, heatmethylbenzene, C6H5CH3 + HCl
    Friedel–Crafts acylationCH3COCl (an acyl chloride) and AlCl3, heatphenylethanone, C6H5COCH3 + HCl
    hydrogenationH2, Pt or Ni catalyst, heat (and pressure)cyclohexane, C6H12
    side-chain oxidation (alkylbenzenes only)hot alkaline KMnO4, then dilute acidmethylbenzene → benzoic acid, C6H5COOH

    Above 60 °C, nitration goes further and gives 1,3-dinitrobenzene. Any alkyl side chain, however long, is oxidised to –COOH by hot alkaline manganate(VII); the benzene ring itself is not attacked.

    Mechanism: electrophilic substitution

    Making the electrophile

    HNO3 + 2H2SO4 → NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4− nitration: the sulfuric acid generates the nitronium ion, NO2+
    Br2 + AlBr3 → Br+ + AlBr4− bromination: the "halogen carrier" polarises Br2 and generates Br+
    CH3Cl + AlCl3 → CH3+ + AlCl4− and CH3COCl + AlCl3 → CH3CO+ + AlCl4− Friedel–Crafts

    The mechanism

    The H+ is picked up to regenerate the catalyst: H+ + HSO4− → H2SO4 in nitration, or H+ + AlBr4− → AlBr3 + HBr in bromination.

    Why substitution, not addition?

    Addition would permanently destroy the delocalised π system, losing about 150 kJ mol−1 of stability. Substitution keeps the ring intact, so it is energetically favoured.

    Side chain or ring?

    Methylbenzene can be chlorinated in two different places, depending on the conditions:

    In the side chain

    Cl2, UV light (or boiling): free-radical substitution, like an alkane, giving (chloromethyl)benzene, C6H5CH2Cl, and further substitution products.

    On the ring

    Cl2, AlCl3 catalyst, room temperature, dark: electrophilic substitution, giving a mixture of 2-chloromethylbenzene and 4-chloromethylbenzene.

    Directing effects

    A group already on the ring decides where a second substituent goes:

    Group on the ringDirects toEffect on reactivity
    –NH2, –OH, –R (alkyl)2- and 4- positionsactivate the ring (donate electron density); –OH and –NH2 strongly
    –NO2, –COOH, –COR3- positiondeactivate the ring (withdraw electron density)

    For example, nitrating methylbenzene gives mainly 2-nitromethylbenzene and 4-nitromethylbenzene, and faster than benzene. Nitrating nitrobenzene gives 1,3-dinitrobenzene, more slowly.

    Questions

    1Quick check

    Methylbenzene reacts with chlorine in bright sunlight. What is the main organic product?

    1. 2-chloromethylbenzene
    2. 4-chloromethylbenzene
    3. (chloromethyl)benzene, C6H5CH2Cl
    4. 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane

    UV light means free-radical substitution in the methyl side chain. Ring substitution needs a halogen carrier such as AlCl3 and no light.

    2Quick check

    What is the electrophile in the nitration of benzene?

    1. NO2−
    2. HNO3
    3. NO3−
    4. NO2+

    HNO3 + 2H2SO4 → NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4−. The nitronium ion is attacked by the delocalised π electrons of the ring.

    3Quick check

    Why does benzene react with bromine by substitution rather than addition?

    1. substitution keeps the stable delocalised π system
    2. benzene has no π electrons
    3. bromine is not an electrophile
    4. addition would need a catalyst

    Addition would destroy the delocalisation, losing about 150 kJ mol−1 of stabilisation. Substitution restores the delocalised ring.

    [1]
    (b)

    [3]

    [1]
    (d)
    Suggest the reagents and conditions to convert benzene into phenylethanone, C6H5COCH3, and name the reaction.
    [2]
    • HNO3 + 2H2SO4 → NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4−
    • Curly arrow from the delocalised π system (ring) to N of NO2+
    • Intermediate with a broken ring of delocalisation, a positive charge, and H and NO2 on the same carbon
    • Curly arrow from the C–H bond back into the ring, releasing H+
    • Substitution keeps the stable delocalised π system; addition would destroy it
    • Ethanoyl chloride, CH3COCl, with an AlCl3 catalyst, heat
    • Friedel–Crafts acylation (electrophilic substitution)

    Halogenoarenes, with the halogen joined directly to a benzene ring, are far less reactive than halogenoalkanes. The reason lies in how the halogen's lone pair interacts with the ring.

    Making halogenoarenes

    React the arene with Cl2 or Br2 and an AlCl3 or AlBr3 catalyst (electrophilic substitution, Topic 30):

    C6H6 + Cl2 → C6H5Cl + HCl benzene → chlorobenzene
    C6H5CH3 + Cl2 → ClC6H4CH3 + HCl methylbenzene → 2-chloromethylbenzene and 4-chloromethylbenzene (the methyl group directs to 2 and 4)

    Why halogenoarenes are unreactive

    Chloroethane is hydrolysed by heating with aqueous sodium hydroxide; chlorobenzene is not hydrolysed under these conditions at all.

    1. A lone pair on the chlorine atom overlaps with the delocalised π system of the ring. This gives the C–Cl bond partial double bond character, so it is stronger (and shorter) than in a halogenoalkane, and harder to break.
    2. The electron-rich π system repels approaching nucleophiles such as OH−.
    3. A nucleophile can't approach from the side opposite the halogen (as in SN2), because the ring is in the way.

    The ease of hydrolysis is: acyl chlorides (fast at room temperature) > halogenoalkanes (need heating with NaOH(aq)) > halogenoarenes (no reaction under normal conditions). See Topic 33.

    Questions

    1Quick check

    Why doesn't chlorobenzene undergo nucleophilic substitution with NaOH(aq) under normal conditions?

    1. the C–Cl bond is very polar
    2. a lone pair on Cl overlaps with the delocalised π system, strengthening the C–Cl bond
    3. chlorine is too electronegative
    4. chlorobenzene doesn't dissolve in water

    The overlap gives the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character, so it is stronger than in a halogenoalkane. The π electrons also repel incoming nucleophiles.

    2Quick check

    Which reagent and conditions convert methylbenzene into (chloromethyl)benzene, C6H5CH2Cl?

    1. Cl2 with AlCl3 catalyst, room temperature
    2. HCl(g), room temperature
    3. Cl2 in UV light
    4. NaCl(aq), heat

    UV light gives free-radical substitution in the side chain. With AlCl3, chlorine substitutes into the ring instead, at the 2- and 4-positions.

    3Paper 4 style
    (a)
    Give the reagents and conditions to make chlorobenzene from benzene.
    [1]
    (b)
    Chloroethane and chlorobenzene are each warmed with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol. Describe and explain the difference in observations.
    [3]
    • Cl2 with AlCl3 (or Fe / FeCl3) catalyst, room temperature
    • Chloroethane: white precipitate (slowly); chlorobenzene: no precipitate
    • In chlorobenzene a lone pair on Cl overlaps with the π system, strengthening the C–Cl bond
    • The π electron cloud also repels the (water) nucleophile
    4Paper 4 style
    (a)
    Describe a test to distinguish 1-chlorobutane from chlorobenzene. Give the observations.
    [3]
    (b)
    Explain the difference in reactivity.
    [2]
    • Warm each with NaOH(aq) (or aqueous ethanolic AgNO3)
    • Acidify with dilute HNO3, then add AgNO3(aq)
    • 1-chlorobutane gives a white precipitate (AgCl); chlorobenzene gives no precipitate
    • In chlorobenzene a lone pair on Cl overlaps with the delocalised π system of the ring
    • So the C–Cl bond is stronger (partial double-bond character) and is not broken / not hydrolysed

    Phenol has an –OH group joined directly to a benzene ring. The ring and the oxygen affect each other: the ring makes phenol much more acidic than an alcohol, and the oxygen makes the ring much more reactive towards electrophiles than benzene.

    Alcohols and acyl chlorides

    Alcohols react with acyl chlorides at room temperature to form esters. Unlike esterification with a carboxylic acid, this is fast and goes to completion:

    CH3COCl + CH3CH2OH → CH3COOCH2CH3 + HCl ethanoyl chloride + ethanol → ethyl ethanoate + steamy fumes of HCl

    Making phenol

    In the lab, phenol is made from phenylamine in two steps:

    1. Diazotisation: phenylamine with HNO2 (made from NaNO2 and dilute HCl), below 10 °C gives benzenediazonium chloride: C6H5NH2 + HNO2 + HCl → C6H5N2+Cl− + 2H2O
    2. Warming with water (above 10 °C) decomposes the diazonium salt, giving off nitrogen: C6H5N2+Cl− + H2O → C6H5OH + N2 + HCl

    The temperature must be kept below 10 °C in step 1, because the diazonium ion decomposes on warming.

    Reactions of phenol

    ReagentConditionsProduct and observationEquation
    NaOH(aq)room temperaturesodium phenoxide; phenol dissolves (it is only slightly soluble in water)C6H5OH + NaOH → C6H5O−Na+ + H2O
    Na(s)room temperature (molten phenol)sodium phenoxide and hydrogen; fizzing2C6H5OH + 2Na → 2C6H5O−Na+ + H2
    diazonium saltin NaOH(aq), below 10 °Can orange-yellow azo dye (precipitate)see Topic 34
    dilute HNO3room temperaturemixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenolC6H5OH + HNO3 → HOC6H4NO2 + H2O
    Br2(aq)room temperatureorange colour disappears, white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenolC6H5OH + 3Br2 → C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr

    Phenol does not react with carbonates: it is too weak an acid to release CO2. This distinguishes phenols from carboxylic acids.

    The acidity of phenol

    Phenol is a weak acid: C6H5OH ⇌ C6H5O− + H+. It is more acidic than water, which is more acidic than ethanol:

    acidity: phenol > water > ethanol

    • Phenol: in the phenoxide ion, a lone pair on the oxygen overlaps with the π system of the ring, so the negative charge is delocalised over the ring. This stabilises the ion, so phenol loses H+ more readily.
    • Water: the charge on OH− is on the oxygen alone.
    • Ethanol: the ethyl group has a positive inductive effect, pushing extra electron density onto the oxygen of C2H5O−. This intensifies the negative charge and destabilises the ion, so ethanol is the weakest acid.

    Why phenol reacts so easily with electrophiles

    Benzene needs concentrated acids or a halogen carrier to react, but phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid and with bromine water at room temperature, without a catalyst. A lone pair on the oxygen is delocalised into the ring, increasing the electron density of the π system (especially at positions 2, 4 and 6). The ring attracts electrophiles more strongly and can polarise a bromine molecule without a catalyst. This is why the –OH group activates the ring and directs to the 2-, 4- and 6- positions, so bromine substitutes three times.

    The same ideas apply to other phenols, such as naphthol (an –OH on a two-ring naphthalene system): they are weakly acidic, form salts with NaOH, react with bromine water and couple with diazonium salts to form dyes.

    Questions

    1Quick check

    Which reagent reacts with phenol but not with ethanol?

    1. aqueous sodium hydroxide
    2. sodium metal
    3. ethanoyl chloride
    4. acidified potassium dichromate(VI)

    Phenol is acidic enough to react with NaOH; ethanol isn't. Both react with Na and with ethanoyl chloride. Dichromate oxidises ethanol, not phenol.

    2Quick check

    Which list shows the compounds in order of increasing acid strength?

    1. ethanol, water, phenol, ethanoic acid
    2. water, ethanol, phenol, ethanoic acid
    3. ethanol, phenol, water, ethanoic acid
    4. phenol, ethanol, water, ethanoic acid

    In the phenoxide ion the negative charge is delocalised into the ring, which stabilises it; in the ethoxide ion the ethyl group pushes electrons onto O, which destabilises it. Ethanoate is stabilised more, by delocalisation over two O atoms.

    3Quick check

    Phenol is added to bromine water at room temperature. What is seen, and what forms?

    1. no change: a halogen carrier is needed
    2. the orange colour disappears and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms
    3. the orange colour disappears and colourless bromobenzene forms
    4. a violet colour forms

    A lone pair on the O atom overlaps with the ring, raising its electron density, so phenol reacts with bromine water without a catalyst, at the 2-, 4- and 6-positions.

    4Paper 4 style
    (a)
    Describe what you would see when aqueous bromine is added to phenol, and write an equation.
    [3]
    (b)
    Explain why phenol reacts with bromine under much milder conditions than benzene.
    [2]
    (c)
    Place phenol, ethanol and water in order of increasing acidity and explain the order.
    [3]
    • Orange (bromine) colour disappears
    • White precipitate
    • C6H5OH + 3Br2 → C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr
    • A lone pair on O is delocalised into the ring
    • Increasing the electron density of the ring, so it polarises / attracts the electrophile (Br2) more strongly
    • ethanol < water < phenol
    • Phenoxide: the negative charge is delocalised over the ring, stabilising the anion
    • Ethoxide: the alkyl group pushes electrons onto O (positive inductive effect), destabilising the anion

    Acyl chlorides are the most reactive carboxylic acid derivatives: they react at room temperature with water, alcohols, phenols, ammonia and amines. This topic also explains the relative acidity of carboxylic acids, phenols and alcohols, and two oxidisable acids.

    More about carboxylic acids

    Making benzoic acid

    An alkylbenzene is oxidised by hot alkaline KMnO4, then acidified with dilute acid: methylbenzene gives benzoic acid, C6H5COOH (Topic 30).

    Two acids that can be oxidised further

    • Methanoic acid, HCOOH, still has a C–H on its carbonyl carbon (it is also an aldehyde). It is oxidised to CO2 and H2O by Fehling's solution (red precipitate), Tollens' reagent (silver mirror), and acidified KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7: HCOOH + [O] → CO2 + H2O.
    • Ethanedioic acid, HOOCCOOH, is oxidised by warm acidified KMnO4 to CO2 (the basis of the titration in Topic 28).

    Making acyl chlorides

    ReagentConditionsEquation
    PCl5room temperatureCH3COOH + PCl5 → CH3COCl + POCl3 + HCl
    PCl3heat3CH3COOH + PCl3 → 3CH3COCl + H3PO3
    SOCl2(warm)CH3COOH + SOCl2 → CH3COCl + SO2 + HCl

    Comparing acidity

    acidity: carboxylic acid > phenol > water > alcohol

    In the carboxylate ion, RCOO−, the negative charge is delocalised over two oxygen atoms (both C–O bonds become equal). This stabilises the ion more than in phenoxide, where the charge spreads into the less electronegative carbon ring.

    Chlorine-substituted carboxylic acids

    AcidCH3COOHClCH2COOHCl2CHCOOHCl3CCOOH
    pKa4.762.861.290.65

    Chlorine is electronegative, so it withdraws electron density from the carboxylate group (a negative inductive effect). This spreads out and stabilises the negative charge of the anion, so the acid dissociates more. The effect is larger with more Cl atoms and when the Cl is closer to the COOH group: 2-chlorobutanoic acid is stronger than 4-chlorobutanoic acid.

    Acyl chlorides

    Acyl chlorides contain –COCl, for example ethanoyl chloride, CH3COCl, and benzoyl chloride, C6H5COCl. They react with nucleophiles at room temperature, always producing HCl (steamy white fumes):

    NucleophileProductEquation
    watercarboxylic acidCH3COCl + H2O → CH3COOH + HCl
    alcoholesterCH3COCl + CH3CH2OH → CH3COOCH2CH3 + HCl
    phenolester (phenyl ester)C6H5COCl + C6H5OH → C6H5COOC6H5 + HCl (phenyl benzoate)
    ammoniaprimary amideCH3COCl + 2NH3 → CH3CONH2 + NH4Cl
    primary aminesecondary amide (N-substituted)CH3COCl + CH3NH2 → CH3CONHCH3 + HCl

    Phenols don't form esters with carboxylic acids easily, so acyl chlorides are the usual way to make phenyl esters.

    Mechanism: addition–elimination

    The carbonyl carbon in an acyl chloride is very δ+, because it is bonded to two electronegative atoms (O and Cl). A nucleophile adds to it, the C=O re-forms, and HCl is eliminated.

    Ease of hydrolysis

    CompoundHydrolysisWhy
    acyl chloride, CH3COClfast, with water at room temperaturethe carbonyl carbon is strongly δ+ (bonded to O and Cl) and planar, so easily attacked
    chloroalkane, CH3CH2Clslow, needs heating with NaOH(aq)the carbon is only δ+ from Cl; attack is via SN1 or SN2
    chloroarene, C6H5Clno reaction under normal conditionsthe C–Cl bond is strengthened by overlap with the ring, and the π system repels nucleophiles

    Questions

    1Quick check

    Which acid is the strongest?

    1. ethanoic acid
    2. 3-chloropropanoic acid
    3. chloroethanoic acid
    4. dichloroethanoic acid

    Two Cl atoms close to the COOH group withdraw the most electron density, stabilising the anion most.

    2Quick check

    Which is the strongest acid?

    1. CH3COOH
    2. ClCH2COOH
    3. Cl2CHCOOH
    4. Cl3CCOOH

    Each electronegative Cl atom draws electron density away from the –COO− group, spreading out the negative charge and stabilising the anion. Trichloroethanoic acid has three.

    3Quick check

    Which compound is hydrolysed most rapidly by water at room temperature?

    1. chloroethane
    2. chlorobenzene
    3. ethanoyl chloride
    4. ethyl ethanoate

    The carbonyl carbon of an acyl chloride is bonded to both O and Cl, so it is strongly δ+ and is attacked rapidly by water, giving ethanoic acid and steamy fumes of HCl.

    4Quick check

    Ethanoyl chloride reacts with methylamine. What is the organic product?

    1. N-methylethanamide, CH3CONHCH3
    2. ethanamide, CH3CONH2
    3. methyl ethanoate
    4. ethylamine

    Nucleophilic addition–elimination: the lone pair on N attacks the carbonyl carbon, and HCl is eliminated (it then reacts with more methylamine).
