    Amines are organic bases, thanks to the lone pair on nitrogen. Phenylamine leads to diazonium salts and azo dyes. Amides and amino acids join together to form the peptide links in proteins.

    Amines

    Amines are classified by the number of carbon groups on the nitrogen: primary (RNH2, e.g. ethylamine), secondary (R2NH, e.g. diethylamine), tertiary (R3N).

    Making amines

    MethodReagents and conditionsExample
    halogenoalkane + ammoniaNH3 in ethanol, heat under pressure (sealed tube)CH3CH2Br + 2NH3 → CH3CH2NH2 + NH4Br
    halogenoalkane + primary amine (gives a secondary amine)amine in ethanol, heat in a sealed tubeCH3CH2Br + CH3CH2NH2 → (CH3CH2)2NH + HBr
    reduction of an amideLiAlH4 (in dry ether)CH3CONH2 + 4[H] → CH3CH2NH2 + H2O
    reduction of a nitrileLiAlH4 or H2 with Ni catalystCH3CN + 4[H] → CH3CH2NH2

    Reducing a nitrile is a useful way to make a primary amine with one more carbon than the halogenoalkane you started from, without the mixture of products that ammonia gives.

    Reaction with acyl chlorides

    Amines (and ammonia) react with acyl chlorides at room temperature to form amides: CH3COCl + CH3CH2NH2 → CH3CONHCH2CH3 + HCl (Topic 33).

    Basicity

    Amines are weak bases: the lone pair on nitrogen accepts a proton. CH3CH2NH2 + H2O ⇌ CH3CH2NH3+ + OH−. With acids they form salts, such as ethylammonium chloride, CH3CH2NH3+Cl−.

    base strength: ethylamine > ammonia > phenylamine

    • Ethylamine is stronger than ammonia: the ethyl group has a positive inductive effect, pushing electron density onto the nitrogen, so its lone pair is more available to accept a proton.
    • Phenylamine is much weaker: the lone pair on nitrogen overlaps with (is delocalised into) the π system of the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept a proton.

    Phenylamine

    Making phenylamine

    1. Nitrate benzene: conc. HNO3 and conc. H2SO4, below 60 °C → nitrobenzene.
    2. Reduce: tin and concentrated HCl, heat under reflux: C6H5NO2 + 6[H] → C6H5NH2 + 2H2O. In the acid, the product is present as the salt C6H5NH3+.
    3. Add NaOH(aq) to release the free amine, which is then separated by steam distillation.

    Reactions of phenylamine

    • With bromine water at room temperature: the orange colour disappears and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine forms: C6H5NH2 + 3Br2 → C6H2Br3NH2 + 3HBr. Like –OH in phenol, the –NH2 lone pair is delocalised into the ring, activating it at positions 2, 4 and 6.
    • Diazotisation: with HNO2 (NaNO2 + dilute HCl), below 10 °C, phenylamine forms benzenediazonium chloride, C6H5N2+Cl−. Warming this with water gives phenol and nitrogen gas (Topic 32).

    Azo dyes

    Benzenediazonium chloride reacts with phenol dissolved in NaOH(aq), below 10 °C (a coupling reaction) to give an orange-yellow precipitate of an azo compound. The diazonium ion acts as an electrophile and attacks the 4-position of the phenol (or phenoxide) ring.

    C6H5N2+ + C6H5OH → C6H5N=NC6H4OH + H+ 4-hydroxyazobenzene (in the alkaline solution it forms as its sodium salt)

    Amides

    Amides contain –CONH2 (primary) or –CONHR (secondary, N-substituted). They are made from an acyl chloride and ammonia or a primary amine, at room temperature.

    ReactionConditionsProducts
    hydrolysis with aciddilute HCl, heat under refluxCH3CONH2 + H2O + HCl → CH3COOH + NH4Cl
    hydrolysis with alkaliNaOH(aq), heat under refluxCH3CONH2 + NaOH → CH3COONa + NH3 (ammonia gas given off)
    reduction of C=OLiAlH4CH3CONH2 + 4[H] → CH3CH2NH2 + H2O

    Amides are much weaker bases than amines (effectively neutral): the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised over the N–C=O group, because the electronegative oxygen of the carbonyl withdraws electron density. So the lone pair is not available to accept a proton.

    Amino acids

    Amino acids have an amine group and a carboxylic acid group on the same carbon (2-amino acids): H2NCH(R)COOH. In all except glycine (R = H), that carbon is chiral.

    Zwitterions

    In the solid, and in solution near neutral pH, the acidic –COOH donates a proton to the basic –NH2 on the same molecule, forming a zwitterion: an ion with both a positive and a negative charge but no overall charge. This explains why amino acids are crystalline solids with high melting points and are soluble in water: they are held by strong ionic attractions.

    Isoelectric point
    The pH at which an amino acid exists as the zwitterion, with no overall charge.

    Amino acids are amphoteric: the –COO− group accepts H+ from acids, and the –NH3+ group gives H+ to bases.

    Peptides

    The –COOH of one amino acid can react with the –NH2 of another in a condensation reaction, forming an amide (peptide) link, –CONH–, and water. Two amino acids give a dipeptide; three give a tripeptide; many give a polypeptide or protein.

    Electrophoresis

    A mixture of amino acids (or peptides) is placed on a gel or paper soaked in a buffer at a fixed pH, and a voltage is applied. At that pH, each amino acid has a charge that depends on its isoelectric point:

    • if pH < isoelectric point, the amino acid is positive and moves to the negative electrode;
    • if pH > isoelectric point, it is negative and moves to the positive electrode;
    • at its isoelectric point, it doesn't move.

    Smaller ions and ions with a larger charge move faster. After separation, the spots are made visible (for example with ninhydrin) and identified.

    Questions

    1Quick check

    Which list shows the compounds in order of increasing base strength?

    1. ammonia, phenylamine, ethylamine
    2. phenylamine, ammonia, ethylamine
    3. ethylamine, ammonia, phenylamine
    4. phenylamine, ethylamine, ammonia

    Phenylamine's lone pair is delocalised into the ring (weakest); ethylamine's alkyl group pushes electrons onto N (strongest).

    2Quick check

    An amino acid is placed in a buffer with a pH below its isoelectric point, and a voltage is applied. What happens?

    1. it doesn't move
    2. it moves towards the positive electrode
    3. it moves towards the negative electrode
    4. it is hydrolysed

    Below the isoelectric point the –COO− group is protonated, so the amino acid is a cation, H3N+CHRCOOH, and moves towards the negative electrode.

    3Quick check

    Why is ethanamide, CH3CONH2, not basic?

    1. the nitrogen atom has no lone pair
    2. the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised over the C=O group
    3. it doesn't dissolve in water
    4. the C=O group accepts the proton instead

    Overlap of the N lone pair with the π system of the C=O group makes it much less available to accept a proton.

    4Paper 4 style
    (a)
    Describe the two-step synthesis of phenylamine from nitrobenzene, then its conversion into benzenediazonium chloride. Give reagents and conditions.
    [4]
    (b)
    Benzenediazonium chloride is added to phenol in aqueous NaOH. Name the type of product, draw its structure, and give one use.
    [3]
    (c)
    Explain why the temperature is kept below 10 °C.
    [1]
    • Tin and concentrated HCl, heat (under reflux)
    • then NaOH(aq) to free the amine from its salt
    • NaNO2 and dilute HCl (to form HNO2)
    • below 10 °C (0–10 °C)
    • An azo compound / azo dye
    • C6H5–N=N–C6H4–OH with the OH in the 4-position
    • Dye (or indicator)
    • The diazonium salt decomposes (to phenol and nitrogen) at higher temperatures
    5Paper 4 style

    Alanine is 2-aminopropanoic acid, CH3CH(NH2)COOH. Its isoelectric point is 6.0.

    (a)
    Draw the structure of alanine at pH 6.0, at pH 2 and at pH 11.
    [3]
    (b)
    Draw the two dipeptides that can form from one glycine (H2NCH2COOH) and one alanine, and circle the peptide link in one of them.
    [3]
    (c)
    Explain why ethanamide is a much weaker base than ethylamine.
    [2]
    • pH 6: CH3CH(NH3+)COO−
    • pH 2: CH3CH(NH3+)COOH
    • pH 11: CH3CH(NH2)COO−
    • H2NCH2CONHCH(CH3)COOH
    • H2NCH(CH3)CONHCH2COOH
    • –CONH– circled
    • In ethanamide the N lone pair is delocalised over the C=O group (by the electronegative oxygen)
    • so it is not available to accept a proton

    Condensation polymers form when monomers with two functional groups join, losing a small molecule each time. Polyesters and polyamides, including proteins, are made this way, and unlike poly(alkene)s they can be broken down by hydrolysis.

    Condensation polymerisation

    Each monomer has two functional groups that can react. Each link formed releases a small molecule: water (from –COOH) or HCl (from –COCl).

    Polyesters

    Made from (a) a diol and a dicarboxylic acid (or a dioyl dichloride), or (b) a single monomer with both an –OH and a –COOH group (a hydroxycarboxylic acid).

    The best-known polyester is PET, poly(ethylene terephthalate), from ethane-1,2-diol, HOCH2CH2OH, and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, HOOCC6H4COOH. It is used for drinks bottles and polyester fibres.

    Polyamides

    Made from (a) a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid (or a dioyl dichloride), (b) an aminocarboxylic acid, or (c) amino acids (giving polypeptides and proteins).

    The best-known synthetic polyamide is nylon-6,6, from 1,6-diaminohexane, H2N(CH2)6NH2, and hexanedioic acid, HOOC(CH2)4COOH (or hexanedioyl dichloride, ClOC(CH2)4COCl). Kevlar is an aromatic polyamide used in body armour.

    nH2N(CH2)6NH2 + nHOOC(CH2)4COOH → (NH(CH2)6NHCO(CH2)4CO)n + 2nH2O

    Repeat units and monomers

    Predicting the type of polymerisation

    Monomer(s)PolymerisationPolymer
    one monomer with a C=Cadditionpoly(alkene); the main chain is all carbon; no small molecule lost
    diol + dicarboxylic acid (or dioyl chloride); or a hydroxy acidcondensationpolyester (–COO– links); water or HCl lost
    diamine + dicarboxylic acid (or dioyl chloride); or an amino acidcondensationpolyamide (–CONH– links); water or HCl lost

    Looking at a section of polymer: if the main chain contains only carbon atoms, it is an addition polymer. If it contains –COO– or –CONH– links, it is a condensation polymer.

    Degradable polymers

    • Poly(alkene)s are chemically inert: their non-polar C–C and C–H bonds aren't attacked by acids, bases or enzymes, so they are non-biodegradable (Topic 20).
    • Photodegradable polymers contain groups (such as C=O) that absorb ultraviolet light, breaking bonds in the chain so the plastic crumbles in sunlight.
    • Polyesters and polyamides can be broken down by hydrolysis of their ester and amide links, by acids or alkalis (and by enzymes in the environment), so they are biodegradable. Poly(lactic acid), made from lactic acid, CH3CH(OH)COOH, is a biodegradable polyester used for packaging and dissolvable stitches.

    Questions

    1Quick check

    Which pair of monomers forms a polyamide?

    1. hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid
    2. ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid
    3. ethene and chloroethene
    4. ethane-1,2-diol and hexane-1,6-diamine

    An amide link forms between –NH2 and –COOH (or –COCl), losing water (or HCl). B makes a polyester, C an addition polymer, and D has no acid group.

    2Quick check

    Which polymer can be broken down by hydrolysis?

    1. poly(ethene)
    2. poly(chloroethene)
    3. poly(propene)
    4. a polyester such as PET

    Ester and amide links can be hydrolysed by acids, alkalis or enzymes, so condensation polymers can be biodegradable. Poly(alkene)s have only C–C bonds in their chains.

    3Quick check

    A polymer has the repeat unit –O–CH(CH3)–CO–. What type of polymer is it, and what is its monomer?

    1. addition polymer; propene
    2. polyester; 2-hydroxypropanoic acid
    3. polyamide; 2-aminopropanoic acid
    4. polyester; propane-1,2-diol

    The repeat unit contains an ester link, –CO–O–. A single monomer with both –OH and –COOH groups, 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid), condenses with itself to give poly(lactic acid).

    4Paper 4 style

    Poly(lactic acid) is made from 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, CH3CH(OH)COOH.

    (a)
    Name the type of polymerisation and draw the repeat unit of the polymer.
    [2]
    (b)
    Explain why poly(lactic acid) is biodegradable but poly(propene) is not.
    [2]
    (c)
    Nylon-6,6 can be made from hexanedioyl dichloride instead of hexanedioic acid. Name the other product of each condensation step, and give one advantage of using the acyl chloride.
    [2]
    • Condensation polymerisation
    • Repeat unit –O–CH(CH3)–CO– with continuation bonds
    • Poly(lactic acid) has ester links that can be hydrolysed (by acid, alkali or enzymes)
    • Poly(propene) has only non-polar C–C and C–H bonds, which are unreactive
    • Hydrogen chloride
    • The reaction is faster / happens at room temperature (acyl chlorides are more reactive)

    Synthesis questions at A Level combine aliphatic and aromatic chemistry. You may be asked to plan routes of several steps, to spot every functional group in a complex molecule such as a drug, and to predict how it reacts with a given reagent.

    The full reaction map

    This map includes every AS and A Level reaction. A Level reactions are tagged.

    Multi-step routes

    Worked example 1: an azo dye from benzene

    1. Benzene → nitrobenzene: conc. HNO3, conc. H2SO4, below 60 °C
    2. Nitrobenzene → phenylamine: Sn and conc. HCl, heat under reflux; then NaOH(aq)
    3. Phenylamine → benzenediazonium chloride: NaNO2 and dilute HCl, below 10 °C
    4. Diazonium salt → azo dye: phenol in NaOH(aq), below 10 °C

    Worked example 2: phenyl benzoate from methylbenzene and phenol

    1. Methylbenzene → benzoic acid: hot alkaline KMnO4, then dilute acid
    2. Benzoic acid → benzoyl chloride: PCl5 (or SOCl2)
    3. Benzoyl chloride + phenol → phenyl benzoate: room temperature (an ester can't easily be made from phenol and a carboxylic acid)

    Worked example 3: a longer amine

    Make propylamine, CH3CH2CH2NH2, from bromoethane without a mixture of amines:

    1. Bromoethane → propanenitrile: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux (adds a carbon)
    2. Propanenitrile → propylamine: LiAlH4 (or H2/Ni)

    Molecules with several functional groups

    Treat each group separately, then check whether a reagent affects more than one.

    Worked example: aspirin and paracetamol

    MoleculeFunctional groupsPredictions
    aspirin, 2-ethanoyloxybenzoic acidcarboxylic acid; ester (phenyl ester); benzene ringfizzes with Na2CO3 (CO2); hydrolysed by NaOH(aq) to a carboxylate, a phenoxide and ethanoate; no colour with neutral iron(III) chloride until hydrolysed (no free phenol)
    paracetamol, N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)ethanamidephenol; secondary amide; benzene ringdissolves in NaOH(aq) (phenol); decolourises bromine water with a precipitate (activated ring); hydrolysed by acid or alkali at the amide link to 4-aminophenol and ethanoic acid
    Checklist for routes

    Give the reagent and the conditions for every step (temperature, solvent, catalyst, reflux or distillation). Watch for reagents that would also attack another group: hot acidified manganate(VII) oxidises alcohols and alkene C=C bonds; LiAlH4 reduces acids, esters, amides, aldehydes, ketones and nitriles; NaBH4 reduces only aldehydes and ketones.

    Questions

    1Quick check

    Which reagent reacts with both functional groups in 4-hydroxybenzoic acid, HOC6H4COOH?

    1. Na2CO3(aq)
    2. NaOH(aq)
    3. ethanol with concentrated H2SO4
    4. 2,4-DNPH

    NaOH neutralises the carboxylic acid and the phenol, giving NaOC6H4COONa. Phenols are too weakly acidic to react with carbonates.

    2Quick check

    Which sequence converts benzene into phenylamine?

    1. Cl2 with AlCl3; then NH3
    2. NaNO2 and HCl; then Sn and HCl
    3. concentrated HNO3 and H2SO4; then Sn and concentrated HCl, followed by NaOH(aq)
    4. CH3Cl with AlCl3; then hot alkaline KMnO4

    Nitration gives nitrobenzene, which tin and hydrochloric acid reduce to phenylamine. Chlorobenzene doesn't undergo nucleophilic substitution with ammonia.

    3Quick check

    Which reagent distinguishes phenylmethanol, C6H5CH2OH, from phenol, C6H5OH?

    1. sodium metal
    2. dilute hydrochloric acid
    3. 2,4-DNPH
    4. neutral iron(III) chloride solution

    Phenol gives a violet colour with neutral FeCl3(aq); phenylmethanol is an alcohol, not a phenol, so it doesn't. Both fizz with sodium.

    4Paper 4 style

    Compound X is HOCH2C6H4CHO (4-(hydroxymethyl)benzaldehyde): a benzene ring with a –CH2OH group and a –CHO group in the 1,4-positions.

    (a)
    Give the structural formula of the organic product when X reacts with (i) NaBH4, (ii) excess acidified K2Cr2O7 under reflux, (iii) HCN with KCN.
    [3]
    (b)
    Describe a test to distinguish X from HOCH2C6H4COCH3. Give the observations.
    [2]
    (c)
    Suggest a two-step synthesis of 4-methylbenzoyl chloride from 4-methylbenzaldehyde, CH3C6H4CHO.
    [2]
    • (i) HOCH2C6H4CH2OH
    • (ii) HOOCC6H4COOH
    • (iii) HOCH2C6H4CH(OH)CN
    • Tollens' reagent (or Fehling's), warm
    • X gives a silver mirror (or red precipitate); the ketone gives no change
    • Oxidise: acidified K2Cr2O7, heat under reflux, giving 4-methylbenzoic acid (side chain CH3 unaffected)
    • Then PCl5 (or SOCl2)

    Chromatography separates mixtures and identifies their components. NMR spectroscopy shows how the carbon and hydrogen atoms in a molecule are arranged, which, with IR and mass spectra (Topic 22), lets you deduce a structure with confidence.

    Chromatography

    Every chromatography method has a stationary phase (which stays still) and a mobile phase (which moves through it). Components of a mixture separate because they distribute themselves differently between the two phases: those that interact more with the stationary phase move more slowly.

    Thin-layer chromatography (TLC)

    • Stationary phase: a thin layer of a polar solid such as aluminium oxide (or silica) on a glass, metal or plastic sheet.
    • Mobile phase: a solvent (polar or non-polar) that rises up the plate.
    • Spots are placed on a pencil baseline; the plate is stood in a little solvent (below the baseline) in a covered tank; it is removed before the solvent reaches the top and the solvent front is marked. Colourless spots are shown with UV light or iodine vapour.
    Retention factorRf = distance moved by the spotdistance moved by the solvent frontLearn it

    For A: Rf = 3.6 / 8.0 = 0.45. For a given stationary phase, solvent and temperature, each compound has a characteristic Rf. A compound has a low Rf if it is strongly adsorbed by (interacts strongly with) the polar stationary phase, for example through hydrogen bonding; it has a high Rf if it is more soluble in the mobile phase.

    Gas/liquid chromatography (GLC)

    • Stationary phase: a high-boiling, non-polar liquid coated on a solid support inside a long, coiled column in an oven.
    • Mobile phase: an unreactive carrier gas, such as helium or nitrogen.
    • The retention time is the time between injecting the sample and a component reaching the detector. Components that are more soluble in (interact more with) the stationary liquid, or that are less volatile, have longer retention times.

    The area under each peak is proportional to the amount of that component, so the percentage composition = area of one peak ÷ total area of all peaks × 100. Peaks are identified by comparing retention times with known samples run under the same conditions (or by passing them into a mass spectrometer).

    Worked example

    The peak areas in a chromatogram are A 1.2 cm2, B 3.6 cm2 and C 3.2 cm2. What is the percentage of B?

    3.6 / (1.2 + 3.6 + 3.2) × 100 = 45%

    Carbon-13 NMR spectroscopy

    Each peak in a 13C NMR spectrum corresponds to one carbon environment: carbon atoms in identical positions in the molecule give a single peak. The chemical shift, δ (in ppm, relative to TMS), shows what type of environment it is.

    Carbon environmentδ / ppm (typical)
    C–C (alkyl)5–55
    C–Cl, C–Br10–70
    C–N (amine)35–60
    C–O (alcohol, ether, ester)50–70
    C=C (alkene) and aromatic C110–160
    C≡N110–125
    C=O in carboxylic acids, esters, amides160–185
    C=O in aldehydes, ketones190–220

    Counting environments: look for symmetry. Propan-2-ol has 2 environments; butan-1-ol 4; butan-2-ol 4; 2-methylpropan-2-ol 2; benzene 1; methylbenzene 5 (the CH3 and four ring environments).

    Proton (¹H) NMR spectroscopy

    A 1H NMR spectrum gives four pieces of information:

    1. Number of peaks: the number of different hydrogen environments.
    2. Chemical shift: the type of environment (table below).
    3. Relative peak areas (integration): the relative number of hydrogens in each environment.
    4. Splitting pattern: the number of hydrogens on the adjacent carbon atoms.
    Type of protonδ / ppm (typical)
    alkyl: R–CH3, R–CH2–R0.9–1.7
    next to C=O: CH3–CO–2.0–2.5
    next to an aromatic ring: CH3–Ar2.2–3.0
    next to N: R–CH2–NH22.3–3.0
    next to a halogen: CH–Cl, CH–Br3.0–4.2
    next to O: CH–O (alcohol, ether, ester)3.3–4.8
    alkene: C=CH4.5–6.0
    aromatic: Ar–H6.0–9.0
    aldehyde: –CHO9.3–10.5
    alcohol O–H0.5–6.0 (variable)
    phenol O–H4.5–7.0
    carboxylic acid O–H9.0–13.0
    amine N–H / amide N–H1.0–5.0 / 5.0–12.0

    Use the Data Booklet's table in the exam; ranges differ slightly between sources.

    Splitting: the n + 1 rule

    The signal from a set of equivalent protons is split into n + 1 lines by n equivalent protons on the adjacent carbon atoms. Protons in the same environment don't split each other. O–H and N–H protons usually appear as singlets and don't split their neighbours, because they exchange rapidly between molecules.

    H on adjacent C, n0123more
    Patternsingletdoublet (1 : 1)triplet (1 : 2 : 1)quartet (1 : 3 : 3 : 1)multiplet

    Practical points

    • TMS, tetramethylsilane, Si(CH3)4, is the reference standard at δ = 0. Its 12 equivalent protons give one strong singlet away from almost all other peaks; it is also inert, non-toxic and volatile (easily removed afterwards).
    • Samples are dissolved in a deuterated solvent, such as CDCl3, which has no 1H atoms, so the solvent doesn't give a signal.
    • Identifying O–H and N–H: run a second spectrum after shaking with D2O. The O–H and N–H protons exchange with deuterium (–OH → –OD), and their peaks disappear.

    Worked example: deducing a structure

    A compound C3H6O has an IR absorption at 1715 cm−1. Its 1H NMR spectrum has one singlet at δ 2.1 ppm. Its 13C spectrum has two peaks, at 30 and 206 ppm. Identify it.

    1. 1715 cm−1 and 206 ppm: a C=O in an aldehyde or ketone.
    2. One 1H environment at 2.1 ppm (H next to C=O), and no aldehyde peak at 9–10 ppm: a ketone with equivalent methyl groups.

    Propanone, CH3COCH3. (Its isomer propanal, CH3CH2CHO, would show three ¹H environments, including an aldehyde H near 9.8 ppm, and three ¹³C peaks.)

    Questions

    1Quick check

    How many peaks are in the 13C NMR spectrum of 2-methylpropan-1-ol, (CH3)2CHCH2OH?

    1. 2
    2. 4
    3. 3
    4. 5

    The two CH3 carbons are equivalent; then CH and CH2OH: 3 environments.

    2Quick check

    In the ¹H NMR spectrum of 1-chloropropane, CH3CH2CH2Cl, what is the splitting pattern of the CH2Cl protons?

    1. singlet
    2. triplet
    3. quartet
    4. sextet

    The CH2Cl protons have 2 H on the adjacent carbon: 2 + 1 = 3, a triplet. (The middle CH2 has 5 neighbours and gives a multiplet.)

    3Paper 4 style

    Compound Y, C4H8O2, is an ester. Its ¹H NMR spectrum (in CDCl3) shows: δ 1.2 (triplet, 3H), δ 2.3 (quartet, 2H), δ 3.7 (singlet, 3H).

    (a)
    Explain why CDCl3 is used as the solvent and what TMS is used for.
    [2]
    (b)
    Use the data to deduce the structure of Y. Explain each peak.
    [4]
    (c)
    Predict the number of peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of Y.
    [1]
    • CDCl3 contains no ¹H, so it gives no signal / doesn't interfere
    • TMS is the reference (standard) for chemical shift, δ = 0
    • δ 3.7, singlet, 3H: an OCH3 group with no neighbouring H
    • δ 2.3, quartet, 2H: a CH2 next to C=O with 3 neighbouring H
    • δ 1.2, triplet, 3H: a CH3 next to a CH2
    • Y is methyl propanoate, CH3CH2COOCH3
    • 4 peaks
    4Paper 4 and 5 style

    A student analyses a painkiller tablet by TLC on aluminium oxide, using a non-polar solvent.

    (a)
    A spot moves 2.7 cm when the solvent front has moved 7.5 cm. Calculate Rf.
    [1]
    (b)
    Explain why a compound containing –OH and –COOH groups has a lower Rf than a hydrocarbon on this plate.
    [2]
    (c)
    Explain why the baseline must be drawn in pencil and must be above the solvent level.
    [2]
    • Rf = 2.7 / 7.5 = 0.36
    • The polar groups interact strongly (hydrogen bond) with the polar stationary phase (aluminium oxide)
    • and are less soluble in the non-polar mobile phase, so they move more slowly
    • Pencil (graphite) does not dissolve in the solvent / move up the plate (ink would)
    • If below the solvent level, the spots would dissolve into the solvent in the tank instead of moving up the plate
